sections.heading: Where Theatre marks are actually lost, and what one session fixes
paragraphs: Theatre candidates in Abu Dhabi rarely lose marks because they cannot act. They lose them in writing, in choices made too early, and in recordings that do not show what the marker needs to see. Each of those has a different cost to fix, and the cheapest fixes are the earliest ones.

The most expensive error is a bad choice in week one. A Higher Level candidate who selects a theorist for the solo piece without testing whether it generates stageable material can spend two months producing work that cannot score well, and then needs a fresh start under time pressure. An hour spent stress-testing three candidate theorists before anything is committed is the highest-value hour in the subject. It is also the hour families almost never book, because nothing looks wrong yet.

The most common error is description instead of justification. A notebook entry that explains the lighting state in detail and never says why it serves the moment has done the work and missed the criterion. The same pattern appears in the research presentation as a narrated history, and in the collaborative project report as a diary of rehearsals. Fixing it is genuinely quick: most students need two or three sessions of working through their own sentences, turning each description into a decision and a consequence. This is the single highest-return intervention in the subject and it costs a fraction of what a late rescue does.

The third category is technical and almost comically avoidable. A recording where the assessed movement happens outside the frame. A presentation where the demonstration is inaudible. A report where the page limit was reached before the strongest material. None of these reflect ability, and all of them lose marks that cannot be recovered after upload. A tutor who asks to see the setup before the recording is made, rather than the file afterwards, prevents all three.

sections.heading: Two Diploma years of Theatre, counted backwards from a May session
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates overwhelmingly sit the May session, and schools build their internal deadlines backwards from the IB's upload windows, which fall well before the examination period. Theatre deadlines therefore arrive earlier than a parent expects, and they arrive while the student is also producing Internal Assessments in five other subjects.

Exact IB session and upload dates are not published on this page, for a deliberate reason: they are set by the IB and revised, and an out-of-date date on a tutoring page is worse than no date. Your child's Diploma coordinator holds the current calendar, and the IB publishes its own assessment timelines. What follows is the shape of the two years in school terms, which is stable, and which is enough to plan a budget against.

The pattern across Abu Dhabi schools looks like this. DP1 term one is course content and the first tentative work on traditions and texts. DP1 terms two and three carry the research presentation and often a first director's notebook attempt, which is where the first real tutoring spend lands. DP2 term one is the heaviest: solo theatre piece work at Higher Level, the collaborative project moving towards performance, and internal draft deadlines stacking up against Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge submissions. By DP2 term two, Theatre is largely finished and uploaded while the rest of the cohort moves into mock examinations.

That shape has a direct budgetary consequence. A family that spreads a Theatre budget evenly across twenty-four months underspends when it matters and overspends in a term where the marks are already fixed. The efficient version concentrates hours into two or three blocks aligned to internal deadlines, and books a single diagnostic hour at the start of DP1 to get the choices right before anything is committed.

sections.heading: What a paid Theatre tutor may not touch
paragraphs: Every Theatre task is assessed as the candidate's own work, and the boundary between teaching and malpractice is sharper in this subject than in most, because so much of the assessment is a document a tutor could in principle improve directly. The IB's academic honesty rules make an authenticity breach a matter for the student's Diploma, not just for the tutor, so the boundary is worth stating plainly in a parent's hearing.

A tutor may teach the criteria and explain what each one rewards. They may discuss a theorist, a text or a tradition. They may read the student's draft and say what a marker would penalise, where justification is missing, which paragraph is description rather than decision, and which section is burning pages for no return. They may watch a rehearsal recording and comment on framing and audibility. They may teach the student how to cut their own work down to a limit. All of that is normal teaching and is what the hours are for.

A tutor may not supply sentences for the student to paste in, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, choose the theorist or text on the student's behalf, script a presentation, or supply a model report from a previous candidate for adaptation. The distinction that matters is authorship: feedback points at the student's own work and leaves them to change it. Material produced by someone else and submitted is malpractice regardless of how lightly it was edited afterwards.

This matters commercially as well as ethically, because the UAE search results for IB coursework contain operations selling completed Internal Assessments outright. One publishes a price for them. A family comparing options should treat any offer to hand over finished assessed work as a risk to their child's Diploma rather than as a service, and should expect a legitimate tutor to decline it in writing.

sections.heading: Finding a Theatre specialist when Abu Dhabi has few, and checking they are permitted
paragraphs: Theatre is a small subject in a small market, and honesty about supply is more useful to a parent than a claim of universal coverage. The number of people in Abu Dhabi who have taught Diploma Theatre and submitted candidates for all four tasks is modest. The number available at 7pm on a weeknight is smaller again. Any platform claiming an instant local match for Higher Level Theatre is describing a tutor pool it does not have.

Our position is that delivery is online precisely because of this. A match is made from the specialists available across our network rather than from whoever is within range of your address, and if no specialist is free for a Higher Level solo piece we say so and give a realistic date rather than putting a generalist in the slot. A family is also told before the trial lesson what the tutor's actual Theatre background is, which is the question that decides whether the hour will be worth its rate.

The legal side is worth getting right, and it is simple. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no figure should be quoted at you by anyone.

Two further points apply specifically in this emirate. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff bar teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct reflects the same restriction, so a family should not be seeking their child's own class teacher as a paid tutor. And a tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit, which is a specific licence issued to training institutes. IB Gram holds no regulator licence or accreditation of any kind, operates no office or centre in the UAE, and says so rather than implying otherwise.

faqs.question: How much does an IB DP Theatre tutor in Abu Dhabi cost per hour?
faqs.answer: Published market rates in the emirate run from about AED 45 an hour at the entry level to AED 650 at the premium end. For Diploma Theatre the realistic band is AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject teacher and AED 200 to AED 450 or more for a specialist with Diploma Theatre submission experience. Those figures come from providers' own published pages read in October 2026: EdFlik from AED 45, Unitors IB from AED 200, TutorChase AED 270, Bestimate 200 to 450 and above, BartyED AED 650. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson, because the right rate depends on the task and the tutor matched.

faqs.question: Why does Theatre support cost less over two years than Chemistry does?
faqs.answer: Because Theatre sets no written examination paper. A Chemistry family typically pays for content teaching through DP1, then heavy weekly revision from January of DP2 through to the examinations, which is a long tail of hours. Theatre marks are all submitted coursework, uploaded months before the examination window, so the spend concentrates into two or three blocks around internal draft deadlines and then stops. Total hours across the Diploma are usually lower. The catch is timing: hours bought in the spring of DP2, when other subjects are at their most expensive, buy nothing in Theatre because the marks are already fixed.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my son with the Higher Level solo theatre piece?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the boundary that the work must be his. A tutor can teach what the task rewards, discuss which aspects of a theorist can actually be staged by one performer in a school studio, read his report and say where justification is missing or where the word limit is being spent badly, and comment on whether the recording shows the assessed moment clearly. What a tutor cannot do is choose the theory for him, supply text for the report, or provide a previous candidate's work to adapt. The most valuable session is the first one, before the choice is locked in.

faqs.question: Does the director's notebook really have a page limit, and what happens if we exceed it?
faqs.answer: Yes. The notebook is submitted within a page limit published in the subject guide, and the limit is binding rather than advisory. Confirm the current figure with your child's Diploma coordinator, because the IB revises task limits between guide editions and a figure on any website can be out of date. The practical risk is not penalty so much as waste: candidates routinely use their pages on description of a set and reach the limit before the moments that would have earned credit. Cutting a notebook down to its strongest material is a skill, and it is one of the quickest things a tutor can teach.

faqs.question: My daughter's collaborative project group has stopped meeting. Can tutoring fix that?
faqs.answer: Tutoring cannot make four teenagers rehearse, and anyone promising otherwise is overselling. What it can do is protect your daughter's own mark, because the collaborative project is assessed through an individual report. A tutor can help her document the process honestly, including what did not work and what she did about it, which is material the criteria actively reward rather than something to hide. Groups that fall apart often produce stronger individual reports than groups that sail through, precisely because there are real decisions to analyse. The school's Theatre teacher should also know the group has stalled.

faqs.question: How many Theatre sessions does an Abu Dhabi Diploma student usually book?
faqs.answer: The common shape is one diagnostic hour early in DP1, a block of four to six hours around the first research presentation or notebook deadline, and a heavier block of six to ten hours in the first term of DP2 when the solo piece and collaborative project overlap. That is roughly twelve to seventeen hours across two years for a Higher Level candidate, and less at Standard Level where there is no solo piece. Standing weekly sessions for twenty-four months are rarely the right structure in this subject, and a tutor who proposes one without looking at the deadlines has not read the course.

faqs.question: Is a Theatre tutor worth paying for when there is no written exam to revise for?
faqs.answer: The absence of an examination is the argument for tutoring rather than against it. In an examined subject a student can recover from a weak term by revising harder in the spring. In Theatre every mark is a submitted document or recording with a fixed upload date, so a weak draft that goes up unchanged is a permanent mark. Hours spent before a submission are therefore worth considerably more than hours spent after one, and the work is exactly the kind that benefits from a second reader. Tutoring is not required for the Diploma, and a strong candidate with an attentive school teacher may need none.

faqs.question: Do you have Theatre specialists based in Abu Dhabi, or are they elsewhere?
faqs.answer: Some are in the UAE and many are not, and we say which before you meet them. Diploma Theatre is a small-cohort subject and the number of people in this emirate who have submitted candidates for all four tasks is limited. Lessons are delivered one to one over live video, so the match is made from specialists across our network rather than from whoever lives near your address. If no specialist is free for the level and task you need, you are told that with a realistic date instead of being given a generalist. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

faqs.question: What does the research presentation need beyond a recorded video?
faqs.answer: It needs a theatre tradition genuinely outside the candidate's own experience, a source base that is more than a few encyclopaedia pages, and a practical demonstration that proves something rather than illustrating a talk. The most common weak submission is an articulate history lesson with a costume. A strong one shows a convention being performed, then explains what performing it revealed about how that tradition works on an audience. A list of sources is submitted alongside the recording, and the time limit is binding, so rehearsing to length is part of the preparation rather than an afterthought.

faqs.question: Can my child take Theatre at Higher Level without much previous drama experience?
faqs.answer: It is possible and it happens often, particularly in schools where MYP Arts runs as a carousel and a student may have had one term of drama in three years. The gap is usually not performance confidence but the habit of justifying a decision in writing, which is what all four tasks are marked on. A student who can explain why they made a choice and what it did to an audience will do well at Higher Level with limited stage time behind them. The Higher Level decision is worth discussing with the school's Theatre teacher before DP1 subject choices are confirmed.

faqs.question: Will a Theatre tutor work to my child's school deadlines rather than a generic plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in this subject there is no sensible alternative. Abu Dhabi schools set internal draft deadlines for each Theatre task, built backwards from the IB's own upload windows, and those internal dates are what the work has to hit. A tutor is given the school's deadline dates at the start and the block of sessions is planned against them. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools these deadlines come from, but the deadlines themselves are set by the school's Diploma coordinator, so that is who to ask for the current calendar.

faqs.question: Does an IB Diploma with Theatre count for UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is assessed by the Ministry of Education against the certificate as a whole, not subject by subject, and the published requirements differ by curriculum track. For the British track, the sourced rule is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. We do not publish an IB points threshold here because we have not read one on an official Ministry page, and an unsourced figure would be worse than none. Check the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with your emirate's attestation channel directly.

faqs.question: Does Ramadan change when Theatre feedback sessions can happen?
faqs.answer: It changes the clock rather than the content. School days shorten during Ramadan across the UAE, family evenings reorganise around Iftar, and the usable session window for most Abu Dhabi families moves to after the meal. Theatre is well suited to this because the work is reading and discussion of documents and recordings rather than long timed practice, so a 75-minute post-Iftar session is productive. Internal Theatre deadlines that fall during or just after Ramadan are worth identifying in advance, since the available working hours in those weeks are genuinely fewer and a draft that slips rarely recovers quietly.

faqs.question: What does the free trial Theatre lesson include, and what is the condition?
faqs.answer: One trial lesson per family, with no card details taken and no obligation to book afterwards. It is a working session rather than a consultation: the tutor looks at whatever exists, a notebook draft, a presentation plan or a recording, and works on it with your child for the session. It ends with a plain statement of what the work needs and roughly how many hours that represents, including the answer that it needs none. The condition is simply that it is one lesson per family, not one per subject or per tutor tried.

intro.heading: TOK is two tasks, and both of them punish answering the wrong question
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is a compulsory part of the Diploma core, taught across both years, and it is assessed by exactly two pieces of work. The first is the TOK exhibition: three objects, each linked to one of the course's internal assessment prompts, with a written commentary explaining the links. The second is the TOK essay, written on one of the prescribed titles issued for the session. There is no examination, no oral and no third component.

The grade that comes out of those two tasks is not cosmetic. TOK and the Extended Essay together contribute points to the Diploma total, and a failing grade in TOK is one of the conditions that can prevent a diploma being awarded regardless of how strong the six subjects are. Confirm the current award and failing conditions with your DP coordinator, who works from the IB's own assessment procedures, because this is precisely the area where secondhand information circulates.

What makes TOK unlike every other Diploma subject is that effort and marks are only loosely related. A student can read widely, think seriously, write fluently, and score in the middle bands, because both tasks are narrow in a way the writing does not advertise. The exhibition asks how knowledge manifests in the world through three specific objects. The essay asks a precise question that is phrased with deliberate care. Most lost marks are answers to adjacent questions.

The exhibition failure is almost always object selection. A student chooses a generic object — a textbook, a map, a telescope — and writes about the category rather than about a specific thing with a real-world context. The commentary then explains what the object is instead of justifying how it links to the chosen prompt, and the mark is capped before the writing quality matters.

The essay failure is almost always the title. Prescribed titles are built from phrases that each demand something specific, and a student who reads the title as a topic rather than as a question writes a general discussion of knowledge in two areas. That earns credit for understanding and loses it everywhere the band descriptors ask for evaluation of the claim actually made.

Abu Dhabi has one local wrinkle worth naming. TOK is timetabled thinly in many schools here, sometimes in a slot shared with other core requirements, and it is the first thing surrendered when internal assessment deadlines pile up in other subjects. That is not a criticism of the schools; it is a structural fact of a crowded Diploma timetable, and it is the main reason families here hire outside help at all. Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi and sends no tutor to an address in this emirate; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.programmesIntro: TOK only exists inside the Diploma, but the students taking it in Abu Dhabi arrive with very different preparation for abstract argument. These notes describe what each route leaves a candidate holding.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: TOK runs across both Diploma years alongside the six subjects, CAS and the Extended Essay. It is assessed by the exhibition, usually completed in the first year, and the essay on a prescribed title, completed in the second. The two together with the Extended Essay feed into the Diploma points total, and TOK carries a failing condition of its own.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi Diploma schools the TOK slot is frequently short and occasionally shared with other core sessions. The practical consequence is that the exhibition is often taught properly and the essay is squeezed, because the essay lands in the same term as internal assessments in several subjects. Families here most often ask for help in exactly that window, which is late but still workable if the title analysis is done first.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP does not teach TOK, but it does teach interdisciplinary work and the Personal Project, both of which build the habit of asking how a claim is justified. Students from a continuum school tend to handle the exhibition more comfortably because the idea of linking an object to a prompt resembles work they have done before.
programmes.countryNote: The emirate's IB continuum schools give students a head start in the exhibition and no particular advantage in the essay, which rewards a different discipline: close reading of a title and sustained evaluation of a single claim. Where a school has a strong MYP tradition, the TOK gap tends to appear in DP2 rather than DP1.

programmes.name: Students joining the Diploma mid-course
programmes.description: A student arriving from a British or American system has usually never met anything like TOK. They are not behind in ability, only in vocabulary: knowledge question, knowledge claim, area of knowledge, perspective. A fortnight of deliberate vocabulary work usually closes a gap that otherwise looks alarming on a first report.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi's employment pattern produces mid-course transfers regularly, including arrivals in DP2 who have missed the exhibition entirely. Where that happens, the priority order is clear: find out what the school requires and by when, then work on the essay title, because the exhibition may already be submitted or waived for that candidate.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.subjectsIntro: TOK support is rarely bought alone, because TOK sits on top of six subjects. Below are the pairings Abu Dhabi families most often ask about, with what each one contributes to a TOK argument.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Assessed by an exhibition of three objects with a commentary and an essay on a prescribed title. Marks are lost through generic object choice, commentary that describes rather than justifies, and essays that discuss a topic rather than evaluating the specific claim the title makes.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: The other half of the Diploma core and the component TOK is most often confused with. The two feed points into the same total, and a student strong in one is not automatically strong in the other: the Extended Essay rewards sustained research, TOK rewards precise evaluation of a claim.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The strongest ally TOK has. The analytical moves overlap almost exactly: identify the claim, test it, consider the counterclaim, evaluate. Students doing well here who underperform in TOK are usually mishandling the task structure rather than the thinking.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: An excellent source of TOK examples and a trap in equal measure. Historians have ready-made material on evidence and interpretation, and they frequently write history essays in TOK, where narrative detail earns no credit and the knowledge question goes unanswered.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Supplies clean examples about method, replication and what counts as evidence in the natural sciences. The common error is describing an experiment at length rather than using it to evaluate a claim about scientific knowledge in two sentences.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The area of knowledge students find hardest to write about and the one that differentiates strong essays, because mathematical knowledge behaves unlike the other areas. Two prepared examples here are worth more than ten from the human sciences.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: A rich source of material on models, assumptions and prediction, which maps neatly onto questions about the human sciences. The risk is importing economic terminology into an essay that then explains terms instead of evaluating knowledge claims.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Useful for the exhibition especially, since arts students are already used to thinking about a specific object in a context. The arts as an area of knowledge is also the easiest place to find a real counterclaim quickly.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Private schools in the UAE teach Arabic alongside their licensed curriculum, and bilingual students carry strong TOK material because translation makes knowledge and language visibly entangled. One prepared example from that experience is worth having in DP1.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.regionsTitle: TOK students across Abu Dhabi, and when the work actually happens
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.regionsIntro: TOK is the piece of the Diploma that gets done in the gaps, so where a family lives determines when those gaps fall. Each note is about the slot that is realistically available for abstract work.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Central and close to several Diploma schools, so early evening slots are achievable. TOK argument work benefits from an earlier slot than most subjects, because evaluating a claim at 20:00 after a full school day produces agreement rather than analysis.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Early finishes and short runs make a 16:30 session realistic, which is the best time available for essay planning. Families here often use a weekly slot through DP2 rather than intensive blocks near the deadline.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long bus journeys from the island schools. Weekend sessions work better here for the essay, because a 75-minute block is enough to take a title apart properly and a tired weekday hour is not.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Bridge congestion pushes weekday starts past 17:00. Exhibition work suits this slot well, since object selection and photographing objects can be done between sessions rather than inside them.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Heavy activity scheduling in the compounds, so TOK often ends up at 18:30 or on a Friday. The Friday block is the better of the two for drafting, and the weekday slot is better used for feedback on what was written.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Longer internal distances and a newer school mix. Students here frequently arrive in DP2 with the exhibition done and no essay plan, which is a two-block problem rather than a weekly commitment.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan
regions.note: Dense and established, with after-school demand concentrated between 16:00 and 18:00. For TOK the quieter 19:00 slot is usable if the session is feedback on written work rather than new argument building.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Mainland communities with the emirate's longest commutes to the island schools. Online delivery is the difference between a weekly TOK slot and none, because an in-home tutor would consume the available hour getting there.

schoolClusters.city: Island and Corniche Diploma schools
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's established Diploma cohorts, where the exhibition is generally well taught and the essay timetable is tight. Worth asking the coordinator two things: when the school's internal essay deadlines fall, and how many comment rounds on a draft the school's own policy allows.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas
schoolClusters.note: Where IB continuum provision sits in the emirate, so students often handle the exhibition confidently. The gap here tends to appear in DP2, when the essay competes with internal assessments in several subjects and the TOK slot is the one that gives way.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.modesIntro: Three patterns cover almost every TOK request from this emirate, and they map onto the two tasks rather than onto a calendar of weekly hours.

modes.title: Exhibition clinic
modes.description: Two or three sessions in DP1 covering prompt choice, object selection and the commentary structure. The work is mostly elimination: testing proposed objects against the chosen prompt and discarding the generic ones before any writing starts. Most exhibition marks are won or lost here rather than in the prose.
bullets: Each candidate object tested for specificity and real-world context
The chosen prompt restated as a question the commentary must answer
A commentary structure that justifies links rather than describing objects

modes.title: Title analysis and essay planning
modes.description: A focused block in DP2: taking the shortlisted prescribed titles apart phrase by phrase, choosing between them on the strength of available examples rather than on interest, and building an argument map with claim, counterclaim and evaluation before any prose is written. Feedback afterwards is on the student's own drafting.
bullets: Each title phrase converted into an explicit requirement
Two areas of knowledge chosen for genuine contrast, not convenience
An argument map the student writes from, not a model answer

modes.title: Weekly argument practice through DP2
modes.description: A standing 60-minute slot for students who need the habit rather than the deadline rescue. Each session takes a claim, finds its strongest counterclaim, and evaluates both in writing under time. The skill is transferable to the essay and to several other subjects, which is why families who start early buy fewer hours overall.
bullets: One claim per session, taken from the student's own subjects
Short timed writing every week, marked against the band descriptors
A running bank of examples the student can use in the essay

sections.heading: The exhibition and the essay, side by side
paragraphs: Families consistently underestimate how different the two TOK tasks are. They share a vocabulary and almost nothing else. The exhibition is a short, object-anchored, internally assessed piece completed in the first Diploma year. The essay is a longer, title-driven, externally assessed piece completed in the second. A student can be strong in one and weak in the other, and treating them as a single subject is the most common planning error.

The exhibition asks the candidate to show how TOK manifests in the world. Three objects, each with a specific real-world context, each linked to one internal assessment prompt chosen by the student from the list in the course. The commentary explains and justifies each link. Marks follow the quality of that justification, not the ingenuity of the objects.

The essay asks the candidate to discuss one of the prescribed titles issued for their examination session, across areas of knowledge. It is marked externally against a single global assessment of how well the title has been discussed, which means every paragraph either advances an answer to the title or it does not. There is no credit for a well-written paragraph that answers an adjacent question.

Word limits and submission mechanics are set by the IB and published in the current TOK guide, which your DP coordinator holds. The commentary and the essay both carry maximum lengths, and work beyond the limit will not be read in the candidate's favour. Confirm the figures and deadlines for your cohort with the school rather than from any third-party page, including this one.

sections.heading: Objects: why a telescope scores badly and a specific telescope does not
paragraphs: The exhibition rewards specificity and families find this counterintuitive, because specificity sounds like a stylistic preference and it is actually the mark scheme. An object in the TOK sense is a particular thing with a particular history: this photograph, taken on this date, by this person; this edition of this document; this item belonging to this family. A category is not an object. A telescope is a category. The telescope in a named observatory, or a specific instrument a student has used, is an object.

The reason sits in what the task asks. The exhibition is about how knowledge shows up in the world, so the object has to be in the world. A generic item cannot carry a real-world context, so the commentary about it immediately slides into a general discussion about the type of thing, which is a discussion about ideas rather than a demonstration of ideas in practice.

The second common failure is the link. The commentary exists to justify why each object connects to the chosen prompt, and students instead explain what the object is and why they find it interesting. A good test to apply before writing: for each object, can you finish the sentence beginning 'this object answers the prompt because'? If the honest answer is a description, the object or the prompt needs replacing, and that discovery is cheap in DP1 and expensive later.

The third is the UAE-specific opportunity most students miss. Candidates in Abu Dhabi have access to objects with genuinely interesting knowledge dimensions: bilingual official documents where translation decisions are visible, museum artefacts with contested attributions, instruments and records from the emirate's own scientific institutions. A specific local object usually produces a stronger commentary than a famous one chosen from the internet, because the student can say something concrete about its context.

sections.heading: Prescribed titles: reading the question phrase by phrase
paragraphs: A prescribed title is not a topic. It is a carefully built question in which every phrase imposes a requirement, and the single most valuable hour of TOK tuition available is the one spent taking a shortlisted title apart before anything is written. Students who skip it write fluent essays about the general area the title mentions and receive a mark that bewilders them.

The phrases do specific work. A title asking 'to what extent' requires a judgement of degree with reasons on both sides, not a yes or a no. One asking 'on what grounds' requires an examination of justification rather than of conclusions. One containing 'always', 'only' or 'must' invites a counterexample and penalises an essay that never looks for one. One naming two areas of knowledge requires both, treated with comparable seriousness rather than one as an afterthought.

The choice between titles should then be made on evidence, not on interest. The right question is which title the student already has two solid examples for, from their own subjects, with a genuine counterclaim available. A title that sounds appealing and offers no counterclaim produces a one-sided essay, and one-sidedness is the most reliable way to stay in the middle bands.

That analysis is work a tutor can legitimately do with a student, because it is teaching. What follows — the argument map, the examples, the drafting — belongs to the student. A tutor who hands over a plan with paragraphs allocated has produced the structure that the essay is largely marked on, and that is help no candidate should accept.

sections.heading: Choosing two areas of knowledge that genuinely contrast
paragraphs: Most prescribed titles require two areas of knowledge, and the choice determines how hard the essay will be to write. Students pick the areas they like. Strong candidates pick the pair where the contrast does argumentative work, because an essay comparing two areas that behave similarly has nothing to evaluate and fills the space with description.

Mathematics is the area students avoid and the one that most reliably lifts an essay, precisely because mathematical knowledge behaves unlike the rest: its claims are established differently, its disagreements look different, and its relationship to evidence is unlike that of the natural sciences. Two prepared mathematical examples are worth a great deal in DP2 and take about one session to assemble.

The natural and human sciences paired together is the most common choice in Abu Dhabi cohorts and often the weakest, because the two share a vocabulary of evidence and method, so students end up making the same point twice. Pairing either with history, the arts or mathematics produces contrast immediately, and contrast is what the band descriptors reward.

The practical move is to build an example bank during DP1 rather than hunting for examples during the essay. Four or five examples, each with enough detail to be used rather than named, drawn from the student's own subjects, with a note on which claims each could support. A student arriving at title selection with that bank chooses on evidence; a student without it chooses on vibe and then writes around the gap.

sections.heading: The five ways a TOK draft loses marks
paragraphs: Marked TOK drafts fail in a small number of recognisable ways, and naming the failure is most of the repair. The first is the substituted question: the student restates the title in their own words, slightly easier, and answers that instead. It is almost always unintentional and it caps the mark immediately, because the essay is assessed on discussion of the title as issued.

The second is the example that is named rather than used. 'The discovery of penicillin shows that knowledge is often accidental' is a gesture at an example. A used example carries enough specific detail to support the claim and enough to be interrogated. Two used examples beat six named ones in every band descriptor.

The third is the missing counterclaim, or the counterclaim that is introduced and immediately dismissed in one sentence. Evaluation requires the opposing case to be made at its strongest before it is weighed. A student who cannot state the best argument against their own position has not finished thinking, and an examiner can see that from the paragraph shape alone.

The fourth is the subject essay in TOK clothing: a history essay, a biology write-up, a literature analysis, with knowledge vocabulary sprinkled over it. The fifth is the unanchored conclusion — a final paragraph that announces a judgement the body never argued for. Both are fixable in a single session once pointed out, which is why a marked draft with the failure named is worth more than three hours of general discussion.
bullets: The substituted question: answering an easier version of the title
Named examples instead of used ones, with no supporting detail
No counterclaim, or one raised and dismissed in a sentence
A subject essay with TOK vocabulary added on top
A conclusion asserting a judgement the body never built

sections.heading: What one TOK session can actually fix
paragraphs: Families asking for TOK help usually ask how many sessions are needed, and the honest answer depends entirely on which task and which failure. TOK differs from a language or a science in that several of its problems are structural and can be repaired in one sitting, while others need a habit built over months.

In one session it is realistic to test three proposed exhibition objects and discard the generic ones, to take two prescribed titles apart and establish which is supportable with the examples the student already has, to diagnose a draft's failure mode and name it precisely, or to convert a one-sided argument into claim, counterclaim and evaluation on paper. These are high-value single hours.

What cannot be done in one session is building the example bank, developing the reflex of looking for the counterclaim, or raising the quality of the student's thinking about knowledge in general. Those take a term of weekly short practice, and families who begin them in DP1 spend far less in total than those who arrive six weeks before the deadline.

The third category is work nobody should buy. Nobody can supply the essay, restructure it into something the student could not have produced, or run a draft past a service that rewrites it. Under IB academic honesty rules the submitted work must be the candidate's own, and the consequence of a breach falls on the student rather than on whoever was paid. A tutor who offers that is selling a risk.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: TOK is where the line gets tested hardest
paragraphs: TOK is unusually exposed to honesty problems for three reasons. The prescribed titles are public, so model answers circulate. The subject matter is abstract, which makes generated text superficially plausible. And the essay arrives at the busiest point of DP2, when a student under pressure is most tempted by a shortcut that looks like editing.

The boundary a tutor works to is specific. Teaching the vocabulary, explaining what a title phrase demands, discussing examples the student brings, marking a draft against the band descriptors, and explaining why a paragraph does not advance the argument are all legitimate and are what the hour is for. Supplying paragraphs, restructuring a draft into a different essay, or rewriting prose to a standard the student could not reach are not.

Text generated by an AI tool sits firmly on the wrong side of that line for submitted work, and in TOK it is easy to spot: the prose is fluent, the examples are generic, the counterclaim is tidy and nothing is used in detail. That profile is exactly what the band descriptors reward least, so the shortcut tends to produce a middling mark in addition to the malpractice exposure. Where such tools are genuinely useful is as TOK material — a live example of a knowledge claim whose justification is hard to inspect.

Schools also set their own rules about how much comment a teacher may give on a TOK draft, and a tutor should work inside them rather than around them. Ask the coordinator how many rounds of feedback the school's policy permits and what form it takes. A tutor who wants to know that answer before starting is behaving correctly; one who treats it as an obstacle is a problem waiting to arrive.

sections.heading: Online delivery, in-home tutoring, and why TOK favours the screen
paragraphs: In-home tutoring is a real market in Abu Dhabi, and published market comparisons put in-home one-to-one at roughly AED 180 to AED 350 an hour with travel inside the fee, against roughly AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. Those are market bands from published rate tables rather than IB Gram prices.

IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in the UAE. We do not send a tutor to an Abu Dhabi address and we run no home visits in Abu Dhabi; in-home tuition is a service we offer only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one online, over live video, on Gulf Standard Time. Saying it before the first conversation is more useful than saying it during.

TOK happens to be the Diploma component best suited to a screen. The work is almost entirely textual: a title on a shared document, an argument map built live, a draft annotated in front of both people, a band descriptor open in a second window. None of that improves by having the tutor in the room, and the shared document means the student leaves the session holding the artefact rather than a memory of agreeing with someone.

The supply point matters too. TOK specialists are thin on the ground in any single emirate, because the course is taught by teachers whose main subject is something else and few have marked it. Online, the pool is everyone who has, free at your hour. For a component with a failing condition attached, that is not a small difference.

process.title: Tell us which task is live
process.description: Exhibition or essay, and what the school's internal deadline is. Send the chosen prompt and proposed objects, or the shortlisted prescribed titles and any draft. Those two documents decide the whole plan, and without them the first session goes on discovery instead of work.

process.title: Free trial lesson used as a clinic
process.description: The trial is a working session: three objects tested against a prompt, or two titles taken apart phrase by phrase. It is free, needs no card and carries no obligation, and you keep the written output — the discarded objects, or the requirements list for each title.

process.title: Ask your school what feedback is permitted
process.description: Schools set their own rules on how many rounds of comment a TOK draft may receive and in what form. We ask you to confirm them with the coordinator before draft work begins, so the support sits inside the school's policy rather than beside it.

process.title: Blocks against the task, not open-ended hours
process.description: An exhibition clinic is two or three sessions. A title and planning block is three or four. Weekly argument practice is a term. Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and each session leaves an annotated document in a shared folder.

process.title: Feedback against the descriptors, in writing
process.description: Drafts come back annotated against the band descriptors with the failure mode named, not rewritten. The next session starts from what the student changed. If nothing changed, that is the conversation, because TOK improves through revision rather than through explanation.

whyPoints.title: Objects tested before anything is written
whyPoints.description: Most exhibition marks are decided by object selection, so sessions start by discarding generic objects and testing each survivor against the chosen prompt. A student who cannot finish the sentence 'this object answers the prompt because' has the wrong object, and finding that out in DP1 is cheap.

whyPoints.title: Titles read phrase by phrase
whyPoints.description: A prescribed title is a question in which every phrase sets a requirement. Sessions convert each phrase into an explicit demand and then choose between titles on the examples the student already has, rather than on which sounds most interesting.

whyPoints.title: Drafts annotated, never rewritten
whyPoints.description: Work comes back with the failure mode named and the band descriptor line quoted, and the student does the revising. A tutor who restructures a draft has produced the thing TOK is largely marked on, which is help no candidate should accept.

whyPoints.title: Mathematics treated as usable
whyPoints.description: Students avoid the area of knowledge that most reliably lifts an essay. One session assembles two mathematical examples with enough detail to be used, which is often the clearest single improvement available in DP2.

whyPoints.title: Online, one-to-one, and stated upfront
whyPoints.description: Every UAE lesson runs over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Abu Dhabi address and runs no home visits in this emirate; that service exists only in India. For a textual component the screen is also the better room.

whyPoints.title: Inside the school's rules, not around them
whyPoints.description: We ask what feedback the school permits on a TOK draft before draft work starts. Working inside that policy protects the candidate, and a tutor who treats the question as an inconvenience is a risk rather than a resource.

faqs.question: What exactly is my child assessed on in Theory of Knowledge?
faqs.answer: Two pieces of work and nothing else. The TOK exhibition: three objects, each with a specific real-world context, each linked to one internal assessment prompt the student chooses, with a written commentary justifying the links. And the TOK essay: a continuous essay on one of the prescribed titles issued for their examination session, marked externally. There is no examination, no oral and no third component. Word limits and deadlines are set in the current TOK guide, which your DP coordinator holds, and should be confirmed with the school rather than taken from a tutoring page.

faqs.question: Why did my son's exhibition score badly when the writing was good?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly object selection. The exhibition rewards specific objects with real-world contexts, and a student who chooses a category — a map, a textbook, a microscope — writes about the type of thing rather than about a particular thing in the world. The commentary then describes the object instead of justifying its link to the chosen prompt, which caps the mark before writing quality counts. The test to apply is whether each object completes the sentence 'this object answers the prompt because' with a justification rather than a description.

faqs.question: How should we choose between the prescribed titles?
faqs.answer: On evidence, not on interest. Shortlist two or three, take each apart phrase by phrase, and ask which one the student already has two usable examples for, from their own subjects, with a genuine counterclaim available. A title that sounds appealing but offers no counterclaim produces a one-sided essay, and one-sidedness is the most reliable way to land in the middle bands. That analysis is one session's work and it is the highest-value hour available in TOK.

faqs.question: Which areas of knowledge give the strongest TOK essay?
faqs.answer: The pair where the contrast does argumentative work. Natural sciences with human sciences is the most popular choice in Abu Dhabi cohorts and often the weakest, because the two share a vocabulary of evidence and method and the essay makes the same point twice. Pairing either with mathematics, history or the arts produces contrast immediately. Mathematics is the area students avoid and the one that most reliably lifts an essay, because mathematical claims are established in a visibly different way.

faqs.question: What does it mean to use an example rather than name one?
faqs.answer: A named example is a gesture: a discovery, a study or an artwork mentioned in a clause as if the reader will supply the rest. A used example carries enough specific detail to support the claim being made and enough to be questioned in turn. Band descriptors reward the second and barely acknowledge the first. Two used examples outperform six named ones consistently, which is why building an example bank during the first Diploma year is worth more than reading more widely in the last term.

faqs.question: Is a weak TOK grade really able to stop the whole diploma?
faqs.answer: TOK carries a failing condition of its own, and together with the Extended Essay it contributes points to the Diploma total, so a very weak TOK result can affect the award rather than just the points. The precise conditions are set in the IB's current assessment procedures and your DP coordinator works from them, so confirm the detail for your cohort with the school. What is safe to say is that TOK is not a subject to leave until the term the essay is due, which is when most families first ask about it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a TOK draft without breaking the rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits. Teaching the vocabulary, explaining what a title phrase demands, discussing examples the student brings, marking a draft against the band descriptors and explaining why a paragraph does not advance the argument are all legitimate. Supplying paragraphs, restructuring a draft into a different essay or rewriting prose beyond the student's reach are not, because the submitted work must be the candidate's own. Schools also limit how many rounds of comment a draft may receive, so ask the coordinator and work inside that policy.

faqs.question: Our daughter used an AI tool to tidy up her TOK writing. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: For submitted work, treat it as one. Generated text in TOK has a recognisable profile — fluent prose, generic examples, a tidy counterclaim, nothing used in detail — which is precisely what the band descriptors reward least, so it tends to produce a middling mark alongside a malpractice exposure that falls on the candidate. Where these tools are genuinely interesting is as TOK material: a knowledge claim whose justification cannot be inspected is a good example to write about rather than a good way to write.

faqs.question: How much TOK help should we book for the exhibition against the essay?
faqs.answer: It depends which task and which failure. An exhibition clinic is two or three sessions. A title analysis and planning block is three or four. Diagnosing a draft's failure mode and repairing a one-sided argument can genuinely be done in one. What takes a term is the habit: looking for the counterclaim automatically and building an example bank. Families who start that in the first Diploma year buy far fewer hours in total than those who arrive six weeks before the school deadline.

faqs.question: Can local objects from Abu Dhabi work for the exhibition?
faqs.answer: They often work better than famous ones, because the student can say something concrete about the context. Bilingual official documents where a translation decision is visible, a museum artefact with a contested attribution, a record or instrument from one of the emirate's own institutions, a family object with a documented history. The requirement is specificity and a real-world context, not prestige. An object chosen from an internet list usually produces a commentary about the category, which is exactly the trap.

faqs.question: Does ADEK set what TOK schools in Abu Dhabi must teach?
faqs.answer: No. ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection outcomes, while the TOK course and its assessment are set by the IB. Separately, private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, which is part of why the Diploma timetable here is crowded and TOK often gets the thinnest slot. School information should be verified on ADEK's own published listings.

faqs.question: Can TOK sessions fit around deadline weeks and Ramadan in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: They have to, because TOK is the component families need most in exactly the weeks it is hardest to schedule. Sessions move at short notice, including to post-Iftar slots through Ramadan when the school day is shortened and afternoons are harder. The practical advice is to put the title analysis block before the deadline crush rather than inside it, since analysis needs a clear head and feedback on a draft does not. Online delivery is what makes the rescheduling workable at all.

faqs.question: My child says they do not understand what TOK wants. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With vocabulary, then with one piece of marked work. Knowledge question, knowledge claim, area of knowledge, perspective, justification: a student who cannot use those five terms precisely will write fluently about nothing in particular. A fortnight of deliberate vocabulary work plus one short timed piece marked against the band descriptors usually converts confusion into a specific, fixable problem. Students joining the Diploma from British or American systems are not behind in ability, only in this vocabulary.

faqs.question: Is TOK support worth buying if the school already teaches it?
faqs.answer: That depends on what the school's TOK slot actually contains. In many Abu Dhabi schools the course is taught by teachers whose main subject is something else, the slot is short, and it is the first thing surrendered when internal assessments crowd the term. Where the exhibition was taught well and the essay was not, a short title block is good value. Where both were taught properly, the honest answer may be that your child needs to revise rather than to be taught, and we will say so.

faqs.question: What should a TOK tutor send us after a session?
faqs.answer: The artefact, not a summary of the conversation. After an exhibition clinic: the list of objects tested, which were discarded and why, and the justification sentence for each survivor. After a title session: the requirement list for each phrase of the title and the examples checked against it. After draft work: the annotated document with the failure mode named and the descriptor line quoted. A parent who cannot judge TOK content can still see whether the student is revising from something concrete.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.closingHeading: Bring the title or the three objects, and we will start there
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Theory of Knowledge home tutor in Abu Dhabi, the useful first step is to send whichever task is live: the chosen prompt with the proposed objects, or the shortlisted prescribed titles with any draft. The free trial lesson then runs as a clinic rather than an introduction, costs nothing, needs no card and carries no obligation, and you keep the written output either way. Ask your school what feedback a draft may receive before we begin, because support that sits inside the policy protects your child. Lessons run online, one-to-one, on Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tuto.tutorsIntro: The tutors below coach TOK as an assessed subject rather than as a discussion club: prompt selection, object justification, prescribed-title analysis, and the structural moves that turn an opinion into a knowledge claim with a counterclaim behind it.

intro.heading: TOK is marked on two documents, not on how well your child argues
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the subject Abu Dhabi parents understand least and worry about latest. It has no textbook, no syllabus content to revise, no past-paper bank and no examination. What it has is two assessed submissions and a grade from A to E that feeds the diploma core alongside the Extended Essay. A student can be brilliant in TOK lessons, admired by the teacher, visibly the sharpest voice in the room, and still finish with a C, because neither assessed document rewards being interesting.

The first submission is the exhibition. The student chooses one of thirty-five internal assessment prompts, selects three specific objects that exist in the world, and writes a commentary of no more than 950 words explaining how each object shows TOK at work in the real world. It is marked by the school and moderated by the IB, and it carries roughly a third of the TOK grade. It is also the component where students lose marks most predictably, because choosing a vague object is easy and justifying a specific one is hard.

The second is the essay: no more than 1,600 words, responding to one of six prescribed titles released by the IB for that examination session, marked externally. It carries the remaining two-thirds. The titles are deliberately strange on first reading, and most of the marks are decided before any writing happens, in whether the student has actually worked out what the title is asking. Students who begin drafting on day one almost always answer a title that was not set.

Between the two sits a documented process. The student has three recorded interactions with the TOK teacher about the essay, from initial ideas through a draft to a final discussion. Those interactions are the school's property and the school's responsibility, which sets a hard boundary on what any external tutor can legitimately do. A tutor who edits a draft that is about to be submitted has not helped; they have created a malpractice problem for the student, and the consequence of an IB malpractice finding reaches further than one grade.

What external coaching can legitimately change is substantial: how to read a prescribed title, how to test whether an object is specific enough to defend, how to construct a knowledge claim and then find a genuine counterclaim rather than a straw man, how to use the knowledge framework as a thinking tool, and how to keep 1,600 words disciplined. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, because TOK coaching is a conversation about a document on a shared screen and nothing about it improves by being in the same room.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tuto.programmesIntro: TOK exists only in the Diploma Programme, but the thinking it assesses is built or neglected much earlier. Here is where each programme touches it for an Abu Dhabi student.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: TOK runs across both years with around 100 taught hours and produces two assessed submissions plus a grade from A to E. It is compulsory for the full diploma. The exhibition typically falls in DP1 or at the start of DP2, and the essay occupies the first half of DP2 under three documented interactions with the TOK teacher.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools timetable TOK very differently: a weekly single period in some, a fortnightly double in others, and in a few an intensive block taught by a rotating team of subject teachers. Where TOK is shared between staff, the exhibition and the essay often get different teachers with different standards, which is the most common reason an Abu Dhabi family looks for outside help with this subject.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: No TOK, but the MYP's interdisciplinary units and the Personal Project rehearse the same habits: holding a question open, using evidence from more than one discipline, and reflecting on process. A student who took the Personal Project seriously arrives in TOK already able to justify a choice rather than assert one.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi IB continuum schools run strong Personal Project programmes and then teach TOK as if nothing preceded it. Where a student has a completed Personal Project, reopening its reflection sheets in the first weeks of TOK is a free head start, and it is usually the fastest way to make the exhibition's justification requirement feel familiar.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP's inquiry structure and its explicit attention to how we know things is the earliest ancestor of TOK in the continuum. Children who are used to being asked how they found something out, rather than only what they found out, carry a real advantage into the diploma core a decade later.
programmes.countryNote: Families moving into an Abu Dhabi IB continuum school from an examination-focused system often notice the difference here first. A child who has spent primary school optimising for the right answer finds TOK's tolerance for unresolved questions genuinely uncomfortable in DP1, and that discomfort shows up as a weak exhibition rather than as a complaint.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The CP does not include TOK. Its core comprises personal and professional skills, service learning, a reflective project and language development. A CP student therefore has no TOK exhibition and no prescribed-title essay, and the reflective project is assessed against entirely different criteria.
programmes.countryNote: This matters because CP and DP students sit in the same Abu Dhabi corridors and swap advice. A CP student being coached for TOK, or a DP student being coached against the reflective project criteria, is a waste of a term. Confirm with the coordinator which core your child is registered for before buying any support for it.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tuto.subjectsIntro: TOK draws its examples from the areas of knowledge and the optional themes rather than from a syllabus. These are the strands a student is actually working with, and what each one is useful for in an assessed submission.

subjects.name: Knowledge and the knower
subjects.description: The starting point of every TOK course: how a person's communities, language, upbringing and biases shape what they take to be known. The richest theme for a student in Abu Dhabi, where most candidates hold two or three cultural frames at once and can speak about it from experience rather than from reading.

subjects.name: Knowledge and language
subjects.description: How language shapes, limits and carries knowledge: translation loss, untranslatable concepts, the vocabulary a discipline invents to see with. Strong material for bilingual candidates, and it overlaps directly with the conceptual work in any Group 1 or Group 2 language subject.

subjects.name: Knowledge and technology
subjects.description: Algorithmic recommendation, machine-generated text, data as evidence, the authority a search result borrows. The theme most likely to produce a lazy exhibition object, because a phone is not a specific object. Done well it is the most contemporary material available.

subjects.name: Knowledge and politics
subjects.description: How knowledge is produced, distributed and contested where power is involved: official statistics, archives, the framing of a news report. Demands care in selecting examples, and rewards a student who can describe a mechanism rather than take a side.

subjects.name: Knowledge and religion
subjects.description: Faith, revelation, interpretation and the relationship between religious and empirical claims. Handled respectfully it suits students in the UAE well, because questions about how different communities justify belief are part of ordinary life here rather than an abstraction.

subjects.name: Knowledge and indigenous societies
subjects.description: Oral transmission, place-based knowledge, the ethics of researching a community you are not part of. Frequently the least-chosen theme and often the most distinctive, since examples are plentiful and the field is uncrowded in student work.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: A field whose methods make the knowledge question visible: sources, selection, hindsight, the difference between an account and the past. The most productive area of knowledge for essays about evidence and interpretation, and the one where students most often find a usable counterclaim.

subjects.name: The natural sciences
subjects.description: Method, replication, falsification, the role of consensus and the place of models. Students taking a science at HL have real material here, but they must resist describing the method they were taught and instead examine what it can and cannot settle.

subjects.name: The human sciences
subjects.description: Economics, psychology, geography and their methodological problems: measurement of the unmeasurable, the observer effect, modelling human behaviour. The area that produces the sharpest essays on whether a discipline's tools fit its object.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Proof, axioms, certainty and the puzzle of why abstract structures describe the physical world. Underused in student work because it seems difficult, and therefore distinctive when a candidate handles it with any confidence at all.

subjects.name: The arts
subjects.description: Whether art produces knowledge, how interpretation works, what a maker's intention is worth. Easy to write badly and strong when anchored to a specific work rather than to art in general, which is the same discipline the exhibition demands.

sections.heading: What a Theory of Knowledge tutor can and cannot do
paragraphs: Searching for an IB DP Theory of Knowledge tutor in Abu Dhabi usually follows one of three moments: a disappointing exhibition mark, a first interaction with the TOK teacher that produced the words start again, or a realisation in DP2 that the essay is due and the title still makes no sense. In each case the useful work is specific and bounded, and in each case there is a boundary a legitimate tutor will not cross.

What coaching changes is method. How to read a prescribed title and identify the knowledge question buried in it. How to test whether an object is specific enough to carry a justification. How to build a knowledge claim and then find a counterclaim that a reasonable person would actually hold, rather than one invented to be knocked down. How to allocate 1,600 words so that the final section is not three hurried sentences. These are teachable in a handful of sessions and they are the difference between a C and an A for most students.

What coaching cannot do is produce the submission. The TOK essay and the exhibition commentary must be the student's own work, the three documented interactions belong to the school, and the final upload is made by the school within the IB's process. A tutor who edits a near-final draft has not helped a student; they have created an academic-honesty problem that falls on the candidate and can put the whole diploma at risk.

The honest version of this subject is also cheaper than most families expect. Two short project blocks, one in DP1 for the exhibition and one in DP2 before any drafting, cover the assessed work. Students who find reflective writing genuinely alien benefit from a lighter habit through DP1, but nobody needs a weekly TOK tutor for two years, and anyone selling that should be asked what the sessions will contain in month fourteen.

sections.heading: The two assessed components and how the TOK grade is built
paragraphs: TOK produces one grade from A to E out of two documents, with the essay carrying the larger share and the exhibition the rest. There is no examination, no paper and no revision in the ordinary sense, which is why a student used to measuring effort in past papers can feel the subject has nothing to work on until the deadline arrives.

The exhibition asks the student to choose a single internal assessment prompt from the thirty-five published by the IB, then to select three objects and write a commentary of no more than 950 words. The objects must be specific and must exist in the world rather than being types of thing, and each needs a justification of how it illustrates the chosen prompt in practice. The school marks it and the IB moderates. Three objects inside 950 words means roughly 300 words each, which is a serious constraint rather than a generous one.

The essay responds to one of six prescribed titles that the IB sets for each examination session, capped at 1,600 words and marked externally. The titles rotate from session to session, so there is no bank to practise against: the skill is reading a title accurately, not recognising a familiar one. Around the essay sit three documented interactions with the TOK teacher, covering initial ideas, a draft and a final discussion. They are not marked but they are required, and they are the school's record.

Component details below reflect the current TOK course. Word limits and the exhibition and essay structure are stable, but the precise internal deadlines and the IB's submission windows differ by school and by session. Confirm those with your child's DP coordinator rather than with any third-party page, including this one.

sections.heading: The exhibition: three objects, one prompt, 950 words
paragraphs: Nearly every weak exhibition fails in the same place, and it is not the writing. It is object choice. A student picks a smartphone, a newspaper, a map, a textbook. Each of those is a category, not an object, and a category cannot be justified in the way the task requires. The fix is a specific instance with a history: this particular photograph, this specific edition, the actual ticket from that event, a named artefact with a date and a provenance the student can describe.

The second failure is the prompt. Thirty-five internal assessment prompts are published and the student chooses one. They are not interchangeable. Some produce natural trios of objects and some are much harder to illustrate in three concrete ways. Choosing the prompt that sounds most interesting rather than the one the student can actually evidence is a decision made in ten minutes that costs the whole component.

The third is the word budget. Three objects inside 950 words leaves roughly 300 each, including the link to the prompt. Students routinely write 500 words on the first object, discover the problem, and compress the remaining two into a paragraph apiece. Allocating the budget before writing and holding to it is mechanical, teachable and worth real marks.

The fourth, less discussed, is that the commentary must explain how the object illustrates the prompt in the real world rather than what the object is. Description is the default register of a sixteen-year-old writing about an artefact, and the task does not reward it. A good session on this component spends most of its time deleting description and asking, each time, what this tells us about how knowledge works here.

Explain how the object illustrates the prompt, not what the object is

sections.heading: The essay: reading a prescribed title before writing anything
paragraphs: Six prescribed titles are released for each session and the student answers one. Most of the available marks are decided before a single sentence is drafted, in whether the student has correctly identified what the title asks. Titles are built around tensions, and the tension is frequently in a small word: whether, to what extent, always, must. A student who reads past that word writes a competent answer to a question nobody set.

The sensible process is slow at the start. Take all six titles. For each, identify the knowledge question, the key terms that need definition, which areas of knowledge could supply contrasting evidence, and whether the student has genuine examples rather than hypotheticals. Only then choose. Two sessions spent here save four later, and they prevent the most common disaster in the subject: a half-finished essay abandoned in week five because the title turned out to have no second side.

Structure matters more in 1,600 words than in 4,000. The essay needs claims with evidence, counterclaims that a reasonable person would hold, and a discussion that goes somewhere rather than concluding that both sides have a point. Two areas of knowledge handled with contrast beat four handled with a sentence each. Examples should be specific, dated and checkable, and they should come from the student's own subjects where possible, because that is where they can defend the detail.

The essay is written by the student, discussed with the TOK teacher in three documented interactions, and submitted by the school. Our work ends at the structure and the reasoning. We will question whether a claim is supported and whether a counterclaim is real; we will not supply prose, rewrite a paragraph, or comment on a draft that is about to be submitted as final.

sections.heading: Where TOK marks are actually lost
paragraphs: The single biggest loss is assertion without evidence. A student makes a confident statement about how scientists work, or what historians do, or why mathematics is certain, and offers nothing to support it. The claim may be true. Unsupported, it earns nothing, and a page of unsupported claims reads as opinion rather than as knowledge analysis.

The second is the straw-man counterclaim. A real counterclaim is a position a thoughtful person actually holds, with reasons behind it. A straw man is one invented to be dismissed in the next sentence. Examiners see the difference immediately, and the straw man costs more than omitting the counterclaim entirely, because it signals the student knows the structure and not the purpose.

The third is the example that does no work. Students collect illustrations and then narrate them: a case study described for 150 words that supports no claim and introduces no complication. Examples must be doing something. If removing an example changes nothing in the argument, it was occupying words that the essay needed elsewhere.

The fourth is the recited knowledge framework. Scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics are a thinking apparatus, not a set of headings to march through. An essay organised as four labelled paragraphs produces a tidy document with no argument in it. The framework is most useful early, in generating questions, and least useful as a structure for the finished piece.

The fifth is length discipline. Going over the word limit is self-harming and going well under is worse, because the discussion that would have earned the top band never happens. Students who draft to 2,400 words and cut to 1,600 generally produce better essays than students who write 1,500 and stop, but only if the cutting is done on purpose.

sections.heading: The knowledge framework against the five areas of knowledge
paragraphs: The most useful thing a TOK student can own is a small grid. Down one side, the five areas of knowledge. Across the top, the four elements of the knowledge framework: scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. Filling in a few cells with real questions turns an abstract course into something a student can work on between lessons.

The point of the grid is not completeness. It is to stop a student answering every title from the natural sciences because that is where they feel competent. A title about evidence handled through history and mathematics produces contrast; the same title handled through physics and chemistry produces repetition with different nouns. Choosing areas of knowledge for contrast is a structural decision made early, not a stylistic one made during writing.

Abu Dhabi students have unusually good access to real examples for several cells of the grid. A city rebuilt within living memory makes questions about historical evidence and oral testimony concrete rather than theoretical. A classroom where five languages are in play makes the language theme immediate. A school community drawn from dozens of nationalities makes perspectives a daily fact rather than a reading.

The table below gives one scope question and one methods question per area of knowledge, with a note on where a candidate here can find material. These are starting points for discussion, not answers to be reproduced, and a student who brings their own version of this grid to a session gets far more out of it.
