sections.heading: What a marked portfolio screen actually looks like
paragraphs: The process portfolio is where Abu Dhabi students lose the most marks for the least reason, because the common weak version is easy to produce and feels like work. It consists of photographs of finished pieces with captions, sometimes beautifully laid out. The criteria are looking for something different: experimentation across art-making forms, evidence of technical development, and critical review of what the student tried and what they learned from it, including the attempts that failed.

A strong screen usually shows three things together. A deliberate experiment with a stated purpose, the result including anything that went wrong, and a written decision about what happens next because of it. That is a small amount of text, but it is the text that carries the marks. A screen with a flawless outcome and the caption describing the technique used demonstrates skill, not development, and skill alone sits in the middle bands.

The second recurring problem is narrowness. The criteria expect engagement with more than one art-making form, and students who have decided they are painters frequently submit two years of painting. In Abu Dhabi this is sometimes a facilities question rather than a preference, which is a legitimate constraint and a solvable one: print, photography, digital work, assemblage and small-scale three-dimensional work are all achievable without a kiln or a spray booth, and all count.

The remedy is interim marking, monthly, on the real screens. The tutor reads what exists, says in writing what each criterion would currently credit, and names one change. Students who get that feedback four times in Year 12 arrive in Year 13 with a portfolio that needs editing rather than rebuilding, which is the difference between a comfortable final term and a crisis.

sections.heading: The exhibition: curating by subtraction
paragraphs: The exhibition is marked on coherence as well as on quality, and coherence is produced by leaving things out. Students arrive in the final term with a body of work made over two years, much of it unrelated, and want to show the best pieces. The best pieces rarely constitute a show. A smaller selection that pursues one idea, where the hanging and the sequence support that idea, scores better than a wider selection of stronger individual works.

The rationale is where that thinking becomes visible, and it has to be the student's own account of their own intention. It should state the idea, explain how the selected works develop it, and be honest about what was excluded and why. A rationale that reads as a general statement about the student's love of art, or that could be attached to any set of works, forfeits the marks the component reserves for articulated intention.

Practicalities shape all of this in Abu Dhabi, and they should be checked early. What space does the school actually provide, for how long, with what hanging system and what lighting? Can three-dimensional work be plinthed? Is there a wall long enough for a sequence? Many students design an installation their school cannot host, then adapt badly under time pressure. Looking at how local exhibition spaces solve the same problems, from museum galleries to converted warehouse rooms, is genuinely instructive here rather than decorative.

The last piece is documentation. Photograph the installed exhibition properly, with even lighting, square to the wall and without visitors in the frame, because those images are part of the submission and a poorly photographed show reads as a weaker show. Plan an hour for it rather than taking pictures on the way out.

sections.heading: Honesty when the work is artwork: appropriation, citation and generated images
paragraphs: Visual Arts has honesty boundaries that essay subjects do not, and students are rarely taught them explicitly. Working from another artist is legitimate and expected: the course asks students to engage with practitioners. What is not legitimate is presenting another artist's image, composition or motif as original work without acknowledgement. The distinction the criteria and the honesty rules both rest on is transformation plus acknowledgement. A study after a named artist, clearly identified, is normal practice. The same image uncredited is not.

Generated imagery has made this sharper. A tool can now produce a competent image in seconds, and submitting it as the student's own making is malpractice, with the consequence falling on the student. Where such tools are used legitimately, for example as a documented ideation step, the use has to be disclosed and must comply with the school's published policy, which most Abu Dhabi schools now have and which is usually stricter than students assume. The simplest safe position is that assessed making is made by the student, by hand or by a process they operated and documented.

The tutoring boundary follows the same logic. A tutor may teach technique, discuss intention, recommend artists to look at, challenge a selection, explain what a criterion credits and give written feedback on the student's own pages and drafts. A tutor may not make or alter the artwork, draw or paint into it, lay out portfolio screens, or supply text for the study or the rationale. We keep a record of what was reviewed and what was advised, which matters in a subject where help can be physical and invisible in the final object.

A note on reproduction of official material: subject guides and assessment documents belong to the IB, and a tutor should cite and link them rather than circulate copies. A provider handing out bundles of restricted material is signalling how they treat rules in general, which is worth noticing before you trust them with a component that carries an honesty declaration.

sections.heading: Tracking progress in a subject where nothing is marked until the end
paragraphs: This is the structural problem with Visual Arts and the reason evidence has to be manufactured deliberately. In Chemistry a parent sees test scores all year. In Visual Arts the first formal mark arrives after submission, by which point nothing can be changed. Schools issue predicted grades, but in a cohort of four or five students those predictions rest on a small comparison set and a teacher's judgement, which may be entirely sound and is still a single opinion.

Interim criterion marking fills the gap. Monthly, the student sends current screens, study drafts and journal pages; the tutor writes criterion-by-criterion notes with an indicative position and the reasons for it, plus one target. Over a year that produces a run of dated, comparable assessments of the same student's work. It will not match the final mark exactly and it is not presented as a prediction, but the direction of travel it shows is reliable, and the targets are specific enough to act on.

What movement looks like differs by component. Comparative study quality moves fastest, often within two drafts, because the fixes are structural: compare in the same paragraph, name the context, cite the source. Portfolio quality moves over months, because it depends on what the student does in the studio between reviews. Exhibition coherence can change in a single session, when a student finally accepts that four works have to come out of the show.

If three consecutive reviews show nothing moving, the honest conclusion is that the plan is wrong or the match is wrong, and that conversation should happen in Year 12 when there is time to act on it. That is the whole purpose of writing it down. Impressions do not accumulate into evidence, and in a subject with a two-year timeline that distinction decides outcomes.

sections.heading: What Visual Arts support costs in Abu Dhabi, plus the materials nobody budgets
paragraphs: Published market rates for private tuition in the UAE run from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, and AED 200 to 450 and above for IB and IGCSE specialists, with one premium provider publishing AED 650. A Dubai rate survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors up to AED 500. Those figures belong to the providers who published them; IB Gram publishes no tariff on this page and quotes nothing different on the phone.

Visual Arts carries a second cost layer that tutoring pages never mention and that families here consistently underestimate: the materials and the presentation. Over two years, paint, paper, canvas, print and photographic costs, digital subscriptions, mounting, framing for the exhibition and documentation photography add up to a real number, and some of it lands in the final term exactly when everything else does. Ask the department what it supplies before planning the portfolio, because the answer varies widely between Abu Dhabi schools.

The table gives indicative figures, flagged as indicative because suppliers and school provision differ. The useful discipline is to budget the materials first, then decide what tutoring is needed, rather than discovering in March that framing for six works has to be paid for in the same month as an examination-season tutoring block. Sessions bought for the comparative study in Year 12 are also cheaper in every sense than sessions bought to rescue it in Year 13.

For tutoring, two questions make quotes comparable. Does the rate include written feedback on submitted work, which is the whole source of the evidence you are buying. And is the rate for online delivery, since in-home bands carry the tutor's travel inside the hour for identical teaching. IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and every UAE lesson is live online, one-to-one, with screen sharing for portfolio pages and work in progress.

sections.heading: Permits, school ethics and choosing a reader for the portfolio
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated and the detail is checkable. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so any amount quoted to you is unverified.

Abu Dhabi adds a rule that matters here. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff bar teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct points the same way. In a subject where the school's art teacher is often the only specialist a family knows, that is a practical constraint, and it is also an argument for an outside reader on its own merits: the person who will write the predicted grade is not the ideal person to assess the evidence you intend to weigh it against.

Choosing that reader is worth doing carefully. Ask how many Diploma Visual Arts cohorts they have taught, whether they will give criterion-level written notes on actual screens rather than general encouragement, and how they handle the honesty boundary when work is physical. Ask for an example of their written feedback with the student's details removed. A practising artist without Diploma experience can be an excellent mentor and a poor guide to this assessment; the two roles are not the same purchase.

Finally, be clear about what nobody can promise. No tutor can promise a particular outcome, and in a subject assessed on judgement, anybody who implies otherwise should be treated with scepticism. What a good reader can do is tell you, in writing and repeatedly, what the criteria are currently seeing in your child's actual work, and what one change would make the biggest difference before the next review.

process.description: Whatever exists, in whatever state. Portfolio screens, journal pages and a comparative study draft tell a specialist more in an hour than a report card does in a year, because the criteria can be applied to them directly.

process.title: Tell us what the school provides

process.title: Set the review rhythm
process.description: Monthly criterion notes on real work, with one named target each time, plus a shorter session between reviews on whatever the notes identified. Three components tracked separately, with dates, so the exhibition cannot quietly eat the study.

process.title: Edit, do not rebuild, in Year 13
process.description: A portfolio reviewed four times in Year 12 needs editing in Year 13. The final block goes on exhibition selection, the rationale in the student's own words, installation within the real space, and photographing the show properly.

whyPoints.title: Interim marking in a subject with no interim marks
whyPoints.description: Monthly criterion-level notes on the student's own screens and drafts, in writing, with an indicative position and reasons. It is the only way to see two years of studio work as something other than a mystery.

whyPoints.title: First-hand research, not screen images
whyPoints.description: A looking protocol for Abu Dhabi's collections and exhibition spaces, so the comparative study is built on scale, surface and installation rather than on composition described from a photograph.

whyPoints.title: Three components, tracked separately
whyPoints.description: Study, portfolio and exhibition each get their own record and their own target. Reporting one overall impression is exactly how the comparative study ends up half-finished in the final term.

faqs.question: Does my daughter need to be the best artist in her year to score well in Diploma Visual Arts?
faqs.answer: No, and that is the most useful thing to understand early. Three components are assessed: a comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition with a written rationale. Two of the three are substantially about documented thinking rather than about finished work, and the exhibition itself is marked on coherence and articulated intention as well as on accomplishment. A quieter artist who compares rigorously, documents experiments honestly and curates with a clear idea routinely outscores the most skilled maker in the cohort. Technical ability helps, but it is not what most of the marks are for.

faqs.question: How do we see whether a Visual Arts grade is moving when nothing is marked until the end?
faqs.answer: By creating interim marks deliberately. Once a month the student submits current screens, study drafts and journal pages, and a specialist writes criterion-by-criterion notes with an indicative position, the reasons, and one target. Over a year that is a run of dated, comparable assessments of the same work. It is not a prediction and should never be sold as one, but the direction of travel is reliable and the targets are specific enough to act on. Comparative study quality usually moves within two drafts; portfolio quality moves over months.

faqs.question: Which Abu Dhabi collections are worth visiting for the comparative study?
faqs.answer: The emirate's museum collections are unusually useful because a student can compare works from different cultures and centuries in one visit, with full label information and provenance. The warehouse and arts-centre spaces add contemporary regional practice, often installation-based, where the relationship between work and space is the subject. The annual art fair offers breadth and commercial presentation, which is useful context for the exhibition component. Permanent architectural and heritage sites add material and craft traditions. Go with a question and a recording protocol rather than browsing, and write the notes up the same day.

faqs.question: Why does seeing work in person matter so much for the comparative study?
faqs.answer: Because the marks sit in analysis, and first-hand observation produces analysis a screen image cannot. Scale relative to a body, surface and brush or tool evidence, condition, framing, lighting and what the work is installed beside are all invisible in reproduction, and they are what lets a student explain how a work operates rather than describe how it looks. Students working only from images write about composition and colour, which is the register of mid-band studies. One properly recorded gallery visit often improves a study more than a week of online research.

faqs.question: What makes a process portfolio screen score well rather than averagely?
faqs.answer: Three things on the same screen: an experiment with a stated purpose, the result including whatever went wrong, and a written decision about what happens next because of it. The weak version is a photograph of a finished piece with a caption naming the technique, which demonstrates skill and not development. The criteria also expect engagement with more than one art-making form, so two years of a single medium limits the mark even when the work is strong. Print, photography, digital work and small-scale three-dimensional work all count and need no specialist facilities.

faqs.question: Our apartment has no ventilation or storage. Which art-making forms still work?
faqs.answer: More than families expect. Drawing, printmaking with water-based inks, photography, digital and lens-based work, collage and assemblage, textiles, and small-scale three-dimensional work all function without a studio, a kiln or a spray booth. Anything requiring solvents, firing or large storage is better done at school if the facilities exist, and the choice is worth making deliberately in Year 12 rather than by accident in Year 13. Tell the tutor what is possible at home in the first session, because a plan that assumes a workshop produces a portfolio that cannot be built.

faqs.question: How does a student decide what to leave out of the exhibition?
faqs.answer: By deciding what the show is about first. Coherence is produced by subtraction: a smaller selection that pursues one idea, where sequence and hanging support that idea, scores better than a wider selection of individually stronger works. State the idea, test each candidate work against it, and be honest in the rationale about what was excluded and why. Most students resist this and nearly all of them score better for doing it. The decision is usually made in a single session, once somebody outside the work asks what the selection is for.

faqs.question: What may a tutor do to the artwork itself?
faqs.answer: Nothing. A tutor may teach technique, demonstrate on their own surface, discuss intention, recommend artists to study, challenge a selection, explain what a criterion credits and give written feedback on the student's own pages and drafts. A tutor may not draw or paint into the work, alter it, lay out portfolio screens or supply text for the study or the rationale. In a subject where help can be physical and then invisible in the final object, we keep a record of what was reviewed and advised, which protects the student if the school asks how the work was supported.

faqs.question: Can my son use generated images in his Visual Arts work?
faqs.answer: Not as assessed making. Submitting a generated image as the student's own making is malpractice and the consequence falls on the student. Where such tools are used legitimately, for instance as a documented ideation step, the use must be disclosed and must comply with the school's published policy, which most Abu Dhabi schools now have and which is usually stricter than students assume. The safe working position is that assessed work is made by the student, by hand or through a process they operated and documented, and that anything else appears in the journal with its use stated.

faqs.question: Where is the line between working from an artist and copying them?
faqs.answer: Transformation plus acknowledgement. Engaging with another artist is expected: the course asks for it. A study made after a named artist, clearly identified as such in the journal and the portfolio, is normal practice and can be credited. The same image presented as original work, or a composition or motif lifted without acknowledgement, is an honesty problem and also a weaker submission, because the thinking that earns marks is the student's own response. Credit every image used, whether photographed by the student or sourced elsewhere; the fix is one line of text.

faqs.question: How much do Visual Arts materials and framing actually cost over two years?
faqs.answer: Enough to budget for deliberately. Indicative figures we see are AED 800 to 3,000 for drawing and painting materials, paper and canvas across both years, AED 300 to 1,500 for print, photographic or digital output, and AED 500 to 2,500 for mounting, plinths and framing in the final term, with documentation photography on top if the school does not cover it. Provision varies widely between Abu Dhabi schools, so ask the department what it supplies before planning the portfolio, and budget materials before deciding how much tutoring the year can carry.

faqs.question: Can a practising artist tutor the Diploma course?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the two things are not the same purchase. A working artist can be an excellent mentor for making and a poor guide to an assessment built on three documented components, screen counts, word limits and published criteria. Ask any candidate how many Diploma cohorts they have taught, whether they will give criterion-level written notes on actual screens, and how they handle the honesty boundary when help is physical. Ask for an example of their written feedback with the student's details removed. Enthusiasm for art is not evidence of experience with this course.

faqs.question: Will Visual Arts weaken a university application from Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: For art, design and architecture routes it is an asset, and a strong portfolio often matters more than the subject grade. For other courses, read the published entry requirements rather than assuming: competitive science, engineering and medical programmes specify the subjects they require, and the question is whether the rest of the timetable meets them. Some UAE and international universities also ask for a separate portfolio submission with its own deadline, which can collide with the exhibition. Check that calendar in Year 12, because two portfolio deadlines in one term is a genuinely difficult position.

faqs.question: When should the comparative study be finished, and what happens if it is not?
faqs.answer: Aim to have it substantially complete before the exhibition work takes over in Year 13, because the exhibition expands to fill whatever time remains. Schools set their own internal deadlines, usually earlier than the IB's upload dates to allow marking time, so ask the arts teacher for those dates and put them somewhere visible. A study left half-finished in the final term is the single commonest avoidable loss in this subject, and it is also the component where improvement comes fastest, which makes the wasted opportunity worse.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send the screens as they are
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.closingBody: Visual Arts is the Diploma subject where parents can see the least and worry the most, because nothing is formally marked until it is too late to change. The remedy is simple and it starts with one reading. Send current portfolio screens, a comparative study draft and a few journal pages, and a specialist will write down what each criterion is currently seeing and what one change would matter most. That is what the free trial lesson is for, and it happens before any payment. Tell us what the school provides and when its deadlines fall, and we will match your child with a Visual Arts specialist for live one-to-one online lessons in Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: How a parent can tell whether Visual Arts is going well
paragraphs: Parents booking an IB DP Visual Arts tutor in Abu Dhabi almost never arrive with a mark in their hand. In Mathematics a bad fortnight produces a number. In this subject it produces a shrug, a half-finished canvas and a teacher comment about developing a personal direction. By the time a predicted grade appears, eighteen months of documentation decisions have already been made, and most of them cannot be revisited. That is the real problem this page is about: evidence, and how to see it in time.

Visual Arts is assessed on three components, and all three are documents rather than performances. The comparative study is an analytical piece comparing artworks and artists. The process portfolio is a record of experimentation across art-making forms. The exhibition is a selected body of resolved work with a short written rationale. None of these is marked on how talented the student is. They are marked on what the submitted screens and pages demonstrate, which is a different thing and a much more checkable one.

So this page is organised around what should exist and when. It sets out the components and their hard limits, what a portfolio should contain by the end of Year 12, what a predicted grade in this subject is actually based on, how to read it, and what questions to put to the art teacher at a parents' evening that will produce a useful answer rather than a reassuring one. It also sets out what a review session returns in writing, because a tutor in this subject who leaves nothing behind is impossible to evaluate.

On delivery: IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with the student's photographed work, portfolio screens or comparative study pages shared on screen. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are a service we run only in India. Reviewing documented work is the actual task in this subject, and a shared screen with the files open does it more precisely than a tutor glancing at a canvas across a studio.

And the boundary, stated plainly. The student makes every artwork, takes every photograph, writes every word of the rationale and the comparative study. A tutor teaches analysis, questions a selection, points at a criterion the screens do not yet evidence, and marks practice work against the published descriptors so the student can see the gap. Nobody at IB Gram writes, edits to completion, or supplies any part of a submission. Providers in this market do sell finished coursework; the risk of using one sits entirely with your child. One more thing worth saying at the outset: nothing on this page requires you to understand art. Every check described here is a question about whether a document exists, how many screens it contains, and whether the writing attached to it explains why rather than what.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.programmesIntro: Visual Arts is examined in the Diploma, and the habits that decide the grade are formed earlier. Here is what each IB stage contributes for an Abu Dhabi student heading towards it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years producing three submitted components: a comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition with a curatorial rationale. The grade rests on documented thinking rather than on finished beauty. Students who photograph only resolved pieces and write the portfolio from memory lose marks they can no longer recover, because the evidence of experimentation no longer exists.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi cohorts in this subject are typically small, often with one specialist teacher carrying both year groups. That makes a second, independent reading of a comparative study or a set of portfolio screens more valuable here than it would be in a large department with internal moderation among several teachers.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Middle Years Arts builds the documentation habit the Diploma assumes: a process journal, recorded experiments, and reflection written at the time rather than afterwards. A Year 11 student who has kept a real journal arrives in DP1 months ahead of one who has produced only finished pieces.
programmes.countryNote: Provision differs across Abu Dhabi schools. Some run a rigorous process journal from Year 7 and some treat art as a making subject with light recording. We ask which a student has had, because the documentation habit takes a term to install and DP1 does not have a spare term.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No bearing on a Diploma grade. What does carry forward is the idea that art is thought about as well as made, which is usually formed in the way a child is asked to talk about their own work rather than in any technical teaching.
programmes.countryNote: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum in UAE private schools under the federal requirement, so Primary timetables here are fuller than the same school's abroad. Specialist art time varies considerably between schools in the emirate.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A route that suits students combining Diploma courses with an art, design or media career study, often with a portfolio for application purposes alongside. Visual Arts taken within it is assessed against the same subject guide and the tutoring work is identical.
programmes.countryNote: This route is uncommon in the emirate, so families rarely find anyone nearby who has supported it. Online matching removes a limitation that was only ever geographic rather than one of expertise.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.subjectsIntro: Visual Arts students in Abu Dhabi often need one other subject supported in the same year. These are the Diploma courses our tutors cover alongside it, and where the skills genuinely overlap.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Comparative study, process portfolio and exhibition. Marks go missing on portfolios that show outcomes rather than experimentation, comparative studies that describe artworks instead of analysing them, and exhibitions selected for variety rather than coherence.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The closest analytical neighbour. A student who can analyse how a text produces meaning has the exact skill the comparative study rewards, applied to images instead of sentences. Students strong here usually need the least help with that component.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: Builds the same close-reading discipline with a tighter focus on form. The transfer into writing about composition, material and context is direct, and one tutor keeping the analytical standard consistent across both subjects saves time.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Shares the habit of analysing how choices create meaning and the problem of documenting a creative process for assessment. Students taking both must keep the two sets of written work distinct in purpose and in referencing.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Shares drawing and modelling skill and very little else in assessment terms. One folder documents a design process against measurable criteria, the other an artistic intention; conflating them costs marks in both.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Useful background for the cultural context work the comparative study demands. Students taking both tend to write stronger contextual analysis because they treat context as evidence rather than as scene-setting.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Perception, memory and culture appear in both subjects with different evidence standards. A student taking both needs to learn which audience expects a cited study and which expects visual evidence.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Questions about interpretation, value and perspective overlap heavily with the comparative study. A student who understands one writes better in the other, and a single tutor can keep the two consistent.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Visual Arts is a popular choice and a common stalling point, usually because the question becomes a biography of an artist rather than an arguable question. Support is process coaching and reading what the student has written.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Included because it is the most common fourth or fifth subject among the Visual Arts students we support in Abu Dhabi, and because a weak grade here is what most often threatens an otherwise comfortable Diploma total.

sections.heading: What should exist by each point in the two years
paragraphs: This is the section most parents in Abu Dhabi actually want, and it is the one competitors in this search do not write. Visual Arts produces no weekly marks, so the only way to monitor it is to check whether the right things exist at the right time. The checks below need no artistic judgement at all. They are questions about whether a document exists, how many screens it has, and whether the writing attached to it analyses or describes.

The pattern of failure is always the same and always visible early. A student enjoys making work, does not enjoy documenting it, and reaches the spring of Year 13 with a portfolio of finished outcomes and no record of the thinking between them. At that point there is nothing a teacher or a tutor can honestly do, because the missing evidence is evidence of something that happened months ago. Caught in Year 12, the same problem takes one session to fix and a routine to maintain.

The table below sets out the milestones, what should exist at each, how a parent can check without expertise, and what it means if the answer is no. Treat the timings as typical rather than official: your school sets its own internal deadlines and those override anything here. Ask the art teacher for the internal deadline calendar at the start of DP1 and keep it somewhere visible. Those internal dates are the ones that matter in practice, because they are the points at which a submission stops being changeable, and they usually sit several months before anything a parent would think of as an exam deadline.

sections.heading: The three components and their hard limits
paragraphs: Visual Arts is one of the few Diploma subjects where a student can lose marks for a purely administrative reason. Each component has a defined number of screens and, where there is writing, a word limit. Exceeding or falling short of them is not a matter of interpretation. A family who learns the numbers at the start of DP1 removes a whole category of avoidable loss, and the numbers are published in the subject guide the school holds.

Higher Level is not simply more of the same. It requires more portfolio screens, more exhibition pieces, a longer rationale and an additional section of the comparative study in which the student connects the artworks studied to their own developing practice. That last requirement is the one Higher Level students most often underestimate, because it cannot be bolted on at the end: it needs the student's own work to have developed in a direction related to what they analysed.

The table sets out the components side by side with their requirements at each level and what the marks actually reward. Confirm every figure against the guide version your child's school is following, because guides are revised and schools adopt revisions at different points. The pattern in the right-hand column, however, does not change between versions: analysis beats description, process beats outcome, and coherence beats variety. The limits themselves are worth writing on a card and keeping with the sketchbook. A student who knows the exhibition needs a specific number of resolved pieces plans the final year differently from one who discovers the number in February and then has to make two more artworks in a hurry.

sections.heading: What a Visual Arts predicted grade is actually based on
paragraphs: Parents in Abu Dhabi often treat a predicted grade in this subject as a judgement of talent, and it is not. It is a teacher's estimate of what the three components will score when they are submitted and moderated, based on what the teacher has already seen. A student with striking work and thin documentation is correctly predicted low, which feels unjust and is in fact the system working exactly as described.

That makes a predicted grade useful to a parent, because it is a statement about evidence and evidence can be improved. The useful conversation with the art teacher is not whether the grade is fair. It is which component is dragging the estimate, which criterion within that component is weakest, and what evidence would need to exist for the estimate to move. Teachers answer those questions readily; they answer a question about fairness defensively, which helps nobody.

Two warnings. First, a predicted grade given in autumn of DP2 is based on a portfolio that is still open, so there is genuine room to move it, while one given in the final term is largely a report on completed work. Second, no tutor can promise a grade change, and anyone who does is describing a sales process rather than an assessment. What a tutor can do is name the criterion and the missing evidence, and show the student what addressing it looks like. It is also worth knowing that predicted grades in this subject move in both directions. A student who closes a documentation gap over one term can be revised upwards, and a student who stops documenting while making ambitious work can be revised down despite the work improving.
bullets: A predicted grade estimates what the submitted components will score

sections.heading: The process portfolio is a record, not a gallery
paragraphs: The single most common and most expensive misunderstanding in this subject is treating the process portfolio as a showcase. It is a record of experimentation. Screens that show a sequence of finished pieces with captions describing how they were made score poorly however good the pieces are, because the component asks what the student tried, what happened and what they did next.

What scores is the uncomfortable material: the medium that did not work, the composition abandoned after two attempts, the technical experiment that failed and the sentence written at the time explaining why. Students resist photographing failures because they look bad, and in doing so they delete the evidence the component is built to reward. The fix is a routine rather than a skill: photograph everything at the stage it is at, write two sentences, date it.

Abu Dhabi students have one specific advantage worth using. The portfolio requires work across art-making forms, and apartment living pushes students towards printmaking, drawing, photography and digital work rather than large-scale painting or sculpture. That is not a compromise. A portfolio that moves between a dry-point print, a photographic series and a digital composition demonstrates range more convincingly than three sizes of the same acrylic painting would. The routine is what makes this work, and it has to be small enough to survive a busy term. Our students who document well generally spend ten minutes at the end of a working session photographing what exists and writing two sentences, which over eighteen months produces far more usable evidence than an occasional ambitious catch-up session that never quite happens.
bullets: Photograph work at the stage it is at, not when it is finished
Failed experiments are evidence and should be documented deliberately
Two dated sentences written at the time beat a paragraph written later
Range across art-making forms is a requirement, not a flourish

sections.heading: The comparative study: analysis against description
paragraphs: The comparative study is an essay in screen form, and it is marked like an essay. The distinction that decides the grade is between describing an artwork and analysing it. Description tells the reader what is in the image. Analysis explains how the formal choices produce meaning, what function the work served, how its cultural context shaped it, and what emerges when it is set beside another work by a different artist.

Students default to description because it is safe and because online sources are full of it. The symptom is easy to spot without any expertise: if a sentence would still be true with the word because removed, it is probably description. Strong studies are full of causal language and comparative language, and they make claims that could in principle be argued with. A study nobody could disagree with is a study nobody can award high marks to.

The table sets out the difference across the things a study must cover, with what a weak and a strong treatment look like in each. Higher Level students should read the final row carefully: the additional screens connecting the studied artworks to their own practice must be genuine, which means the connection has to exist in the work before it can be written about convincingly. Choice of artworks is the decision that sets the ceiling on this component. Two works that share a medium but nothing else give a student very little to compare, while two that share a problem and solve it differently give them a whole study. We spend the first review on that choice rather than on the writing, because the writing cannot outperform the pairing.

sections.heading: The exhibition, the rationale and the discipline of leaving work out
paragraphs: The exhibition is where students lose marks for being generous to themselves. The component asks for a coherent body of work, and coherence means that the pieces belong together and that the order in which they are presented does something. A student who submits their strongest individual pieces regardless of relationship has submitted a portfolio of highlights, which is a different and less well-credited thing.

Selection is therefore the main act of judgement in the component, and it is almost always an act of exclusion. The strong piece that does not belong has to come out. Students find this very difficult, partly because the piece took three weeks and partly because nobody has told them that leaving it out is a decision the examiner can credit. A tutor's most useful contribution here is asking what the body of work is about and then asking which piece contradicts the answer.

The curatorial rationale is short, and shortness is the difficulty. There is room to state an intention and show how the selection and arrangement deliver it, and no room for the story of the two years. The common failure is spending the word count on process that belongs in the portfolio. Write the intention first, then test every remaining sentence against it, and the limit stops being a constraint and becomes a filter. Arrangement is the part students forget entirely. The order and grouping of the pieces is part of what is assessed, and a sketch of the hanging plan made before the rationale is written tends to produce a sharper rationale, because the student has to decide what the sequence is arguing before they describe it.
bullets: Coherence of the body of work is credited; a highlights reel is not
Excluding a strong but unrelated piece is a decision, and a creditable one
The rationale states an intention the selection visibly delivers
Process belongs in the portfolio, not in the rationale's word count

sections.heading: Photographing work, and using Abu Dhabi's cultural sites properly
paragraphs: Every mark in this subject is awarded on a photograph or a scan. That makes documentation quality a genuine assessment issue rather than a presentational nicety, and it is one of the few things in the course that costs nothing to fix. Work photographed at an angle, under a yellow ceiling light, against a patterned wall, loses detail the marker cannot recover. Daylight near a window, the work flat and square to the camera, a plain background, no flash: four rules and the problem is solved.

Abu Dhabi's cultural infrastructure is the second underused asset. Students writing a comparative study from online reproductions alone produce analysis that reads like a summary of other people's analysis. A student who has stood in front of a work and recorded its scale, surface and the way the room places it writes differently, and the difference is visible in the marks. The cultural district on Saadiyat Island, the exhibition spaces around Mina Zayed and the historic sites in the city centre all offer accessible, specific material.

Two practicalities. Check photography rules at any venue before relying on images, and keep a dated record of what was seen first-hand; both matter for referencing and for honesty. And note what is permitted in a submission: reproductions of other artists' work are used under the conditions the guide sets out, credited fully, and the school's art teacher is the right person to confirm the current referencing requirement for screens.
bullets: Daylight, square to the camera, plain background, no flash
First-hand viewing produces analysis that reproductions cannot
Keep a dated record of what was seen and where
Credit every reproduction and confirm the referencing format with the school

sections.heading: What a review session returns, and where the line sits
paragraphs: A tutor in an essay subject leaves a marked paper behind. In Visual Arts the equivalent has to be deliberately constructed, or there is no way to tell a useful session from a pleasant one. Every review we run returns three things in writing: which criterion the work currently evidences and which it does not, a numbered list of changes in priority order, and a note of what was checked, including screen counts and word limits. The student acts on all of it themselves.

That is also where the boundary sits, and it is set by IB academic-honesty rules rather than by preference. A tutor may teach analysis, question a selection, name an unaddressed criterion, mark a practice piece of analysis against the descriptors, and explain what a stronger version would do differently. A tutor may not write, rewrite, edit to completion, or supply screens, images or sentences for a submission. Appropriation of another artist's work without acknowledgement, and submitted text a student did not write, are both malpractice.

A practical consequence worth stating: because everything we hand back is a change list rather than a changed document, progress in this subject is slower and more visible than in subjects with weekly marks. Over a term a parent can read six change lists and see whether the same criterion keeps appearing. If it does, either the advice is not landing or the student is not acting on it, and both of those are worth knowing about in November rather than in May.
bullets: Each review returns criteria notes, a numbered change list and a limits check
A tutor teaches, questions, names criteria and marks practice work

whyPoints.description: Abu Dhabi cohorts are small and often taught by one specialist carrying both year groups. A second experienced reading of a comparative study or a set of portfolio screens catches what a single reader, however good, has stopped seeing.

whyPoints.title: No promises about grades
whyPoints.description: Nobody can guarantee a mark in a subject assessed on two years of documented work. What a review offers is a named criterion, the missing evidence, and a change the student can make this week.

faqs.question: How will I know whether Visual Arts tutoring is actually working?
faqs.answer: Read the change lists. Every review we run returns criteria notes, a numbered list of changes in priority order, and a check of screen counts and word limits. Across a term a parent can see whether the same criterion keeps reappearing: if analysis of cultural context is listed in November, January and March, either the teaching is not landing or the student is not acting on it. Both are worth knowing early. In a subject with no weekly marks, that written record is the only honest measure available.

faqs.question: What should be in the process portfolio by the end of Year 12?
faqs.answer: Dated evidence of experimentation across more than one art-making form, including things that did not work, with short reflections written at the time rather than afterwards. By the end of DP1 the portfolio should be well advanced towards its screen count, not starting. A quick parental check needs no expertise: ask to see three dated pages from different weeks and look for abandoned directions. A portfolio containing only successful finished pieces is the most common and most expensive problem in this subject.

faqs.question: Who marks Diploma Visual Arts, the school or the IB?
faqs.answer: The work is submitted and assessed against published criteria, with external moderation of the school's marking. The practical consequence for a parent is that the teacher's judgement is not the final word, and that everything rests on what the submitted screens and documents evidence rather than on what the teacher knows about the student's ability. A student whose strongest qualities are visible in the studio but absent from the submission will be marked on the submission. Your school's IB coordinator can explain the exact moderation route for the current session.

faqs.question: What is a Visual Arts predicted grade actually based on?
faqs.answer: The teacher's estimate of what the three components will score when submitted, based on what has been seen so far. It is a judgement about evidence rather than about talent, which is why a student with striking work and a thin portfolio is correctly predicted low. That also makes it actionable. Ask the art teacher which component is dragging the estimate and which criterion within it is weakest, rather than whether the grade is fair; the first question gets a useful answer and the second rarely does.

faqs.question: What are the screen counts and word limits for each component?
faqs.answer: Standard Level requires 10 to 15 comparative study screens, 9 to 18 process portfolio screens across at least two art-making forms, 4 to 7 exhibition artworks and a curatorial rationale of up to 400 words. Higher Level requires the same comparative study plus 3 to 5 screens connecting it to the student's own work, 13 to 25 portfolio screens across at least three forms, 8 to 11 artworks and a rationale of up to 700 words. Confirm every figure against the guide version your school follows, because guides are revised.

faqs.question: Why would a tutor say the portfolio screens are too finished?
faqs.answer: Because the component rewards experimentation rather than outcomes. Screens showing a sequence of resolved pieces with captions about how each was made answer a question nobody asked. What scores is the medium that failed, the composition abandoned after two attempts, the test that produced a surprising result, and the sentence written at the time explaining what changed as a result. Students avoid photographing failures because they look bad, and in doing so they remove the evidence the marks are attached to.

faqs.question: How does an online tutor see enough of a painting to comment usefully?
faqs.answer: The same way a moderator does: from photographs. Every mark in this subject is awarded on a photograph or scan of the work, so reviewing documented images is not a compromise, it is the actual task. What matters is photograph quality, and four rules cover it: daylight near a window, the work flat and square to the camera, a plain background, no flash. Work shared before the session means the hour is spent on analysis rather than on uploading files.

faqs.question: Can a tutor annotate my daughter's comparative study screens?
faqs.answer: A tutor can tell her, in writing, which criteria a screen does not yet evidence and what a stronger treatment would do differently, and can mark a practice piece of analysis against the published descriptors. A tutor cannot write, rewrite or edit her screens to completion, or supply sentences for a submission. The distinction matters: a change list she then acts on herself is teaching, and a document handed back improved is malpractice that puts her whole Diploma at risk.

faqs.question: Our Abu Dhabi school has one art teacher. Is a second opinion worth paying for?
faqs.answer: In small cohorts it usually is, and not because the teacher is weak. A single reader who has watched a student's work develop for eighteen months stops seeing what an unfamiliar reader sees immediately, which is exactly what external moderation will do to the submission. An independent reading against the criteria catches omissions that have become invisible through familiarity. The sensible pattern is one review per component, placed before the school's internal deadline, rather than regular weekly sessions.

faqs.question: How do we photograph artwork properly in an Abu Dhabi apartment?
faqs.answer: Natural light does most of the work. Photograph near a window in the morning or late afternoon, with the work flat and square to the camera, against a plain wall or a sheet of white card, with the flash off and the room lights off so the colour is not contaminated by warm bulbs. Three-dimensional work needs one consistent light direction and several angles. Shoot everything at the stage it is at rather than waiting until it is finished, because mid-stage images are the ones the portfolio needs.

faqs.question: Does taking Visual Arts weaken a university application?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the destination and should be checked against each university's published requirements rather than assumed. Art, architecture and design courses frequently want it and often ask for a portfolio in which the exhibition work is central. Competitive science and medicine routes expect specific subjects, and Visual Arts does not substitute for them. The decision belongs in the Year 12 option conversation, with the actual entry requirements of the shortlisted courses on the table rather than a general reputation.

faqs.question: Which Abu Dhabi cultural sites are genuinely useful for the comparative study?
faqs.answer: Any that let the student stand in front of a work and record its scale, surface and setting. The cultural district on Saadiyat Island, the exhibition spaces around Mina Zayed and the historic sites in the city centre all provide specific, local, first-hand material. A study written from online reproductions alone tends to read as a summary of other people's analysis. Check each venue's photography rules before relying on images, keep a dated record of what was seen, and credit every reproduction used on a screen.

faqs.question: My daughter is in DP2 with very little documented. What can still be done?
faqs.answer: An audit first, then a plan for what remains. What can still move is the comparative study, which is written rather than accumulated, the rationale, and the exhibition selection. What cannot be recovered is eighteen months of experimentation that was never photographed, because a portfolio cannot acquire a past. The honest approach is to document everything from this week on a sustainable weekly routine, concentrate effort on the components that are still open, and plan around a realistic outcome rather than a hoped-for one.

faqs.question: How many review sessions does a comparative study usually need?
faqs.answer: In our Abu Dhabi caseload, typically three to five across DP1 and the first term of DP2: one on the choice of artworks and the reason for pairing them, one or two on turning description into analysis, and one before the school's internal deadline checking criteria coverage and screen counts. A student starting the study late needs more hours for less movement, because the choice of artworks is the decision that determines how much analysis is even possible, and by then it is usually fixed.

faqs.question: Does an online art tutor need a UAE private tuition permit?
faqs.answer: A tutor resident in the UAE giving private lessons, including online lessons, needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no schedule of amounts has been published. A tutor resident abroad falls under their own jurisdiction's rules. Ask any provider and expect a direct answer.

In a free trial lesson your child shares photographed work and portfolio screens with the tutor who would teach them, and afterwards you receive a written view of which components are evidenced, which criteria are unaddressed, and how many review hours a realistic plan needs across the remaining terms. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, scheduled backwards from the school's internal deadlines, and every review returns a change list your child acts on themselves.

intro.heading: Price the phase, not the hour
paragraphs: Parents searching for IB exam preparation in Abu Dhabi are usually asking a cost question underneath the subject question. They have been quoted an hourly rate, sometimes two very different ones, and they cannot tell what either number buys. The hourly rate is the least informative figure in this market. What decides the bill is how many weeks you buy, in how many subjects, at which phase of the final year, and whether the hours are spent on something the remaining time can actually change.

The final year of the Diploma divides into phases that behave differently and cost differently. There is the pre-mock phase, where content gaps can still be closed and an hour of teaching is cheap relative to what it returns. There is the mock-aftermath phase, where the useful work is diagnosis and reallocation. There is the study-leave phase, where sessions get shorter, more frequent and more expensive per hour of calendar time because slots are scarce. And there is the week before each paper, which is worth almost nothing to buy and a great deal to plan.

Rates in this emirate are not a mystery either, they are simply unpublished by most providers. Rate trackers and provider pages put qualified online subject tutoring at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, in-home visiting work at AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the fee, and premium named tutors above that again. Monthly estimates for a weekly hour run around AED 240 to 600 at the budget end and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Those are market observations from October 2026, attributed to the sources that published them, and they are not IB Gram's price list.

What a family can control is allocation. Six subjects plus the core is more surface area than any budget covers properly, so the spending decision is really a triage decision: which two or three subjects have the most recoverable marks per hour, which ones are safe enough to leave alone, and which are so far behind that money spent there buys a smaller grade change than the same money spent elsewhere. That judgement needs a marked paper, not a conversation.

So this page is organised as a spend plan. It sets out what each phase is worth, what the market charges for it, the four ways exam-season money is most reliably wasted in Abu Dhabi, how to read a mock before you buy anything, and what the November session costs a family who decides a subject needs a second attempt. Every figure is labelled with where it came from. Where we do not have a sourced number, including for examination entry fees, the page says so and points you at the body that sets it.

abu-dhabi/ib-exam-preparation.programmesIntro: Exam preparation means something different at each stage of the IB continuum, and the cost profile changes with it. Three stages matter to an Abu Dhabi family planning spend across the school years rather than just the final term.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced assessment with no external written papers for most students, so exam preparation here is really preparation for being examined later: timed writing under pressure, reading a criterion as a specification, and keeping a usable set of notes. Money spent in MYP 4 and 5 is the cheapest exam preparation a family will ever buy, because it is preventative.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi families often move children into the Diploma from MYP within the same school, which hides the size of the step. The jump that catches candidates here is the shift from criteria written in sentences to mark schemes that reward specific command-term behaviours, and a few hours in the final MYP year is the least expensive way to meet it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, assessed through internal work completed across two years and written papers sat at the end. Exam preparation spend concentrates in the second year, and the allocation question is which of the six subjects returns the most marks per hour once the internally assessed components are already submitted.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma candidates in this emirate normally sit the May session, which puts the heaviest spending window in the first months of the calendar year. Abu Dhabi's school calendars, Ramadan timings and study-leave arrangements all land inside that window, which is why the plan is built against the family's real availability before any hours are priced.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme and course candidates
programmes.description: Students taking individual IB courses rather than the full Diploma, or combining IB courses with a career-related study, still sit the same external papers in those subjects. The budget is usually smaller and more focused, often a single subject where a grade is needed for a specific university or progression requirement.
programmes.countryNote: This is the group most likely to be quoted for a short, single-subject block in Abu Dhabi, and the group for whom the phase question matters most: buying six weeks before the paper and buying six months before it are different products at a similar hourly rate.

abu-dhabi/ib-exam-preparation.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are where Abu Dhabi families most often concentrate final-phase spend, with a note on what the written papers reward. Confirm the exact components and weightings for your child's course in the current subject guide the school issues, because these are revised between cohorts.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The usual first call on an exam-season budget, because its lost marks are patterned and recoverable: method marks sacrificed by writing no working, proof questions abandoned at the first line, and calculator papers attempted without the calculator strategy the paper assumes.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Rewards modelling and interpretation in context, which candidates trained on pure technique find harder than the algebra. Final-phase hours go on reading a scenario, choosing a model and justifying the choice in writing rather than on computation.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Marks concentrate in the extended-response and data-analysis questions, where candidates who know the physics lose marks for not quoting values from the graph or stating an assumption. Uncertainty treatment is a finite, drillable gap.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics are the recurring content gaps, but the faster recovery is usually in command-term discipline: stating an observation where the paper asked for an explanation costs marks on knowledge the candidate already has.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume makes re-reading feel productive and practice feel punishing, which is why the marks sit in precise terminology and in data questions where the trend is described without the figures that earn the mark.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is an examinable skill: axes labelled, the correct curve shifted, the new equilibrium marked. Evaluation marks are the other recoverable block, lost by candidates who analyse thoroughly and then stop before judging.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study papers reward application to the specific organisation in front of the candidate. Generic answers that would fit any firm score in the lower bands, and that habit is correctable inside a few weeks of focused practice.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Written papers reward a controlled argument about how a text produces meaning, not a summary of what it says. Final-phase work is mostly timed essay practice with annotated marking against the assessment criteria.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Study recall is finite and therefore cheap to finish, while the expensive gap is evaluation: candidates describe a study accurately and then fail to say what it fails to show. Short repeated drills move this faster than content revision.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: By the final phase these are usually submitted and the mark is fixed, which matters for the budget: money spent here late buys nothing. Where they are still open, support is feedback on the student's own draft and nothing beyond that.

abu-dhabi/ib-exam-preparation.regionsIntro: In exam season the scarce resources are evening slots and the student's own energy, and both vary by community. These are the Abu Dhabi areas families most often book from, with the scheduling point each raises once study leave begins.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Small Diploma cohorts and wide subject spreads, so a household often needs two different HL specialists rather than one generalist. Morning slots during study leave fill first here, which is worth booking before April.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Activity-heavy weekday evenings mean the realistic slot is often 19:30 or later, and the lesson recording gets used more than anywhere else. Short twice-weekly sessions outperform one long block in this pattern.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment living with both parents working, so sessions are booked around commutes rather than around school. Families here most often ask for a fixed weekly slot locked for the whole exam term rather than rolling bookings.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long school runs across the mainland corridor already consume the late afternoon, which is why the pre-mock phase here is usually bought as weekend mornings and the study-leave phase as weekday mornings.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Dense, central and close to several large schools, so group revision is easy to find and individual diagnosis is not. The spend question here is usually whether to add one-to-one work on top of what the school already provides.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Established family areas with multiple children in the same household, where the budget is being split across siblings in different year groups. A single shared schedule planned once saves more than negotiating the hourly rate.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Zayed City
regions.note: Newer communities a long way from the island, where a visiting tutor's travel would be inside the fee. In the final phase that travel cost competes directly with the number of sessions the same money buys.

schoolClusters.city: The island and Saadiyat
schoolClusters.note: Established Diploma provision with internal mock timetables set early in the calendar year, which is what fixes when diagnostic spending is useful. Students we support attend schools in this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and the mainland
schoolClusters.note: Larger year groups and broader option blocks, so subject combinations differ widely between households in the same street and a single spend plan rarely transfers from one family to the next.

abu-dhabi/ib-exam-preparation.modesIntro: Exam-season support is bought in three shapes in this market, and they price very differently per unit of calendar time. All three run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

modes.title: Phase block, pre-mock
modes.description: A fixed number of weeks bought before the school's mock window, aimed at closing content gaps while there is still time for content to matter. This is the cheapest phase per mark recovered, because an hour spent here can still change what a candidate knows rather than only how they write it down.

Content-led, with one timed section each week to check transfer

modes.title: Diagnostic and reallocation, post-mock
modes.description: Two to four sessions per subject whose only purpose is to mark and interpret the mock scripts and produce a written allocation plan. Families frequently buy fewer total hours after this than they had budgeted, because the scripts show two of the six subjects do not need them.

modes.title: Study-leave clinic
modes.description: Short, frequent sessions in the weeks when papers are actually sat, built entirely around scripts the candidate has already attempted. Per hour this is the most expensive phase in the market because slots are scarce, and the hours bought should be fewer and more targeted than earlier blocks.

sections.heading: What IB exam preparation costs in Abu Dhabi, phase by phase
paragraphs: The direct answer: a specialist IB tutor working online in this market is quoted in the region of AED 200 to 450 an hour, a qualified non-specialist subject tutor AED 150 to 300, and premium named tutors above that. A rate tracker's monthly estimates for one weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. All of those are market figures published in October 2026 by providers and trackers, not IB Gram prices, which are quoted after a diagnostic.

The number that decides your bill, though, is the number of hours, and that follows the phase. A pre-mock block in two subjects at one session a week for ten weeks is twenty hours. A post-mock diagnostic across four subjects is eight to twelve hours and then stops. A study-leave clinic in one subject at four short sessions a week for three weeks is around nine hours. Those are very different totals at a similar hourly rate, and families who negotiate the rate while leaving the hours unplanned usually spend more.

The phase also changes what the money buys per mark. Content teaching before the mock is cheap per mark because the candidate still has time to consolidate. Diagnosis after the mock is the highest-value purchase in the whole year, because it decides where everything else goes. Technique work in study leave is narrow but reliable. The week before a specific paper is close to worthless to buy and genuinely valuable to plan, which costs nothing.

sections.heading: Four ways exam-season money gets wasted here
paragraphs: The first is paying for content re-teaching after the mock. Once the mock script shows that marks are being lost to working omission, command-term misreading and timing, buying more content coverage treats the wrong fault at full price. This is the single most common exam-season purchase in this market and the one with the weakest return, because it is also the easiest thing for a tutor to sell and to deliver.

The second is buying hours in the subject the family worries about most rather than the subject with the most recoverable marks. Worry is not evidence. A candidate frightened of Physics and quietly losing fifteen reachable marks in Economics should be spending on Economics, and only a marked script says so. Spreading hours evenly across six subjects is the same error in a politer form.

The third is the two-hour minimum. In-home visiting work in this emirate is commonly quoted at two hours, because the travel has to be worth the trip, and market rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour include that travel. In exam season, four forty-five-minute sessions beat one two-hour visit for technique work, because technique is built by frequent correction. Paying for the length of a session that exists to justify a drive is paying for the drive.

The fourth is late spending on components that are already closed. Internal assessments, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge are usually submitted before the final phase, and once submitted the mark is fixed. Hours bought against them buy nothing. A provider who takes that booking without saying so is selling calendar time, and the honest answer costs them the hours.

sections.heading: Reading a mock script before you release a budget
paragraphs: A mock percentage is the least useful artefact the school will give you, and it is the one most families buy tutoring from. Two candidates on 54 can need completely different interventions costing completely different amounts. The script tells you which, and it tells you in four categories: marks lost to content not known, marks lost to technique on content that was known, marks lost to timing, and marks lost to question selection or misreading.

Those four categories price differently. Content gaps are the most expensive to close and the slowest. Technique faults are cheap, fast and transfer across every paper in the subject. Timing is a two or three session fix. Question selection is often a single conversation. A script with eighteen marks in the technique and timing categories is a far better purchase than a script with eighteen marks of missing content, at the same hourly rate.

So the order is: get the scripts, have them marked against the published scheme, categorise the losses, then decide the budget. A diagnostic of eight to twelve hours across four subjects, bought once, routinely reduces the total spend because it closes two subjects down. Families who skip it tend to buy a flat weekly commitment in four subjects for twelve weeks and never find out which two mattered.
Ask the school for the scripts rather than the grades. Schools in this emirate vary in how readily they release them, and it is worth asking early, before the mock rather than after it.

sections.heading: The November session and the cost of a second attempt
paragraphs: Where one subject is clearly not going to land, a family's real options are to spend more on it now, to accept the grade, or to plan a retake in a later session. That last option has a cost structure most providers never discuss, and it is worth setting out before the May papers rather than after the results. A retake means a further entry through a centre, a further period of tutoring at the same market rates, and a delay to whatever the grade was needed for.

Diploma candidates in Abu Dhabi normally sit the May session, and a November sitting exists as an alternative. We do not publish IB session or results dates on this page, because the IB's own site cannot be verified by automated checking and an unverified date on a fee-paying decision is worse than no date. Confirm every IB date with your child's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org directly, and plan the retake decision around what they confirm.

The entry fee question gets the same treatment. Examination entry is handled through the school as the centre, or through an approved centre for a candidate entering independently, and those bodies set the fees. We do not quote figures we have not read on the setting body's own page. Ask the coordinator for the entry cost, the deadline and whether the school will enter a candidate for a later session at all, because not every school does.

sections.heading: What you are entitled to ask before paying anything
paragraphs: Exam season is when providers are least likely to be questioned and most likely to be paid in advance, so it is the right time to be awkward. There are five questions that cost nothing to ask and change what you buy. Which exact components of this subject has the tutor taught before. Will a marked script be produced in the first fortnight. What happens to unused hours. Who is actually teaching, as opposed to who appears on the website. And what is the stated limit of what these weeks can do.

The fifth is the one that separates a tutor from a salesperson. Nobody can promise a grade or a point improvement, and any provider promising a particular score, a fixed rise in points, or money back against a result is describing something they cannot control. The honest version is a written statement of what the remaining weeks can address and what they cannot, produced after the diagnostic and before the hours are committed.

The permit question is also legitimate and easy to ask. Individuals giving private lessons in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023; it is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules also indicates that Abu Dhabi school staff may not take paid private tutoring work with students enrolled at their own school, which is a reason to be wary of any arrangement marketed that way.

IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and nothing on this page should be read as implying one. Any provider claiming such status is making a specific factual claim that can be checked with the body named.
