abu-dhabi/ib-myp-design-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach MYP Design as an assessed subject built on a documented design cycle. Each one has marked student folders against the four criteria and can read a draft folder and tell you, page by page, which band it sits in and what the next piece of evidence needs to show.

intro.heading: Why a good product and a poor grade keep happening in MYP Design
paragraphs: The commonest conversation in MYP Design support starts the same way. The student built something that works, the family saw it, the teacher was complimentary about it, and the grade came back as a 4. Nothing has gone wrong with the marking. The student has misunderstood what the subject assesses. MYP Design is marked against four criteria of 8 marks each, and only one of them - criterion C, creating the solution - is substantially about making. The other three are awarded for research, specification, planning, testing and evaluation, all of which live in the folder.

The four criteria are specific and in a fixed order. Criterion A, inquiring and analysing, asks the student to explain and justify the need, research it from relevant sources, analyse existing products, and write a design brief. Criterion B, developing ideas, asks for a design specification, a range of feasible designs, a justified choice and accurate planning drawings. Criterion C, creating the solution, asks for a plan with logical steps and time estimates, the solution itself, and documented changes to the plan. Criterion D, evaluating, asks for a testing method, an evaluation of the solution against the specification, improvements, and the impact of the product on the client or target audience.

Read that list and the shape of the problem becomes obvious. A student who begins by building and documents afterwards cannot score above the middle bands anywhere, because the evidence will not exist in the order the criteria require. A specification written after the product is finished is not a specification; it is a description. Testing invented at the end to match the thing that was built does not evaluate anything. Marks are lost at the start of the cycle and only become visible at the end of it.

Abu Dhabi adds some particular texture. Design provision varies substantially between schools in the emirate: some run well-equipped workshops with laser cutters and 3D printers, others teach digital design almost entirely, and newer schools in the Khalifa City and Yas corridors are still building up their facilities. That changes what a student can realistically make, which changes what a sensible design brief looks like. A tutor who pushes a workshop-heavy project at a student with access to a laptop and a printer has set them up to lose criterion C marks on something that was never achievable.

What follows is written around evidence rather than encouragement. What each criterion needs to see on the page. What a weak folder looks like at each stage and what moves it up a band. A twelve-week schedule showing what should exist by when, so a parent can check progress rather than take a view on it. The academic-honesty position on generated images, borrowed research and a parent who is an engineer. And a plain statement of delivery: lessons are one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-design-tutor.programmesIntro: Design appears in three IB programmes with a different evidence requirement at each stage, and the habits built in MYP are what make the Diploma version manageable. The sequence below is worth reading as a progression of documentation demands.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The programme in the URL. Design is assessed against inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating - each out of 8. Students work through the design cycle for each unit and submit a folder of evidence. Schools set their own units, so the context varies widely, but the criteria and the evidence they require do not. The folder is the assessment; the product is one quarter of it.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP Design units run on school-specific contexts, often tied to local themes - sustainable packaging, shading structures, water use, visitor information for a cultural site. That local framing is an advantage for criterion A, because a student can research a real need in the emirate rather than a generic one, and criterion A rewards a need that is explained and justified rather than assumed.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Design Technology at SL or HL continues the same logic with heavier documentation and an externally assessed design project. Students who learned in MYP to write a specification before they build arrive able to do the Diploma version; students who learned to build first spend DP1 unlearning it. The transferable skill is not making - it is evidencing decisions in a form someone else can mark.
programmes.countryNote: Not every Abu Dhabi school that runs MYP Design also runs DP Design Technology, because it needs facilities and a specialist teacher. Families should check at option-choice time rather than assume continuity, and a student intending to continue should keep their strongest MYP folders as a portfolio.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Design thinking in the PYP sits inside transdisciplinary units rather than as a graded subject. There is no criterion marking, and the useful groundwork is habitual: sketching before building, writing down what the thing has to do, and saying afterwards whether it did it. Those three habits are the whole of MYP criteria B and D in embryonic form.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi primary sections run maker spaces and design challenges from Year 4, which is why some MYP 1 cohorts in the emirate arrive already comfortable with an iterative cycle while others meet it for the first time at eleven. That difference shows up in criterion A scores in the first term.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Where a school runs the Career-related Programme, design work can appear inside the career-related study and the reflective project, both of which are portfolio-evidenced rather than examined. The demands are different from Design Technology - more about applied practice and reflection than about a formal design cycle - but the documentation discipline is identical.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is run by very few Abu Dhabi schools, so most readers will not need it. It is listed because parents weighing a design-oriented sixth form sometimes meet it as an option and need to know the evidence model differs.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-design-tutor.subjectsIntro: Design sits next to several MYP subjects that are marked on process evidence in the same way, and a student who gets the habit right in one usually improves in the others. The grid names what each is assessed on so a parent can see whether the problem is Design or documentation generally.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, evaluating - 8 marks each. The characteristic failure is a strong product with a thin folder: no justified need, a specification written retrospectively, and testing invented to match what was built.

subjects.name: Digital design and computing contexts
subjects.description: Where a school runs Design as digital rather than product work, the criteria are unchanged but the evidence looks different - wireframes and iterations replace planning drawings. Students often document digital work less carefully because the files feel like the record. They are not.

subjects.name: Arts - visual and performing
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, responding. The process journal carries the marks here as the folder does in Design, and a student who keeps one well for either subject finds the other considerably easier.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating among the four criteria. The evaluation strand is assessed on almost exactly the logic of Design criterion D: test against a stated expectation, judge honestly, propose a specific improvement.

subjects.name: Mathematics - Standard and Extended
subjects.description: Investigating patterns and communicating are the criteria that overlap with Design. Students lose marks in both subjects for reaching a correct outcome and not evidencing the route to it.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Investigating is marked on a research plan and source evaluation, which is Design criterion A in a different costume. A student weak on criterion A research is usually weak here too, and one fix serves both.

subjects.name: English - Language and Literature
subjects.description: Organising and producing text. A folder is a written document, and students whose English organisation is weak lose Design marks for folders that contain the right thinking in an order a marker cannot follow.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Investigating, planning, taking action, reflecting, evidenced in a process journal and report. It is the design cycle applied to a self-chosen goal, and students with two years of disciplined Design folders find it dramatically less daunting.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Students designing anything structural, mechanical or electrical hit physics they have not met yet. A Design tutor who can handle the underlying mechanics saves a student from a planning drawing that cannot work.

subjects.name: Mathematics for scale and tolerance
subjects.description: Accurate planning drawings need scale, tolerance and unit discipline, and criterion B explicitly rewards accuracy. A surprising share of lost criterion B marks are arithmetic rather than design.

sections.heading: What a marked MYP Design folder actually contains
paragraphs: The folder is the assessment. Everything a marker can award is in it, and everything not in it is unmarkable regardless of how good the product was. The table below sets out, criterion by criterion, the evidence that has to be present, what a weak folder shows instead, and the specific thing that moves it up a band.

Two patterns account for most of the lost marks. The first is assertion in place of justification. A student writes that there is a need for better shading at a bus stop, and never establishes that the need exists - no observation, no data, no user comment, no analysis of what current shading fails to do. Criterion A rewards a need that is explained and justified from research, and a sentence of opinion cannot reach the upper bands however reasonable it sounds.

The second is retrospective documentation. A student builds, then writes the specification, then designs a test that the product obviously passes. Every piece of that evidence is in the folder, so the student believes the work is complete, and every piece of it is worth the lower band because the order has destroyed its function. A specification exists to constrain a design that has not yet been chosen; written afterwards, it constrains nothing.

This is why a folder review is the first session rather than a later one. A tutor reading the folder can say which of those two patterns is present, in which sections, and what specifically to add. It is also why the review produces a written summary: a student who walks into a conversation with their Design teacher holding a page of named gaps has a far better conversation than one who asks how to improve.

sections.heading: Criterion A: the research almost nobody does properly
paragraphs: Criterion A is the cheapest eight marks in the subject and the most commonly thrown away. It asks four things: explain and justify the need for a solution, identify and prioritise primary and secondary research, analyse a range of existing products, and develop a design brief. Each is a discrete piece of evidence, and the folder should show four of them.

Justifying the need is where students start badly. The instinct is to state a problem and move on, because the problem feels self-evident to the person who chose it. Marks come from the evidence that it is a problem for somebody: a photograph of the existing situation, a short survey of three or four users with the responses included, a measurement, a quotation from a source. In an Abu Dhabi context these are easy to come by - shade, heat, water use, visitor wayfinding and sports facilities all generate observable, local, documentable needs, and a local need is more defensible than a global one because the student can actually research it.

Analysing existing products is the second common failure, and the word is analysing. A student describes a product - its material, its colour, its price - and scores in the lower bands. Analysis asks what it does well, what it does badly, for whom, and what that implies for the new design. Two products analysed properly beats six described. The useful discipline is to end every product analysis with a sentence beginning 'this means my design must', because that sentence is what feeds the specification under criterion B.

The design brief is the shortest piece of evidence and the one most often missing entirely. It is a statement of what will be designed, for whom, and within what constraints. A marker reading a folder with no brief has nothing to judge the later work against, and criterion B and D both become harder to score as a result. Written properly it takes a paragraph.
bullets: Evidence the need exists: photographs, a short user survey, a measurement, a cited source
Primary and secondary research identified and prioritised, not just collected
Two existing products analysed properly beats six described superficially
End each product analysis with 'this means my design must...'
A design brief: what, for whom, within what constraints - one paragraph, never omitted

sections.heading: Criterion B: the specification is where the grade is decided
paragraphs: If criterion A is the cheapest marks, criterion B is the most consequential, because the design specification written here is what criterion D will later test against. A weak specification makes a high criterion D score arithmetically impossible, and students never see that connection because the two criteria are assessed months apart.

A specification point is useful only if it can be measured or checked. 'The product must look modern' cannot be tested and is worth nothing later. 'The product must shade a seated adult between 11am and 3pm' can be tested, and a student who writes six points like that has handed themselves a criterion D structure for free. The most efficient single intervention in MYP Design support is rewriting a specification into testable points before the student starts designing.

The rest of criterion B is a range of feasible designs, a justified choice and accurate planning drawings. Feasible is the operative word in a UAE school context: a design requiring a laser cutter in a school without one is not feasible, and the student will lose criterion C marks building something they were never equipped to build. The justification for the chosen design must refer to the specification, not to preference - a student who says they chose design two because it looked best has not justified anything, where a student who says design two meets four specification points against design one's two has.

Planning drawings are marked on accuracy and on whether someone else could make the thing from them. Dimensions, scale, materials and a sense of assembly are what is wanted, not presentation quality. A clear annotated sketch with real measurements outscores a beautiful render with none, which surprises students who have spent a weekend on the render.

sections.heading: Criteria C and D: the plan, the changes, and a test that could fail
paragraphs: Criterion C is the only criterion substantially about making, and even here the marks are split. The student needs a logical plan with steps and realistic time estimates, the solution itself, and - the part that is almost always missing - a record of how the plan changed during making and why. Every real build deviates from its plan. A folder that shows no deviation shows a plan written afterwards, and markers read it that way.

The fix is mechanical: a dated line each working session saying what was done, what went wrong, and what was changed as a result. Three sentences a session. Over a six-week build that produces exactly the evidence criterion C asks for, and it costs the student about four minutes a week. Students resist it because it feels like admin, which is why the arrangement works better when a tutor asks for it weekly than when a teacher asks for it once.

Criterion D is testing and evaluating, and the single diagnostic question is whether the test could have failed. A test designed to pass tells a marker nothing and scores in the lower bands. A test taken from the specification - each measurable point checked, with the result recorded whether or not it is flattering - scores well even when the product underperforms, because the criterion rewards honest evaluation rather than a successful product.

The last strand of criterion D is impact on the client or target audience, which students usually answer with a sentence about how the client liked it. What is wanted is evidence of use or opinion: a user trying the product and saying what happened, a photograph of it in situ, a measurement taken with it in place. In an Abu Dhabi school context this is easier than it sounds, because classmates, siblings and teachers are available clients and three minutes of recorded reaction is legitimate, documentable evidence.

sections.heading: Twelve weeks of evidence, week by week
paragraphs: The most common request from Abu Dhabi parents in this subject is not for better marks but for visibility: a way to tell whether the work is going well while there is still time to act. Design is unusually good for this, because the folder accumulates and each stage has a checkable artefact. The table below sets out what should exist by the end of each week of a typical twelve-week unit, what a tutor marks that week, and the signal that progress is real.

Treat the schedule as a template rather than a timetable. Schools in the emirate run units of different lengths, and a department running two short units a term works to a compressed version of the same sequence. The order never changes, though: research before brief, brief before specification, specification before designs, plan before build, test method before testing. A folder in which that order has broken down is the one reliable early warning sign, and it is visible by about week four.

The parent's version of the check is simpler still and takes two minutes. Weeks one to three: is there evidence the need exists, from more than the student's own opinion? Weeks four to five: does the specification contain points that could be measured? Weeks six to nine: is there a dated record of changes during making? Weeks ten to twelve: does the testing refer back to the specification by point? Four questions, four weeks apart, and a parent who asks them will catch almost every folder problem while it is still cheap to fix.

Where support is running weekly, each session ends by agreeing the next evidence target and the date it is due. That is also what makes it possible to stop: when the folder contains what the criteria require, the block ends. A tutoring arrangement in a documented subject should be able to say what finished looks like, and in Design it can.

sections.heading: Digital or product: matching the brief to what the school has
paragraphs: Design in Abu Dhabi schools is delivered in two broadly different ways, and the difference matters more to a student's grade than anything about their ability. Some departments run equipped workshops - hand tools, a laser cutter, 3D printing, materials budgets - and expect a physical prototype. Others teach Design largely as digital work: app interfaces, websites, information graphics, product visualisation. Newer schools in the emirate often sit between the two while facilities are still being built.

The criteria are identical in both cases, but the evidence looks different. A digital unit's criterion B planning drawings are wireframes and annotated screens with real dimensions and interaction notes. Its criterion C change log records iterations and why each was abandoned. Its criterion D testing is user testing - handing the interface to three people, recording what they failed to find, and measuring against specification points about findability or speed.

Digital students tend to document less, and they lose marks for it. The reason is understandable: the files feel like a record. They are not a record of thinking - a version history shows that something changed, not why, and criterion C asks for the why. A student working digitally needs a change log just as much as one working in a workshop, and arguably more, because the intermediate states are so easy to overwrite.

The practical rule before any brief is written is to establish what the student can actually access, at school and at home. Apartment living on Al Reem Island constrains messy prototyping; a villa in Al Raha Gardens does not. A school in the newer corridors may expect a model rather than a working product. Matching the brief to that reality is a criterion B feasibility judgement, and getting it wrong costs criterion C marks for a build that was never possible.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in Design: generated images, borrowed research and a helpful parent
paragraphs: Design carries three academic-honesty questions that come up constantly in Abu Dhabi households, and all three have clear answers. Submitted work must be the student's own, and a tutor teaches, reviews and gives feedback on it - we do not supply assessed work, and the consequence of misrepresenting someone else's work as a student's own falls on the student.

Generated images are the newest of the three. A model-generated render presented as the student's own planning drawing misrepresents authorship, and it also scores badly on its own terms: criterion B wants dimensions, materials and buildability, which a generated image does not provide. Where a department permits generated imagery for mood or inspiration, it must be labelled as such and cited, exactly like any other source. The safe position is that anything presented as the student's own design work should be drawn by the student.

Borrowed research is the oldest. Criterion A rewards research that has been identified, prioritised and analysed, and every source needs citing - a folder with uncited images, data or product information has an integrity problem as well as a marks problem. The practical habit is to cite as you collect rather than at the end, because reconstructing sources in week eleven is where students take shortcuts they would not take in week two.

The third is the most delicate: a parent who is an engineer, an architect or a designer. That expertise is genuinely useful and entirely legitimate used in one way and damaging used in another. Explaining a principle, asking why a dimension was chosen, pointing out that a joint will fail - all fine, all teaching. Drawing the plan, choosing the specification points or building the prototype is not, and it is visible, because the folder's thinking will not match the student's classwork. The same line applies to a tutor: we comment on the student's drawing, we do not redraw it.
bullets: Work submitted for assessment must be the student's own

sections.heading: What the first session establishes
paragraphs: The first session is a folder review and it is free: one trial lesson per student, booked with no card details, nothing payable before or after, no obligation to continue. The student shares whatever exists - even if that is three pages and a photograph - and the tutor reads it against the four criteria.

What comes back is a written note with three parts. A band judgement for each criterion that currently has evidence, with the reason stated. A list of missing evidence in priority order, because a folder four weeks from submission cannot fix everything and some gaps cost whole bands while others cost a mark. And an honest view of what is achievable in the time remaining, which sometimes means telling a family that the realistic target is a 5 rather than a 7 and that the time is better spent on criterion D than on rebuilding criterion A.

The note is written to be shown to the Design teacher. That matters more in this subject than in most, because the department sets the unit, knows the equipment and marks the folder, and a student arriving with specific named gaps gets a specific answer. Vague requests for feedback get vague feedback, in every school in the world.

Where the student is mid-unit, the ongoing arrangement is one session a week aligned to the class timeline, each ending with the next evidence target and its date. Where no MYP Design specialist is free for the slot a family needs, we say so and offer a different slot, an alternative with the limitation stated plainly, or a referral back when availability opens - rather than putting a generalist in front of a folder they cannot band.

faqs.question: What has to be inside an MYP Design folder for full marks?
faqs.answer: Four blocks of evidence, one per criterion. Criterion A needs a justified need, a research plan, analysis of existing products and a design brief. Criterion B needs a specification with measurable points, a range of feasible designs, a justified choice and accurate planning drawings. Criterion C needs a plan with steps and time estimates, the solution, and a record of changes made during making. Criterion D needs a testing method drawn from the specification, an honest evaluation, specific improvements and evidence of impact on the client. Anything not in the folder cannot be awarded marks, however good the product was.

faqs.question: Why did my child's Design product score well but the grade come back low?
faqs.answer: Because only one of the four criteria is substantially about making. Criterion C carries 8 marks of the 32, and even that is split between the plan, the solution and the documented changes. The other three criteria reward research and justification, specification and planning, and testing and evaluation - all of which live in the folder. A student who built something excellent and documented it afterwards will sit in the middle bands across three criteria, because the evidence exists in the wrong order to do the job the criteria ask of it.

faqs.question: How measurable do the specification points have to be in MYP Design?
faqs.answer: Every point has to be measurable or checkable by somebody else. 'The product must look modern' is worth nothing; 'the product must shade a seated adult between 11am and 3pm' can be tested. This matters twice over, because criterion D later asks for testing against the specification - so a vague specification caps the evaluation marks months before anyone notices the connection. Six testable points is a better specification than fifteen aspirational ones. Rewriting a specification into testable points before the student starts designing is the most efficient intervention in the whole unit.

faqs.question: Does my child need specialist software or a workshop for MYP Design?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on how their school runs the subject, which is why that is the first thing to establish. Some Abu Dhabi departments have equipped workshops and expect a physical prototype; others run Design largely as digital work where the deliverable is an interface or an information graphic. The criteria are identical either way. What matters is feasibility: a design requiring equipment the student cannot access loses criterion C marks for a build that was never possible, so the brief should be written around real access at school and at home.

faqs.question: How does criterion D testing work if there is no real client?
faqs.answer: A client does not have to be external. A classmate, a sibling, a teacher or a parent who genuinely has the need the student identified counts, provided their involvement is documented. The testing itself comes from the specification: take each measurable point and check it, recording the real result. The diagnostic question is whether the test could have failed - a test designed to pass earns lower-band marks. Impact on the client needs evidence of use rather than a sentence about approval: someone using the product, what happened, and what they said about it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor look at a Design folder before my child submits it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and reviewing a draft is exactly what a tutor should do. The boundary is clear: we read the folder, state which band each section sits in, name the evidence that is missing and explain what the criterion is asking for. We do not rewrite sections, redraw planning drawings or supply research. That line protects the student, because work submitted for assessment must be their own and the consequence of misrepresenting someone else's work falls on them. A list of named gaps is also more useful than a corrected version, since the student still has to understand the criterion.

faqs.question: How long does a Design unit run in an Abu Dhabi school?
faqs.answer: Commonly eight to twelve weeks, though departments vary and some run two shorter units in a term. The sequence never changes even when the length does: research, then brief, then specification, then designs, then plan, then build with a change log, then testing against the specification. The useful parental check is four questions spread across the unit - is the need evidenced, are the specification points measurable, is there a dated change log, and does the testing refer to the specification by point. Asked a month apart, those four catch almost every folder problem early.

faqs.question: Is digital design marked differently from product design?
faqs.answer: The criteria are identical; only the evidence looks different. Planning drawings become annotated wireframes with real dimensions and interaction notes. The criterion C change log records iterations and why each was abandoned. Criterion D testing becomes user testing: hand the interface to three people, record what they could not find, and measure against specification points about findability or speed. Digital students tend to document less because the files feel like the record, and they lose marks for it - a version history shows that something changed, not why, and the why is what carries the marks.

faqs.question: Can my child use an AI image generator in their Design work?
faqs.answer: Not as their own design work. A generated render presented as the student's planning drawing misrepresents authorship, and it scores poorly in any case, because criterion B wants dimensions, materials and buildability rather than a picture. Where a department permits generated imagery for mood or inspiration, it must be labelled and cited like any other source - check the department's position before using it at all. The safe rule is that anything presented as the student's own design should be drawn by the student, and anything from a tool should be cited as coming from one.

faqs.question: What should we see after a month of Design support?
faqs.answer: Four specific artefacts, not a feeling. Evidence that the need exists from more than the student's own opinion. Two or three existing products analysed, each ending in a stated design implication. A design brief naming what is being designed, for whom, and within what constraints. And a specification whose points could be checked by somebody else. If those four exist and are dated, the work is on track. If the folder still opens with an asserted problem and three sketches, it is not, and that is worth raising with the department.

faqs.question: Does MYP Design matter for Diploma subject choices?
faqs.answer: It matters as preparation rather than as a prerequisite. Design Technology at SL or HL in the Diploma runs on the same logic with heavier documentation and an externally assessed project, so a student who learned in MYP to specify before building arrives able to do it. Not every Abu Dhabi school that runs MYP Design also offers DP Design Technology, since it needs facilities and a specialist teacher, so check at option-choice time rather than assuming continuity. A student intending to continue should keep their strongest MYP folders as a portfolio.

faqs.question: Who can be the client for an MYP Design project?
faqs.answer: Anyone who genuinely has the need the student identified and whose involvement can be documented - a classmate, a sibling, a teacher, a sports coach, a parent. What matters is that they are real and that the folder evidences them: what they said about the problem, what they said about the specification, what happened when they used the product. A client invented at the end to justify a finished product is visible to a marker and costs marks under both criterion A and criterion D. Abu Dhabi school contexts make this straightforward, because real local needs are easy to find.

faqs.question: How do we evidence the making stage if the work happens at school?
faqs.answer: With a dated log kept during the sessions themselves, which takes about three sentences a time: what was done, what went wrong, what changed as a result. Photographs of intermediate states help, but the log is what criterion C asks for, because the criterion wants documented changes to the plan rather than a smooth account. Students resist it as admin, which is why it works better as a weekly ask than a one-off instruction. A folder showing no deviation from its plan reads to a marker as a plan written after the fact.

faqs.question: Is the Design ePortfolio marked outside the school?
faqs.answer: Where a school registers Design for MYP eAssessment, the portfolio is externally moderated rather than marked solely in-house, and the components a school enters vary. Not every Abu Dhabi school takes that route - many assess Design internally against the same criteria - so confirm with your MYP coordinator which applies to your child before planning around it. Either way the criteria and the required evidence are the same, which is why a folder built properly serves both. The difference is mainly in deadlines, since an externally moderated portfolio has fixed submission dates the school works backwards from.

faqs.question: My child thinks Design is an art subject - does that cause problems?
faqs.answer: It causes a specific and predictable problem: effort goes into presentation and renders, and marks are lost on measurements, justification and testing. Design rewards defensible decisions, and the aesthetic quality of a folder earns very little. A clear annotated sketch with real dimensions outscores a beautiful visualisation with none, which genuinely surprises students who spent a weekend on the visualisation. The useful reframing is that Design is closer to the Sciences in its marking logic than to Arts - state what you expect, test it, and report honestly what happened, including when it did not work.

Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, aligned to where the class has reached, each ending with one evidence target and a date.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-eassessment-preparation.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach MYP subject groups at Year 5 level and mark against the criterion descriptors the student's own school uses. Each profile names the subject groups covered, the on-screen components they prepare, and the ePortfolio work they can give process feedback on.

intro.heading: A Year 5 report tells you the grade; it rarely tells you what moved
paragraphs: Most Abu Dhabi parents arrive at this page holding a Year 5 report card with four criterion levels on it and no idea which of them is fixable before the May session. The report says 5, 4, 5, 3. It does not say that the 3 is the criterion where the student describes when the task asked them to explain, and that this is a question-shape problem rather than a knowledge problem, and that it is the single cheapest level to move. IB MYP eassessment preparation in Abu Dhabi is useful exactly to the extent that it makes that distinction visible, in writing, in the first fortnight.

So this page is built around evidence rather than reassurance. It sets out what a marked on-screen task should look like when it comes back, what the four criterion bands actually reward at levels 1-2, 3-4, 5-6 and 7-8, what the process journal has to contain for an ePortfolio subject, and what the file of dated drafts does for a Personal Project supervisor who has to sign an authenticity declaration. It also sets out the numbers: what MYP-level support costs across the Abu Dhabi market, who publishes those figures, and what the hour does and does not include.

There is a practical reason to be this specific. MYP eAssessment is not a paper examination sat on a laptop. The on-screen components are built around stimulus material the student reads inside the interface, and a student who revises content but never practises the interface loses marks to navigation and clock management rather than to physics or history. The ePortfolio subjects are won in term one, because what is submitted is a record of process compiled over months. By March, an ePortfolio either exists or it does not, and no amount of weekly tutoring conjures one up.

Abu Dhabi adds its own constraints. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools here and publishes its own inspection ratings, so a parent comparing two schools is reading an ADEK judgement rather than a Dubai one. School runs along the Sheikh Zayed and Al Maqta corridors put many Khalifa City and Al Raha students home closer to a quarter to five than four o'clock, which decides whether a weekday session is realistically a five-thirty or an eight o'clock. Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies sit on the timetable alongside the MYP in every private school in the emirate, which is minutes a revision plan has to work around rather than wish away.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video with a shared whiteboard and the student's own work on screen. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; that is a service offered only in India. The reason to prefer the online route here is not cost, it is supply: a Year 5 student who needs a design teacher who has moderated ePortfolios gets that person rather than whoever can reach Al Reef by half past five.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-eassessment-preparation.programmesIntro: Four IB programmes run in Abu Dhabi schools, and a Year 5 family is usually looking at two of them at once: the MYP their child is finishing and the Diploma the same school will offer in Year 12. Here is what each one assesses and what it means in this emirate specifically.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria marked out of 8, with the criterion totals converted to a 1-7 grade using published boundaries. The criteria are named differently in different subject groups, but the mark allocation does not change. Assessment is continuous and internal for MYP 1-4, which is why a Year 5 family often meets external marking for the first time in the eAssessment year and finds the standard unfamiliar.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi has a smaller MYP cohort than Dubai, concentrated in the IB continuum schools on the island and in the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor. That matters for supply: a family needing a Year 5 design or arts specialist is drawing on a thin local pool, and the subject groups least covered by in-emirate tutors are usually design, arts and language acquisition at phase 4 or above.

programmes.name: The eAssessment year
programmes.description: The final MYP year is where on-screen examinations and ePortfolios are externally marked and moderated, and where the Personal Project is externally moderated against its own criteria. Schools choose how far to go: some enter candidates for the full IB MYP Certificate, others for individual course results. The two routes carry different requirements, and a parent should know which one their school has chosen before buying a single hour of support.
programmes.countryNote: Ask the MYP coordinator at your Abu Dhabi school, in writing, which components your child is entered for and on what date each is due. Entry decisions are made by the school, not the family, and the registration window closes months before the session. Several Abu Dhabi schools enter course results in two or three subject groups rather than the full certificate, and the preparation plan is materially different in each case.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Internal assessment carries roughly a fifth to a third of the grade depending on the subject, and the external papers carry the rest. The step up from MYP Year 5 is less about content than about the length of the written answer and the amount of independent reading a Higher Level subject assumes.
programmes.countryNote: Most Abu Dhabi MYP students continue into the Diploma at the same school, which makes Year 5 criterion data genuinely predictive. A student sitting at 4s in the analysis-and-evaluation criterion in a science subject group will meet the same demand again in a Diploma Paper 2 extended response. Fixing the question-shape problem in Year 5 is cheaper than meeting it again in Year 12 with a Higher Level syllabus on top.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary units of inquiry with no external examinations, finishing with the Year 6 exhibition. Reporting is against learning outcomes rather than numerical criteria, so the first time most families see a criterion level out of 8 is in MYP 1. That jump in reporting style, not a jump in difficulty, is what unsettles parents of a Year 7 student in their first MYP term.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi IB continuum schools run PYP through to MYP on one campus, so a Year 5 student may have been in the same building since FS1. That continuity is useful: the school holds years of internal evidence. Ask for it. A portfolio of Year 9 and Year 10 work tells a tutor more in twenty minutes than a diagnostic test does in an hour.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-eassessment-preparation.subjectsIntro: MYP subject groups are assessed against four criteria each, and the criterion that is weak is usually the same one across several subjects. These are the groups we cover at Year 5, with the specific place marks go missing in each.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Marks go on analysing how a text produces its effect, not on summarising what happens in it. The commonest Year 5 pattern is a student who can identify a technique and name it correctly but never links it to the reader's response, which caps the analysing criterion at the 3-4 band however much terminology appears.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Four criteria across listening, reading, speaking and writing, with the phase deciding the standard. Students lose marks by writing at the right level in the wrong register: an informal reply where the task set a formal letter scores badly on the criterion that rewards appropriate conventions, regardless of grammatical accuracy.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: The on-screen component hands the student source material and asks for use of it. Answers that could have been written without opening the source lose the investigating and communicating marks. The fix is mechanical: every paragraph must cite a line, a figure or a date from the stimulus provided.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: The criterion that rewards processing and evaluating is where Year 5 science marks disappear. Students calculate correctly, then stop, where the descriptor asks them to evaluate the method's limitations and suggest an improvement that follows from the data rather than a generic one about repeating the experiment.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: Standard and extended, on-screen examination at Year 5
subjects.description: Two things cost marks: unjustified steps in the criterion that rewards communication, and real-life application questions where the model is set up but never interpreted back into context. Extended mathematics adds proof-style reasoning that standard students have usually never been asked to write out.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: An ePortfolio subject, so the submission is a documented design cycle rather than a product. Marks sit in the inquiring and analysing stage and in the evaluating stage, both of which demand evidence collected months earlier. A beautiful final artefact with no research record scores in the lower bands.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.levels: Visual arts, music, drama; ePortfolio at Year 5
subjects.description: Assessed on the developmental record as much as the outcome: investigation, process, presentation and reflection. The process journal is the evidence, and it cannot be reconstructed in April. Students who photograph and annotate as they work score in bands their finished pieces alone would not reach.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: The criteria reward planning for performance and reflecting on it, which means written and video evidence rather than athletic ability. A strong athlete with no plan, no data and no reflection sits lower than a moderate performer who documented a training cycle properly.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary learning
subjects.description: Assesses whether a student can bring two disciplines together and say what the combination reveals that neither would alone. Answers that run the two subjects in parallel paragraphs without integrating them score in the middle bands at best, which surprises strong single-subject students.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Marked on planning, applying skills and reflecting, with the process journal and the report as the evidence. The product itself carries no marks of its own. Students lose bands by leaving the journal until the end, which makes the reflection generic and the planning criterion impossible to evidence.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-eassessment-preparation.regionsTitle: Where in Abu Dhabi our Year 5 students actually live
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-eassessment-preparation.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi enrolment spreads across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the newer mainland communities, and the practical consequence is the clock. These are the areas Year 5 families contact us from and what the school run does to a weekday session.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense residential towers with island and city-centre schools within a short drive. Students are usually home by a quarter past four, which makes a five o'clock session realistic on a weekday without cutting into homework time.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities feeding the Al Raha and Khalifa City school cluster. The afternoon run along the Sheikh Zayed corridor commonly lands students home closer to half past four, so a half past five or eight o'clock slot works better than a five.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: A short school run by Abu Dhabi standards, with several large international schools inside the corridor. Year 5 families here often take a weekday evening slot plus a longer Saturday morning block during the ePortfolio submission months.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A small, concentrated cohort with the shortest commute in the emirate and the earliest arrival home. Sessions from a quarter to five onwards are straightforward, and Saadiyat families are the most likely to use the earlier slot through term time.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Mushrif
regions.note: Established island neighbourhoods with a mix of British-curriculum and IB schools. Traffic around the corniche in the late afternoon pushes arrivals past four, and five o'clock onwards is the dependable window here.

regions.name: Al Reef, Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Mainland communities where many students travel by school bus, which can mean an arrival after five. Later evening sessions and weekend blocks suit these families, and a two-hour Friday or Saturday slot is common in the run-up to a submission deadline.

regions.name: Yas Island and Al Jubail Island
regions.note: Newer residential areas with short, predictable runs to island schools. Families here frequently book a fixed weekday slot for the whole term because the arrival time barely varies, which is what makes criterion tracking week on week actually comparable.

schoolClusters.city: The island: Al Bateen, Al Mushrif, Al Reem and Al Maryah
schoolClusters.note: The older IB and British-curriculum schools sit here, and the MYP cohorts are small enough that a single subject group may have one teacher. Students we support attend schools in this cluster; naming them is ecosystem context rather than any claim of a relationship.

schoolClusters.city: The Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor
schoolClusters.note: The largest concentration of international enrolment in the emirate and the cluster most of our Year 5 enquiries come from. Design, arts and language acquisition at the higher phases are the subject groups families here most often ask about.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Saadiyat, Yas and the newer mainland communities
schoolClusters.note: Newer campuses with growing secondary cohorts, where a Year 5 year group may be the first to sit eAssessment at that school. Families in this cluster ask more questions about what the components actually look like, because the school has less history to point to.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one on one criterion at a time
modes.description: A fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time, each session targeting the criterion the evidence says is weakest rather than working through a textbook. The student produces a timed task, the tutor marks it against the published descriptors, and both the mark and the descriptor sentence go into the record so the next session starts from a number rather than an impression.

modes.description: Longer sessions built around the on-screen format rather than the content: reading stimulus material inside the interface, moving between tasks, managing the clock across a two-hour component. These run as two-hour blocks at weekends because a timed component cannot be practised in a forty-minute weekday slot after an Abu Dhabi school run.

The student writes every word themselves and the school marks the work; we keep dated copies of what was discussed so the supervisor can see the sequence.

sections.heading: What an on-screen MYP component actually produces as evidence
paragraphs: An MYP on-screen examination is a timed component sat inside a software interface that presents stimulus material alongside the questions. That one structural fact changes what preparation means. A student revising from a textbook is practising recall. A student sitting an on-screen task is being asked to read unfamiliar material under time pressure, work out which criterion a question is testing, and produce a response of the right shape inside a box that does not scroll the way a page does.

The evidence this produces is unusually good, because every task comes back with a criterion level and a reason. After one timed task you can see three separate things: whether the content is known, whether the question shape was recognised, and whether the clock ran out. Those are three different problems with three different fixes, and a report card that says 4 collapses all of them into a single number. This is why the first lesson is spent generating a marked script rather than talking about study habits.

Which subject groups are examined on screen and which are submitted as an ePortfolio is a decision set out in the current MYP assessment arrangements and chosen in part by the school. Confirm it with your child's MYP coordinator in writing before planning anything, because the preparation for a two-hour timed component and the preparation for a portfolio compiled across two terms have almost nothing in common. Getting that wrong in October is the single most expensive planning error available to a Year 5 family.
bullets: A marked script separates missing content from a missed command word
Time-per-question data shows where the clock, not the knowledge, failed
Stimulus-use can be counted: how many paragraphs cite the source
Interface handling improves with practice and is worth real marks

sections.heading: The evidence file: what you should be able to see after four weeks
paragraphs: A month of weekly sessions should leave a file, not a feeling. By the end of week four an Abu Dhabi parent should be able to open a folder and find a dated starting criterion level for each criterion in the target subject group, the descriptor sentence that level came from, at least four marked tasks, and one full-length timed attempt with notes on where the clock ran out. If that file does not exist, there is nothing to judge progress against and the next three months are being bought on trust.

The second thing the file should show is the student marking their own work. A Year 5 student who can mark their own script against the published descriptors and land within one level of the tutor has internalised the standard, and that single skill is worth more in the examination than any individual topic. Disagreement of two or more levels tells you the student does not yet know what the criterion rewards, which is a diagnosable and fixable problem rather than a vague lack of effort.

The table below is the shape of the file we keep, week by week. It is deliberately dull. The point of writing it down is that a plan which is not working becomes visible in week five or six, while there is still time to change the subject group, the criterion or the tutor, rather than in March when the only remaining option is to hope.

sections.heading: Criterion levels one to eight, read as bands rather than as marks
paragraphs: MYP criteria are marked out of 8 and the descriptors come in pairs of bands: 1-2, 3-4, 5-6, 7-8. Treating the number as a score out of eight is the most common parental misreading in Abu Dhabi and elsewhere, because it suggests a 4 is halfway to full marks. It is not. A 4 means the response described where the descriptor at 5-6 asks for explanation with reasoning, and the jump between those two bands is a change in the kind of sentence written, not an increase in the amount of content known.

That reframing is what makes the number useful. Each band has a characteristic missing move, and the missing move is teachable in a known number of sessions. Moving from the 3-4 band to the 5-6 band in a science or humanities subject group is mostly a matter of carrying reasoning through to a judgement and tying every paragraph to the stimulus. Moving from 5-6 to 7-8 is a different order of work: it needs evaluation of limitations and counter-cases offered without prompting, and that depends on reading the student does alone.

The table sets out the four bands, what each descriptor rewards, the move usually missing at that band, and a realistic amount of work to shift one band. The session counts are a planning tool rather than a promise; they come from what the work actually involves at each band, and a student arriving in February with a 3 in two criteria has a materially different plan from one arriving in October.

sections.heading: ePortfolio subjects are judged on the record, and the record is built in term one
paragraphs: In design, arts, physical and health education and language acquisition, the Year 5 submission is an ePortfolio: a compiled record of work with the student's development visible across it. The grade rests on evidence of process. For design that means the inquiring and analysing stage, the research that justified the specification, and an evaluation that tests the outcome against criteria set before it was made. For arts it means the developmental workbook. For physical and health education it means a plan, the data collected while following it, and an honest reflection on what the data showed.

The operational consequence is brutal and worth stating plainly in October rather than March. A process record cannot be assembled retrospectively. A student who photographs and annotates a design iteration in November has evidence; the same student reconstructing that iteration in April has a paragraph of recollection that a moderator will read as exactly that. Every term one session that produces two annotated journal pages is worth more to the final band than a term three session spent polishing the artefact.

What a tutor does here is narrow and it matters that it stays narrow. The tutor reads the journal, asks the questions a moderator would ask, names the stage with no evidence behind it, and sends the student back to collect it. The tutor supplies no text, suggests no wording for the submission and edits nothing. We keep a dated note of each session so the school supervisor can see the sequence of work and confirm it is the student's own.
bullets: Journal pages dated as they are made, not compiled at the end

A dated session record the school supervisor can inspect

sections.heading: The Personal Project, the supervisor's record and the line a tutor stays behind
paragraphs: The Personal Project is externally moderated against criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting, and the product carries no marks of its own. Students and parents find this counter-intuitive: a genuinely impressive outcome with a thin process journal sits in a lower band than a modest outcome documented properly. The report and the journal are the assessed artefacts. A tutor who understands that spends the sessions on the record of thinking rather than on the thing being made.

There is a hard boundary around this component and it protects the student rather than us. The work must be the student's own, the school supervisor signs an authenticity declaration, and a breach is an academic-honesty matter with consequences that reach the certificate. So the support offered is process coaching: planning the stages, choosing a realistic goal, interrogating the reflection, checking that the journal evidences what the criteria ask for. No sentence of the submission comes from a tutor, and nothing is edited into it.

That boundary is also a differentiator in this market. There are operators in the Gulf selling finished coursework, including completed assessed pieces at prices that imply the work is done for the student. Buying one of those is an academic-honesty breach for the student and a malpractice trigger for the school, and no price makes that a sensible purchase. Saying so explicitly on a page like this is deliberate: it is the position a parent should insist on from anyone they pay.

sections.heading: ADEK, the inspection report and what an Abu Dhabi MYP school's grades tell you
paragraphs: In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, private schools are the responsibility of the Department of Education and Knowledge, which the UAE government's own portal describes as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai schools answer to KHDA, Sharjah to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah to its Department of Knowledge, and schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah to the federal Ministry of Education. A parent moving from Dubai to Khalifa City is reading a different regulator's judgements on arrival, not a differently formatted version of the same ones.

What an inspection rating does and does not predict is worth being honest about. A rating describes a school's provision at the time of inspection across a basket of measures. It does not forecast one student's criterion levels in one subject group, and it says nothing about whether the Year 5 design teacher has moderated an ePortfolio before. Parents comparing two Abu Dhabi schools on their published ratings are comparing institutions; parents trying to explain one child's 3 in one criterion need the child's own marked work instead.

The regulator matters to tutoring in a second way. Press reporting of ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, with the MoHRE private tuition work permit required for teachers tutoring outside school hours. Treat that as press-reported and verify it against the current ADEK policy document, but the practical advice holds: do not arrange paid tuition with your child's own class teacher in this emirate.

sections.heading: What MYP-level support costs in the Abu Dhabi market, and who published the figure
paragraphs: Three of the six ranking pages in this market publish no price at all, and two of the others quote United States dollars, which is not the currency an Abu Dhabi family transacts in. So here are the market bands in AED per hour, with the provider that published each figure named and the date they were read. These are market rates, not IB Gram prices. Our own model is a free trial lesson first and a consultation that quotes against the actual subject group, criterion target and number of weeks remaining.

Two things move the number more than anything else at MYP level. The first is whether marked work comes back. An hour of conversation and an hour that returns a criterion-level mark with the descriptor quoted are priced similarly in this market and are not the same product, and the difference is invisible until you ask to see a sample marked script. Ask for one before paying. The second is travel: a tutor driving to Al Reef or Al Shamkha in late afternoon traffic is charging for the drive inside the hourly rate, whether or not the invoice itemises it.

Read the table as a map of what exists rather than as a recommendation. The lower bands are typically university students or generalists; the upper bands are advertised as specialists. Nothing about a price confirms that the person holds a MoHRE private tuition work permit, has marked at Year 5 standard, or has seen an ePortfolio moderated. Those are separate questions, and they are the ones worth asking.

sections.heading: The Abu Dhabi school-run clock and when a Year 5 session can realistically start
paragraphs: A tutoring plan that ignores the commute collapses in week three. Abu Dhabi spreads its international enrolment across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the mainland communities, and bus routes from Al Reef, Al Shamkha and Al Falah can put a Year 5 student through the door after five. A session booked for half past four looks fine on a calendar in October and becomes a weekly argument by November, which is how good plans die.

The honest version is that most Abu Dhabi weekday sessions work at one of two times: shortly after the student is home and fed, or after eight when homework is done. Timed on-screen practice is a different problem again, because a two-hour component cannot be rehearsed in a forty-minute weekday slot. Families who take timed work seriously put it at the weekend and keep the weekday slot for single-criterion work on shorter tasks. Two hours on a Friday or Saturday morning costs a family less in friction than four interrupted weekday evenings, and it produces a comparable script.

Ramadan reorganises all of it. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing, concentration in the late afternoon drops, and schools shorten the day. Planning around it rather than pretending it will not happen is the difference between losing four weeks and losing one. The table below lists the areas our Year 5 families contact us from, the school clusters they typically use, when students are actually home, and the slots that hold up across a full term.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies inside a Year 5 week
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must otherwise adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal rule is why your child's Abu Dhabi school teaches those subjects alongside the MYP rather than instead of it, and why a revision plan built as though the week contains only eight MYP subject groups is already over-committed before it starts.

KHDA's published guidelines for Dubai schools give the clearest public picture of how the requirement is implemented, and they are worth reading even for an Abu Dhabi family because the underlying federal obligation is the same. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, advises that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than twenty-five minutes, requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and prohibits additional or different content without prior Ministry permission.

For planning purposes the arithmetic is simple. Those lessons occupy real timetable minutes, they carry their own assessments and homework, and in Year 5 they land in the same weeks as ePortfolio submissions. A family choosing between a second MYP subject group and Arabic support should make that choice deliberately in October, not discover in February that both were needed. Where Arabic is the pressure point, it is worth asking the school which stream the student sits in before arranging anything, because the content and language of instruction differ between the streams.
