abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Three programmes run in Abu Dhabi IB schools and the Middle Years one is the longest, covering five school years and the whole of adolescence. What a household needs to provide changes completely across that span, which is why the programme matters more than the subject when you are planning the week.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Five years, eight subject groups, and assessment against four published criteria per subject rather than against examinations. The early years are about habits and written structure; the last two bring the Personal Project and, in many schools, the choice of what comes next.
programmes.countryNote: Across an Abu Dhabi week the MYP years divide sharply. An MYP 1 or 2 student needs a short, early, supervised session and will not survive a 19:00 start. An MYP 4 or 5 student can work late and often prefers to, which is why households with children at both ends of the programme cannot run a single shared slot.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary education with no external examinations, evidenced through portfolios, observation and whatever standardised measures a school chooses. The final year carries the Exhibition. Sessions at this age are short, heavily parent-supported and best scheduled immediately after school.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi households often have a PYP child and an MYP child at once, and the instinct is to book one tutor for both. It does not work: the formats, the session lengths and the time of day that works are all different, and the primary child will take the better slot every time.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. External written papers plus an internally marked and externally moderated component in every subject.
programmes.countryNote: The reason to get the household operating system right during the MYP years is that the Diploma will not tolerate a vague one. A sixteen-year-old carrying four internal assessments in the same fortnight needs study habits that were built at thirteen, which is the best available argument for acting in MYP 2 rather than waiting.

programmes.name: The Year 10 alternative
programmes.description: Several Abu Dhabi schools run Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE in Years 10 and 11 in place of MYP 4 and 5. Assessment becomes externally examined, with syllabus codes, tiering and published series dates replacing criterion descriptors.
programmes.countryNote: If your school takes this route, the household rhythm changes in Year 10 as well as the assessment model. Timed paper practice needs a quiet, uninterrupted hour at a desk, which is a different demand on the house than a criterion-marked task a student can build over a fortnight.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: What each subject needs from the house is as practical a question as what it needs from a tutor. The notes below describe the physical and scheduling demand of each MYP subject group, which is the part a parent arranging an evening actually has to solve.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Needs paper, a pencil and a visible working surface. Over video this means a second camera or a phone propped over the page, because a tutor who cannot see the working cannot diagnose anything. Set that up once and it takes ten seconds thereafter.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Mostly discussion and written work, with the investigation criteria requiring the student to talk through a method rather than perform it. Practical work stays at school; what happens in a session is designing, processing data and writing the evaluation.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Needs the text to hand and a quiet enough room for reading aloud, which younger students resist in a shared space. Thirty minutes of close reading with a tutor is worth more than two hours of silent revision at this age.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: The one group where the student must talk continuously, so the room matters most. Headphones with a microphone rather than laptop speakers, and a door that closes. Speaking is the least rehearsed strand in the whole programme precisely because households find it awkward.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Source material, note-taking and structured writing. The practical need is a device the student can type on while still seeing the tutor, which rules out working entirely on a phone. A cheap second screen solves more problems here than an extra hour.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: The assessed work is largely the design folder, not the artefact, so sessions are spent on documentation. That is good news for an online format and bad news for students who assumed the making was the subject.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: The process journal carries most of the assessable thinking. A session can review photographs of work in progress and the written reflection around them; the practical work itself continues at school and at home unsupervised.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Families are regularly surprised that this subject has written components at all. Planning for performance and reflecting on performance are both desk tasks, and they are where a capable athlete loses levels.

subjects.name: Arabic and the federally required subjects
subjects.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies run alongside the licensed curriculum in every UAE private school. Confirm which stream your child sits in before booking anything, because the Arab and non-Arab routes use different material and different languages of instruction.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Supervised inside school and assessed substantially on the process journal. A household's useful contribution is time, a quiet hour and asking what the entry for last week shows. Nobody outside the student may contribute to the work itself.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.regionsTitle: What the Abu Dhabi evening looks like by community
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: The practical constraint on Middle Years tutoring in this emirate is the shape of the evening, and that varies by where you live and which school the bus serves. The notes below are about logistics rather than academics, because logistics is what decides whether a weekly slot survives past October.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long bus routes into the island schools mean a 16:30 arrival is common and a 16:00 start is not realistic for most households here. A 17:30 slot works, and it is one of the reasons families in this community find visiting tutors hard to schedule at all.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Further out, with the longest school commutes in the emirate for island-based schools. Parents here routinely report that the child is too tired to work before eating, which argues for a later start or a weekend morning session.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Larger households, often with three or more school-age children, where the limiting resource is a quiet room rather than money. A set of headphones and a defined session corner does more for outcomes here than a higher hourly rate.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Mixed-curriculum neighbourhood with siblings at different schools on different timetables. Families here usually need two different weekly slots rather than one shared one, and that is cheaper online than with a visiting tutor.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Bandar
regions.note: Apartment living with thin walls, which makes Language Acquisition sessions genuinely awkward. The fix is headphones and a scheduled time when the room is free, not a different subject or a different tutor.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Short commutes to several of the emirate's IB schools, so an earlier session is possible here than almost anywhere else. MYP 5 households dominate, and the Personal Project drives most autumn enquiries.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Activity-heavy weeks, with sport and swimming on multiple evenings. The realistic answer is one fixed academic slot per child plus a weekend morning, rather than trying to fit sessions between commitments.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: High turnover of mid-year arrivals from other school systems. These households need a diagnostic session early rather than a long-term plan, because the first question is which criteria the new system is actually marking.

schoolClusters.city: Island and Saadiyat schools
schoolClusters.note: Short commutes and earlier evenings for families living nearby, longer ones for the mainland communities these schools draw from. Internal assessment calendars here set the rhythm of the term. Students we support attend schools in this cluster; no relationship with any school is implied.

schoolClusters.city: Mainland and Khalifa City schools
schoolClusters.note: Longer bus routes, later arrivals home and a mix of IB and British-curriculum provision in the same streets. This is where the Year 10 route question comes up most, and where the evening window is narrowest.

modes.description: A single 45 or 60-minute session each week at the same time, taken at a table in a shared room rather than in a bedroom. The consistency is the active ingredient at this age: a slot that moves every week is abandoned by November regardless of how good the tutor is.

sections.heading: Home tutoring in Abu Dhabi: what it costs and what the visit adds
paragraphs: A visiting tutor for a Middle Years student in Abu Dhabi costs between roughly AED 180 and AED 500 an hour at published market rates. Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, with home tutors quoted from AED 200 to 500, and monthly in-home packages in this market have been advertised around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour sessions. Online one-to-one rates sit below that range: Unitors publishes IB from AED 200 and IGCSE from AED 150, while EdFlik and Tutopiya publish budget online hours from AED 45 to 65 and AED 33 to 52. Those figures were read in October 2026 and each provider revises its own.

What the premium buys is physical presence, and for a particular kind of student that is worth paying for. A twelve-year-old who will not open a laptop without an adult beside them is better served by a person in the room than by a video call. So is a student with a diagnosed need that requires close physical prompting, and so occasionally is a household where the internet is genuinely unreliable. Those cases are real and this page is not pretending otherwise.

What the premium does not buy is subject match. The pool of tutors willing to drive to Al Shamkha for a 17:30 session with a Year 8 Design student is small, and it shrinks further for Language Acquisition in a specific phase or for a subject group with a documentation-heavy assessment model. A household choosing the visiting route is choosing from whoever is nearby and available, which is a trade most parents have never been invited to see written down. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India, and the reason the online route is worth your attention is this match question rather than the price.

sections.heading: Who is in the room with an eleven to sixteen-year-old
paragraphs: This is the part of the home-tutoring decision that families think about privately and rarely discuss. A visiting tutor is an adult, usually unknown to you at the point of booking, spending an hour alone with your child in your home, often in a bedroom because that is where the desk is. Most tutors are entirely professional and nothing ever goes wrong. The question is not about likelihood; it is about what arrangement you would be comfortable describing to somebody else.

The practical safeguards for a visiting arrangement are worth stating plainly. Sessions in a shared room with the door open rather than in a bedroom. A parent or another adult in the house throughout, not out on an errand. No lifts, no sessions moved to another address, no messaging between tutor and student outside an account the parent can see. Those are not accusations about anybody; they are the conditions under which the arrangement is sound regardless of who the tutor turns out to be.

An online session changes the shape of this rather than removing the question. Nobody enters the house. The session happens on a screen in a room you choose, and for a younger student that room should be a shared one, which also happens to be better for concentration. Communication stays inside a platform rather than on a personal phone. A parent walking past hears the lesson, which is the single most informative form of monitoring available and costs nothing. For a Middle Years student in particular, the shared-table arrangement solves the supervision question and the attention question with one decision.
bullets: Shared room, not a bedroom, for any student under about fifteen

sections.heading: What a parent in the next room can actually tell
paragraphs: You do not need to understand MYP Sciences criteria to judge whether a session is working. Several reliable signals are audible from the next room, and they are more informative than the tutor's own report. The first and strongest is the ratio of voices. In a good session with an eleven to sixteen-year-old, the student talks at least as much as the tutor. A session you can hear as a continuous adult monologue is a lecture, and lectures do not move criterion levels.

The second signal is silence of the right kind. Genuine working silence, lasting a minute or two while a student attempts something, is the sound of the most valuable part of a lesson. If there is never any silence, the tutor is probably doing the thinking and the student is agreeing with it. The third is whether you hear the student asking questions by about week four. A student who has never asked the tutor a question has not yet decided the tutor is useful.

The fourth is what happens in the last five minutes. A session that ends with the student writing something down, reading back a plan, or stating what they will do before next week has closed properly. A session that ends with the tutor summarising while the student packs up has not. None of this requires subject knowledge, all of it is observable from a shared room, and together these four signals will tell you more in a fortnight than a term of written reports.

sections.heading: The Abu Dhabi week, and where the session can actually go
paragraphs: A tutoring plan that ignores the shape of the week fails in October rather than in June. Across this emirate the usable window is narrow: buses into the island schools get mainland families home between 16:00 and 16:45, after which there is food, activities on two or three evenings, and a homework load that increases sharply from MYP 3 onwards. Two of the three things a parent wants to schedule cannot both happen at 17:00.

The pattern that holds is one academic slot per child at a fixed time, protected from everything else, plus a weekend morning for anything longer. Weekend mornings are the most undervalued hours available to Abu Dhabi households: the student is rested, nothing else is scheduled, and a ninety-minute block is possible in a way it never is on a Tuesday. Families who move their heavy work there stop losing sessions to fatigue.

Ramadan reshapes all of this for a month and is worth planning in advance rather than improvising around. School hours shorten, evenings reorganise around Iftar, and the productive window for a teenager often shifts later rather than disappearing. A post-Iftar session works for MYP 4 and 5 students and rarely for MYP 1. Schools also compress assessment into the weeks before and after, so the useful move is to front-load the term, accept a lighter month, and plan the catch-up for afterwards rather than pretending the month will be normal. Agree the reduced schedule with the tutor in advance, in writing, so nobody is improvising a cancellation on the day.

sections.heading: Two children, one tutoring budget
paragraphs: A great many Abu Dhabi households have two or three children in the school system at once, often in different programmes, and a single realistic tutoring budget. The instinct is to split it: half an hour each, or one tutor covering both, or alternating weeks. Two of those three work and one does not.

One tutor covering two children in different MYP years almost never works, and it is the option families try first because it looks efficient. The subjects are different, the criteria are different, the attention span is different and the time of day that suits each child is different. In practice the stronger or louder child takes the session and the other gets homework supervision. If a tutor genuinely holds both subject groups at both year levels, two separate shorter sessions are the honest version of the same purchase.

What does work is sequencing. Put the whole budget on one child for a term, with a defined target criterion and a review date, then move it. A term of focused work that shifts one criterion and builds a habit outlasts a year of thin coverage across two children, and the habit transfers to the subjects you are not paying for. The other thing that works is a fortnightly cycle per child with written tasks in between, which halves the cost per child without halving the assessment opportunities, because the limiting factor in the MYP is how often a criterion is marked rather than how many hours are taught.

sections.heading: Who does what on the Personal Project
paragraphs: In MYP 5 the Personal Project becomes the piece of work most likely to draw a household into trouble, because it happens largely at home, it is assessed substantially on a process journal, and the adults nearby can all see how to improve it. The project is supervised inside the school, and the school's supervisor is the only person with a formal role. Everybody else, including a paid tutor and including you, works within limits that are narrower than they feel.

The allocation is clearest set out as a table, which is below. The short version: the student chooses the goal, writes every entry, makes every decision and produces the outcome. The school supervisor holds the formal check-ins and the criteria. A tutor may ask questions, explain what a criterion rewards, and respond to entries the student has already written. A parent provides time, a quiet hour and the question what does last week's entry show. Nobody outside the student contributes material.

Where a tutor is genuinely useful is scope. Stalled projects usually fail because the goal is too broad to evidence or the success criteria were written so loosely that nothing can be measured against them, and both are fixable by questioning rather than by contributing. Asking a student to say in one sentence how they would know the project had succeeded will often restart it inside a single session. Keep the journal dated and written as things happen; reconstructing a term of entries in the final fortnight produces weak criterion levels and raises exactly the authorship question nobody wants.

sections.heading: The permit, category by category, and how a parent checks it
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit, and most households have never asked about it. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is applied for through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system under the service name Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, which states a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so any amount quoted to you is unsourced and should be treated as such.

The eligible categories are broader than parents expect: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. That last category surprises people, and it is a legitimate route for a sixth-former tutoring a younger child. What matters is that the permit exists for the person you are paying, whatever category they sit in.

There is a separate and important Abu Dhabi rule. ADEK's professional-ethics requirements for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's own code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's school. This has been press-reported and is worth verifying against the current ADEK document, but the direction is clear, and it rules out the first person most families think of. Asking is straightforward: whether they hold the permit, which category it was issued under, and whether they teach at your child's school. An evasive answer to any of the three is an answer.

sections.heading: What home tuition will not fix in MYP 5
paragraphs: Two problems arrive in the final Middle Years year that no amount of tutoring addresses, and it is worth saying so before a household spends a term discovering it. The first is the route decision. Whether your child should take the Diploma or move to IGCSE, and which subjects at which level, is a judgement about the criterion profile and the student's temperament. A tutor can supply evidence for that decision and a reasoned view, and should. They cannot make it, and a tutor who offers a confident answer in week one is guessing.

The second is motivation that has nothing to do with the subject. A fifteen-year-old who does not start work is sometimes missing a skill, often avoiding a specific fear of being wrong, and occasionally simply uninterested in a subject they did not choose. The first of those is a tutoring problem. The other two are not, and an hour a week of paid attention can mask them for a term while the underlying thing stays put. An honest tutor says by week four which of the three they think they are looking at.

The third thing, though families rarely frame it as a problem, is time. A criterion level moves when a task assessing it is next marked, and in some subjects that is twice a term. Tutoring begun in the final weeks of MYP 5 cannot change a report. It can still be worth buying, for the handover into the next programme and for the habits, but the expectation should be set to what the assessment calendar actually permits rather than to what a parent hopes for.

sections.heading: Grade movement, and what a household can honestly claim
paragraphs: The question every parent wants answered is whether this worked. The honest instrument is a comparison between what existed before the tutoring and what exists now, and the only reason it can be answered at all is if somebody wrote down the baseline. That is the single most common failure in private tutoring: three terms of sessions, a vague sense of improvement, and no way to tell whether the child grew up or the teaching worked.

What can honestly be claimed is narrow and still useful. A named criterion level that has moved on a school-marked task. An error pattern that has stopped appearing. A habit that happens without prompting, such as checking work against each descriptor strand before submitting. A piece of written work that is structured where the previous one was not. Each of those is observable, attributable and dated. None of them is a grade promise, and no honest tutor offers one.

What cannot be claimed is a grade, a percentage improvement or a comparison against other students. Nobody can separate the effect of a weekly hour from the effect of a child being six months older, a teacher being different, or a topic happening to suit them. That is not a reason to skip the measurement; it is the reason to measure the specific things instead. Set the review at eight weeks, look at the four artefacts, and make the continue, change or stop decision on what is written down rather than on how the sessions felt.
bullets: Write down the baseline, or nothing can be claimed later
Claim criterion levels, error patterns and habits, never grades
Eight weeks is the honest first review point
Stopping is a legitimate outcome and should be available without friction

process.title: Ask the school first
process.description: Most Abu Dhabi schools run departmental clinics, catch-up sessions or coordinator meetings that are already paid for inside your fees. Ask which exist and which your child is eligible for before paying anybody. It costs an email and occasionally removes the need for tutoring altogether.

process.title: Send the report and the last two marked tasks
process.description: Those three documents name the problem faster than any conversation. Include the task-specific clarifications if your child still has them. A tutor who reads them before the trial lesson can tell you which criterion is costing levels rather than which subject is difficult.

process.title: Set the room before the slot
process.description: Decide where in the house the session happens: a shared table, headphones with a microphone, a phone propped over the page for mathematics. Ten minutes of setup once removes the commonest reason online sessions underperform at this age, and it also keeps the lesson audible to you.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: One lesson at no charge, no card required. Listen from the next room. Judge it on the voice ratio, on whether there was working silence, and on whether your child ends by saying what they will do before next week in their own words.

process.title: Protect one slot and review at eight weeks
process.description: One fixed weekly time per child in Gulf Standard Time, defended against activities, plus a weekend morning for longer work. At week eight, read the session notes and the marked tasks and decide to continue, change the target, change the tutor or stop.

whyPoints.title: The delivery position is stated before you enquire
whyPoints.description: IB Gram runs no home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. You are told that at the top of the page rather than in week three, which is more than most providers in this market put in writing.

whyPoints.title: Rates on this page carry their source

whyPoints.title: Matched on the subject group, not the postcode
whyPoints.description: Your child works with somebody who has taught that MYP subject group, rather than with whoever was willing to drive to Al Shamkha for a 17:30 session. For Design, Language Acquisition phases and the documentation-heavy groups this is the whole difference.

whyPoints.title: Built for a parent to monitor
whyPoints.description: Shared-room sessions, communication inside an account you can see, dated notes written for you rather than for a file, and four audible signals you can judge from the next room without knowing the subject.

whyPoints.description: A tutor asks questions, explains what a criterion rewards and responds to entries the student has already written. No content is contributed by anyone outside the student. The allocation table on this page is the version we work to.

whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education or the IB, and occupies no UAE office. The permit and ethics rules on this page are explained because they affect who you should hire.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel to our villa in Abu Dhabi for MYP lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Middle Years sessions for Abu Dhabi families are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. The practical gain is the match: your child works with somebody who has actually taught that MYP subject group rather than with whoever was willing to make the drive to your community at 17:30 on a Tuesday. The practical cost is that you set up a table, a device and headphones once at the start.

faqs.question: How much does a visiting tutor for a Year 8 student cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market rates put in-home one-to-one tutoring at AED 180 to 350 per hour in Bestimate's 2026 survey, with home tutors quoted between AED 200 and 500, and monthly in-home packages advertised around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour sessions. Online one-to-one sits below that: Unitors publishes IB from AED 200 and IGCSE from AED 150. Those were the published positions in October 2026. Most of the premium covers travel time and the smaller pool of tutors willing to drive, rather than better teaching.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring effective for an eleven-year-old who cannot sit still?
faqs.answer: It can be, with two conditions. Keep the session to 45 minutes rather than an hour, and run it at a table in a shared room where an adult passes through, not in a bedroom. The shared room does more for attention at this age than any software. What genuinely does not work is a long evening session on a laptop in a closed room, in any format. If your child needs an adult physically beside them to begin a task at all, a visiting tutor is the better fit and we would say so.

faqs.question: Where in the house should an online session happen?
faqs.answer: A table in a shared room, with headphones that have a microphone rather than laptop speakers, and for mathematics a second device or phone propped so the tutor can see the written working. Avoid bedrooms for students under about fifteen: it is better for supervision and better for concentration. If the room is noisy, headphones solve more of the problem than moving to a quieter but private space. The setup takes ten minutes once and then ten seconds a week.

faqs.question: Should I sit in on my child's tutoring session?
faqs.answer: For the first session, listen from the next room rather than sitting at the table; most eleven to sixteen-year-olds perform rather than work with a parent beside them. What you learn by listening is more useful anyway: whether your child talks at least half the time, whether there are one or two minutes of genuine working silence, whether they ask the tutor questions by about week four, and whether the session ends with your child stating the plan in their own words rather than the tutor summarising.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take two of my children in different MYP years?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and it is the first thing families try because it looks efficient. Different subjects, different criteria, different attention spans and different workable times of day mean that in practice the louder or stronger child takes the session and the other receives homework supervision. If a tutor genuinely holds both subject groups at both year levels, book two shorter separate sessions. The alternative that does work is sequencing: put the whole budget on one child for a term with a named target, then move it.

faqs.question: What support might our school already provide before we pay for a tutor?
faqs.answer: More than most families use. Abu Dhabi schools commonly run departmental clinics, lunchtime or after-school catch-up sessions, learning-support referrals and coordinator meetings, all inside the fees you already pay. Ask which exist, which your child is eligible for, and what the subject teacher thinks the actual problem is. That last conversation often changes the brief entirely, because a teacher will name a criterion or a habit where a report card only shows a number.

faqs.question: How do we keep sessions going through Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Plan for a lighter month rather than a normal one. School hours shorten, the evening reorganises around Iftar, and for MYP 4 and 5 students a post-Iftar session genuinely works. For MYP 1 to 3 it usually does not, and the honest approach is to front-load the term before, accept reduced output during, and schedule catch-up afterwards. Schools often compress assessment into the weeks either side, so the planning question is which tasks fall where rather than whether to continue.

faqs.question: Can we pause over the summer and restart in September?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for many Middle Years students that is the right decision rather than a compromise. Two things make a pause work. Agree before you stop what the restart point is, so the first September session is not spent rediscovering the problem. And ask for a short handover note covering the target criterion, what moved and what did not. Students who continue through the summer usually do so for a specific reason: a transition into a new programme, a language that decays quickly without use, or a project deadline.

faqs.question: What should I do if my child refuses to work with the tutor?
faqs.answer: Separate the three possible causes before changing anything. A mismatch of personality is real and the fix is a different tutor, which should be available without friction. Avoidance of a subject because being wrong in front of someone is uncomfortable is common at this age, and the fix is a tutor who starts with work the student can do. Genuine disinterest in a subject the student did not choose is not a tutoring problem at all. An honest tutor will tell you which of the three they think it is by about week four.

faqs.question: Is it safe to record my child's online lessons?
faqs.answer: Recording can be useful for revision, and it needs a decision rather than a default. Ask who holds the recording, where it is stored, how long it is kept and how to have it deleted. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs personal data, and a minor's lesson recording is personal data. If a recording is not going to be rewatched, the simpler option is a written session note instead. Keep any recording inside a platform account you can access rather than on a tutor's personal device.

faqs.question: What information should a tutoring provider ask about my child?
faqs.answer: Enough to match a tutor and no more: programme, year, subjects, levels or phases, the target criterion, and the school if you choose to give it. A recent marked task is genuinely useful. What should not be collected without a stated purpose is a photograph, a full academic history, medical detail or anything about siblings. Ask what is collected, why, how long it is kept and how to have it deleted, and expect a privacy link on the page. That is the standard any provider handling a minor's data should meet.

faqs.question: Does a private tutor in Abu Dhabi need a permit, and how do I check?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is obtained through MoHRE's app, website or e-services under Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Ask three questions: whether they hold it, which category it was issued under, and whether they teach at your child's school. ADEK ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of their own enrolled students, so that last answer matters.

faqs.question: How long before a Year 9 report shows any change?
faqs.answer: Longer than most parents expect, because of how the programme is assessed rather than because of the tutoring. A criterion level only moves when the school next marks a task assessing that criterion, which in some subjects happens twice a term. Tutoring started in week three may produce no report change until the following term even where the underlying work is sound. What should change inside a month is the record: tutor-marked tasks, a shrinking error log, and a habit the student runs without prompting.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor is not the right match after two sessions?
faqs.answer: Say so and change, and expect that to be straightforward rather than a negotiation. A mismatch in the first fortnight is common and is nobody's failure: age, subject group and personality all have to line up, and a tutor who is excellent with an MYP 5 student can be wrong for an MYP 1 one. What is worth doing before you switch is writing down what specifically did not work, so the second match is better informed than the first. Bring the same marked tasks to the new tutor.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.closingHeading: Set the room, protect the slot, review at eight weeks
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-home-tutor.closingBody: If you came here looking for a visiting tutor, the numbers and the trade-offs are above and they are honest ones. What we offer instead is one-to-one Middle Years support over live video, matched on the subject group rather than on the drive, with no home visits anywhere in the UAE. Send the latest report, two recent marked tasks and the time of day your child can actually work. Take the free trial lesson and listen from the next room. Then decide at week eight, on what is written down, whether to continue, change the target or stop.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach the individuals and societies subject group: integrated humanities in MYP 1 to 3, and history, geography, economics or business where an Abu Dhabi school runs discrete courses in MYP 4 and 5. Each marks practice work against the published criterion rubric and works from your school's own unit planner.

intro.heading: What individuals and societies assesses, and where the levels actually go
paragraphs: The subject group most often misunderstood by parents in this emirate is individuals and societies, partly because its name tells you nothing and partly because it shares territory with a different, federally required subject. It is the MYP's humanities group. It can draw on history, geography, economics, business management, politics, civics, sociology, psychology, philosophy and anthropology, and in MYP 1 to 3 most Abu Dhabi schools teach it as one integrated course before splitting into named disciplines in MYP 4 and 5.

It is assessed on four criteria, each marked out of eight by your child's own school. Criterion A is knowing and understanding, which rewards using subject terminology in context and demonstrating knowledge through descriptions, explanations and examples. Criterion B is investigating: formulating a clear and focused research question and justifying its relevance, following an action plan, collecting varied and relevant information using research methods, and evaluating the process and the results. Criterion C is communicating: using a style appropriate to the audience and purpose, structuring ideas in the required format, and documenting sources using a recognised convention. Criterion D is thinking critically.

Criterion D is where the subject actually lives and where Abu Dhabi students lose the most. Its strands ask a student to discuss concepts, issues, models and theories, to synthesise information into a valid argument, to analyse and evaluate sources in terms of origin, purpose and value, and to interpret different perspectives and their implications. That is a serious analytical demand for a thirteen-year-old, and almost nobody is explicitly taught it. Students instead write more, more fluently, about what happened, and are puzzled when the level does not move.

So the diagnosis that matters is not whether your child is good at humanities. It is which of four quite different skills is missing. A student with a 7 on criterion A and a 3 on criterion D is knowledgeable and uncritical, and needs source work and argument construction. A student with a 6 on criterion D and a 3 on criterion C has good ideas presented in an unstructured, unreferenced piece, and needs structure and a citation convention. Those two students need opposite terms, and a provider who sells both of them the same package will fail one of them.

Lessons run one to one, live over video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. For a research subject the online format fits the work closely: sources open in a second window, a draft is annotated on a shared screen while the student watches, and a reference list can be built and corrected live rather than described from memory down a telephone line.

Criterion C explicitly includes documenting sources using a recognised convention
Criterion D requires evaluating sources by origin, purpose and value, and interpreting perspectives

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.programmesIntro: Humanities changes shape three times across the IB continuum, and the skills that transfer are not the ones parents expect. Content barely carries over. Research question writing, source evaluation and referencing carry over entirely.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Individuals and societies is one of the eight subject groups. MYP 1 to 3 is usually integrated humanities drawing mainly on history and geography. MYP 4 and 5 may split into named courses such as history, geography, economics or business management. Assessment is on criteria A to D through tasks the school writes, with an optional on-screen examination available in MYP 5.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools licensed by ADEK report these criterion levels to parents, and the humanities ones are the least understood on the report because the criteria names are abstract. ADEK inspects these schools and publishes ratings, which is a useful second reading: a department rated well, with a student scoring low on criterion B, points at a specific research-skills gap rather than at the teaching.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The group becomes named subjects with external papers and an Internal Assessment: history, geography, economics, business management, psychology, global politics. Source evaluation becomes formal and heavily weighted, particularly in history, and the Extended Essay requires an independent research question and a full reference list.
programmes.countryNote: For an Abu Dhabi student intending Diploma history or economics, MYP criterion B and criterion D are the two things worth paying for early. Every Diploma humanities course assumes a student can narrow a question, find varied sources and judge them. Students who arrive without that spend their first Diploma year learning it while also learning content, and the Extended Essay then lands on top of both.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Social studies within transdisciplinary units of inquiry, with no criterion grading. Children ask questions, gather information and present findings, which is the same cycle the MYP later formalises and marks. There is no humanities level to diagnose and therefore nothing for a paid tutor to act on.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi family is in a continuum school, the genuinely useful preparation before MYP 1 is reading non-fiction and talking about who wrote it and why. A child who asks who made a claim is already doing the first part of criterion D. That costs nothing, and we would rather say so than sell humanities tutoring to a ten-year-old.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.subjectsIntro: Individuals and societies is a group rather than a subject, and in MYP 4 and 5 an Abu Dhabi school may run any combination of the courses below. These are the ones families most often ask about, with what each assesses and where the levels go.

subjects.name: Integrated humanities
subjects.description: History and geography content taught together through key concepts. Marks are lost on criterion B, because students are asked to investigate before anyone has taught them to narrow a question, and on criterion C, where sources go undocumented.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Causation, consequence, continuity and change, usually across two or three depth studies chosen by the school. Criterion D carries the weight here: a student must evaluate sources by origin, purpose and value and handle more than one perspective on the same event.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Physical and human geography with a strong data component. Criterion C work includes map and graph conventions, and criterion B often involves primary data collection, which makes fieldwork method and sampling the places levels are won.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Scarcity, markets, intervention and development, taught with diagrams. Students lose levels for describing a diagram instead of using it as an argument, and for writing about an economy in general where a named example was required.

subjects.name: Business management
subjects.description: Organisations, functions, stakeholders and decision-making. Favours students who can structure a report, which is criterion C, and penalises students who present opinion as analysis, which is criterion D.

subjects.name: Civics and global politics
subjects.description: Power, governance, rights and participation. The most perspective-dependent course in the group, and therefore the one where interpreting different perspectives and their implications is most directly assessed.

subjects.name: Psychology and sociology
subjects.description: Behaviour, groups and research methods. These courses expose weak research methodology fastest, because a student has to explain how evidence about people is gathered and what it can and cannot support.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Separately assessed units pairing individuals and societies with another group, often sciences in this emirate. They carry their own criteria and their own grade, and the humanities half is frequently the half students neglect.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: Analysis, organisation, text production and language use. Booked alongside humanities more often than any other subject, because an unstructured argument loses levels on criterion C regardless of how good the thinking behind it is.

subjects.name: Arabic and the federally required subjects
subjects.description: Arabic, Islamic education and social studies are required in UAE private schools alongside the licensed curriculum. They occupy real timetable space and are a separate assessment stream from MYP individuals and societies, which confuses a great many families.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.regionsTitle: Abu Dhabi communities and the humanities requests that come from each
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so none of this concerns a tutor's commute. What differs between communities is what families ask for and when a student can still concentrate on an argument, which is a later hour than most parents assume and an earlier one than most students claim.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: Older island schools with established humanities departments. Requests here are usually criterion D: a student writing fluently and uncritically, whose essays describe events competently and never weigh a source.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Early bus returns support four o'clock sessions, which suits humanities because source work needs a fresh reader. Al Reem requests often concern MYP 4 history depth studies specifically.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Later arrivals push sessions past five. The most common request from this corridor is criterion B: an investigation has been set, the research question is far too broad, and the deadline is ten days away.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Cultural institutions within reach make primary research unusually practical here, and museum-based investigations give a student something to evaluate that is not a web page.

regions.name: Al Zahiyah and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Dense central communities with several schools in short distance. Requests skew to MYP 5 and the Diploma choice between history and economics, where criterion levels are read as a predictor.

regions.note: Longer journeys home mean weekend sessions carry the heavier work. An investigation plan written on a Saturday morning is better than one written at eight on a Tuesday evening.

regions.note: Sustainability and urban planning are visible locally, which makes the geography and economics units land concretely. Criterion D paragraphs from here tend to have real examples in them already.

This is the highest-value purchase in the subject group and the one schools have least time to teach individually.

modes.description: Sessions aimed squarely at criterion D. Unglamorous, quick to move and routinely worth a level on its own.

sections.heading: Individuals and societies is not UAE social studies, and the confusion costs marks
paragraphs: This is the first thing to settle, because a surprising number of Abu Dhabi families are working with the wrong mental model. MYP individuals and societies is an IB subject group, assessed against four IB criteria on tasks your child's school writes. UAE social studies is a separate, federally required subject. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So your child is studying both, in different lessons, assessed in different ways.

In Dubai, the KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidance sets out the detail: separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students for Arabic as a first language, Islamic education and social studies, with combined classes for the two groups prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. It specifies Standard Arabic as the language of instruction for Islamic education for Arab students and Arabic for social studies for Arab students, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs. It also states that using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is prohibited. In Abu Dhabi the licensing and inspection authority is ADEK rather than KHDA, so check the detail of the local requirement with your school, but the federal baseline is the same.

The practical consequence is that a tutor has to ask which subject a piece of homework belongs to before teaching it, and the answer changes everything. A UAE social studies task follows prescribed Ministry content and cannot be supplemented with other material without permission. An MYP individuals and societies task is judged against criteria A to D and can draw on any relevant sources the student can justify. Treating the second like the first produces timid, content-recall writing that scores badly on criterion D. Treating the first like the second produces work that does not match what the Ministry prescribed.

sections.heading: The four criteria in plain humanities language
paragraphs: Criterion A, knowing and understanding, has two strands. The student must use a wide range of subject terminology in context, and demonstrate knowledge and understanding of content and concepts through descriptions, explanations and examples. The failure mode is terminology used as decoration: a word deployed correctly in a sentence that does not require it, with no example attached. Fixing it means insisting that every technical term is followed by an instance.

Criterion B, investigating, has four strands and is the one nobody has time to teach in class. The student must formulate a clear and focused research question and justify its relevance, formulate and follow an action plan, use research methods to collect varied and relevant information, and evaluate the process and results of the investigation. Three of those four are usually absent from student work. The question is too broad, the action plan does not exist as a document, and the process evaluation at the end gets left out entirely because the student thought the essay was the task.

Criterion C, communicating, also has three strands: an appropriate style for the audience and purpose, information structured appropriately for the specified format, and sources documented using a recognised convention. That third strand is a gift, because it is entirely mechanical. A student who picks one citation convention and applies it consistently has secured marks that do not depend on the quality of their thinking at all, and a great many Abu Dhabi students lose those marks by referencing nothing or by mixing three formats in one piece.

Criterion D, thinking critically, is the hard one. Discuss concepts, issues, models and theories. Synthesise information to make a valid argument. Analyse and evaluate a range of sources in terms of origin, purpose and value. Interpret different perspectives and their implications. Each of those is a taught skill, and together they are what separates a humanities student from a well-informed one. The table below gives the typical strand failure per criterion and what moves it.

sections.heading: The research question decides the investigation before it starts
paragraphs: More humanities investigations are lost at the question than anywhere else, and the loss is invisible until the writing stage, by which point it is too late. A student sets out to answer why the First World War happened, or whether globalisation is good, or how tourism affects Abu Dhabi. None of those is answerable in the words available, so the student writes general material, cannot use sources precisely, and ends with a conclusion that does not follow from anything.

A workable MYP research question passes three tests. It can be answered within the word count. It requires the student to weigh something rather than to list. And it specifies a place, a time or a group so that evidence can be found about it. Compare 'how does tourism affect Abu Dhabi' with 'to what extent has visitor growth on Saadiyat Island changed local employment patterns since 2015'. The second is harder to ask and far easier to answer, and it makes criterion D possible because real sources exist about a defined thing.

Justifying relevance is the second strand of criterion B and the one students skip completely. It asks why the question is worth asking, and a sentence will do, provided the sentence says something. 'This is an important topic' is not a justification. 'This matters because the emirate's development plans assume tourism employment will grow, and whether it has is checkable' is. Teaching a student to write that sentence takes one session and it also improves their question, because an unjustifiable question is usually a vague one.

The action plan then becomes straightforward. Dates, the sources to be consulted, the method for recording information, and when the draft will exist. Students resist writing it because it feels like admin, and they lose a criterion B strand for not having it. The habit transfers directly: the Diploma Extended Essay requires exactly this and rewards it far more heavily, so a student who learns it at fourteen arrives at seventeen with the hardest part already routine.

sections.heading: Source evaluation: origin, purpose and value, practised rather than defined
paragraphs: Criterion D asks the student to analyse and evaluate a range of sources in terms of origin, purpose and value. Most students can recite that triplet and cannot use it, because it has been defined for them rather than practised. The result is a paragraph that states who wrote a source and when, and then uses the source as though that statement had no consequences.

Doing it properly means asking what the origin implies about what the source can and cannot tell you. A government publication about a development project knows things nobody outside the project knows, and has a reason to present them favourably. A newspaper report from the week of an event captures reaction accurately and cannot know the outcome. An interview with a participant decades later has perspective and faulty memory. None of those sources is bad. Each is good for something specific and misleading about something else, and saying which is what the criterion rewards.

The method that works in sessions is volume and contrast. Four to six short sources per session, including at least one that is genuinely unreliable, judged out loud and then in writing. Within three or four sessions students stop producing the formulaic origin-purpose-value paragraph and start writing sentences like 'because this figure comes from the operator's own annual report, it is reliable about capacity and not about demand'. That sentence is a level-7 move and it takes practice, not explanation, to produce.

Perspective is the final strand and the one that most changes a piece of writing. Interpreting different perspectives and their implications means the student has to find the serious version of the opposing view rather than a weak version to knock down. For Abu Dhabi students writing about development, migration, labour or environment, the local material is rich and the temptation to write the comfortable answer is strong. A tutor's job is to require the other perspective in every argument, which students resist for about two sessions and then find makes writing easier, because disagreement gives an essay something to do.
