sections.heading: The same text, analysed twice, six weeks apart
paragraphs: The hardest question in writing tuition is whether the student has improved or whether the tutor has. One heavily supported essay answers nothing. The measure that does answer it is a repeat under identical conditions: the same passage, the same time limit, no notes, no help, in week one and again in week six. Both pieces are kept, and the difference between them is the result.

This works because criterion A is a skill rather than a body of knowledge. A student who can analyse the structure of a passage, identify the effect of a writer's choices and justify an opinion with an example and a term can do that on any passage, which means improvement shows up on a repeat rather than on a new topic. It also exposes the opposite case honestly. A student whose second attempt is no stronger has not learned the skill, whatever happened in the sessions in between, and six weeks is early enough to change course.

Choosing the passage matters. It should be something the school is not assessing, long enough to have structure, and unfamiliar at the start. A short non-literary text often works better than an extract from a novel, because it removes the advantage of having read the book. The conditions should be written down: the time limit, whether a dictionary is allowed, whether the student may plan on paper. Parents can run the repeat themselves if they prefer, which some do, and it makes the comparison harder to argue with.

The second part of the record is the draft sequence. For each assessed task, the first draft, the annotated version and the student's rewrite are all kept. Over a term that produces three or four sequences, and the useful pattern is in the first drafts rather than the final ones. If the week-twelve first draft is already doing what the week-two annotated version had to be told to do, the teaching has landed. If the first drafts are identical and only the final versions improve, something else has been happening.

sections.heading: Where analysis stops and retelling begins
paragraphs: The most common reason a well-written essay scores a 4 in this subject is that it describes the text instead of analysing it. The student explains what happens, in order, accurately and fluently, and then states that this is effective. Criterion A asks for something different: analysis of content, context, language, structure, technique and style, and analysis of the effects of the creator's choices on an audience. The word doing the work is choices.

The practical distinction is easy to teach and hard to habituate. Retelling says what is in the text. Analysis says what the writer did and what it does to a reader. 'The narrator describes the room in detail' is retelling. 'The narrator catalogues the room's objects without naming a single person, which delays the reader's sense that anyone lives there' is analysis, because it identifies a choice and names an effect. Students can usually produce the second sentence when asked directly, and revert to the first when writing at length, which is why the fix is repetition on short passages rather than discussion on long ones.

The third strand of criterion A compounds the problem: opinions must be justified using examples, explanations and terminology. Students supply the opinion and omit one of the three, most often the explanation, so the essay becomes a list of quotations with labels attached. Teaching the three-part move, which is claim, evidence, then the explanation of how the evidence supports the claim, is worth a level on its own and takes two or three sessions of deliberately short paragraphs.

The fourth strand asks for evaluation of similarities and differences by connecting features across and within genres and texts. This is where MYP 4 and 5 students lose most heavily, because comparison is treated as two essays stapled together. A comparative paragraph has to move between texts within itself, and the organising idea must be a feature rather than a text. That reorganisation is a criterion B skill as much as a criterion A one, which is why the two are usually taught in the same term.

sections.heading: Criterion B: the essay that has good ideas and no shape
paragraphs: Criterion B, organizing, has three strands: employing organisational structures that serve the context and intention, organising opinions and ideas in a sustained, coherent and logical manner, and using referencing and formatting tools to create a presentation style suitable to the task. It is the criterion that most rewards planning and the one students are most confident they do not need.

The failure is recognisable at a glance. Paragraphs that each contain two or three ideas, in the order the student thought of them. An introduction that announces the topic without stating a position. A conclusion that repeats the introduction in different words. Transitions that signal sequence rather than logic, so the essay moves from one point to the next without any point following from the one before. None of that is a writing-quality problem, which is why students who write attractive sentences are so often surprised by a criterion B level of 3.

The repair is structural and quick, because it happens before the writing. One idea per paragraph, written as a single sentence in a plan. The plan read back in order to check that the sequence argues something rather than lists it. A position stated in the opening. A conclusion that answers rather than restates. Five sessions of planning essays without writing them moves criterion B more than twenty sessions of writing essays without planning them, and students resent it for about two weeks before they notice their drafts taking half the time.

The third strand, referencing and formatting, is the cheap part. Quotations punctuated and attributed consistently, a format that matches what the task asked for, and a presentation style suited to the intention. A student who writes an essay when a speech was set has lost a strand before the content is read. Reading the task sheet for the required form takes thirty seconds and is skipped routinely.

sections.heading: Criterion C: producing text, and the difference deliberate choices make
paragraphs: Criterion C is the one most often misread as a reward for creativity. Its strands ask for texts that demonstrate thought, imagination and sensitivity while reflecting critically on new perspectives arising from personal engagement with the creative process, for stylistic choices in linguistic, literary and visual devices with awareness of their impact on an audience, and for relevant details and examples selected to develop ideas. The operative word again is awareness.

A student who writes a vivid piece without being able to say why they made any of their decisions will score in the middle. A student who can point to a deliberate choice, name the effect intended and explain why it suits the audience will score higher on a piece that reads less impressively. This is counter-intuitive to most families and it is also the most teachable thing in the subject, because it is a habit of annotation rather than a talent. Writing a short reflective note alongside each creative piece, naming three decisions and their intended effects, trains it quickly.

The reflective strand is where Abu Dhabi students have an unusual advantage worth using. Many are writing in a second or third language, in a city where several languages are audible in one afternoon, and that experience produces genuine material about voice, register and audience. A piece that uses code-switching deliberately, and a reflection that explains why, is doing exactly what criterion C asks for. Students often assume their multilingual experience is a disadvantage in an English course; in this criterion it is the opposite, provided the choices are conscious and explained.

sections.heading: Criterion D: the marks a spell-check cannot earn
paragraphs: Criterion D, using language, has five strands and is the most mechanical criterion in the MYP. Appropriate and varied vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression. Writing and speaking in a register and style that serve the context and intention. Correct grammar, syntax and punctuation. Spelling, legible writing and clear pronunciation. Appropriate non-verbal communication in oral work. Nothing on that list requires insight, and all of it requires practice.

Variety is the strand students lose without noticing. A whole essay built from one sentence shape, usually subject-verb-object with a subordinate clause attached, reads competently and scores in the middle. The repair is specific drills: rewriting the same idea five ways, starting sentences with something other than the subject, varying length deliberately so that a short sentence lands after three long ones. Ten minutes a session for a month changes a writer's texture permanently.

Register is the strand that catches strong writers. A formal essay written in the voice of a text message loses marks, and so does a personal reflection written as though it were a legal document. The task sheet implies the register, and students who read only the question and not the form consistently misjudge it. Correctness is the strand parents notice, and it is also the one most improved by reading aloud: a student who reads their own draft out loud will hear a missing clause or a run-on sentence that their eye skipped past four times. That costs nothing and is the single most effective piece of advice in this section.

sections.heading: Oral tasks, recordings and the strands nobody prepares for
paragraphs: Two of criterion D's five strands concern speech: clear pronunciation and appropriate non-verbal communication. Oral tasks appear throughout MYP language and literature, and they are the assessments students prepare for least, partly because there is nothing to hand in and partly because practice feels embarrassing. The consequence is predictable: a student who writes at a 6 speaks at a 4, and the grade carries both.

The fix is recording. A student who records a three-minute response, listens to it once and records it again improves measurably on the second attempt, and the gap between the two is the clearest evidence of progress available in the whole subject. Listening is uncomfortable for the first few attempts and then becomes routine. What they hear is usually not pronunciation but pace, filler words, and sentences that lose their grammar halfway through because the thought changed mid-clause.

Structure matters in speech as much as in writing, and is harder, because there is no page to see. A spoken response needs a stated position in the first fifteen seconds, two or three supporting moves, and a close. Students who plan on paper first and then speak from three words rather than from a script sound both more organised and more natural than students who either improvise or read aloud. Where the school's task involves responding to questions, the rehearsal that helps is someone asking harder questions than the teacher is likely to, which is a thing a tutor can do and a parent generally cannot.

sections.heading: Where a tutor stops and the student starts
paragraphs: In a subject whose raw material is text, the honesty line has to be explicit, because the easiest way to improve an essay is to write part of it. The IB's position is that submitted work must be the student's own, and a tutor who supplies sentences has both broken that and destroyed the only record worth keeping. What a tutor may do is teach analysis, mark practice work against the strands, ask questions about a draft, explain what a criterion rewards and model a technique on a text that is not being assessed.

The question-led method is what makes this workable in practice. Annotating a draft with 'you say this is effective, but effective at doing what, for whom?' teaches the analysis strand without writing it. Annotating with 'this paragraph contains three ideas, which one is it about?' teaches criterion B. The student answers in their own language, in the document, with the tutor watching. The rewrite is theirs, it is in their voice, and they can explain every sentence if their teacher asks.

The same boundary applies to the MYP 5 personal project where writing is involved, and the stakes there are higher because a supervisor signs off on authenticity. A tutor can discuss the inquiry cycle, ask about the process journal and explain what the criteria reward. The report itself must be produced by the student alone. Students should know that a teacher may ask them to talk through any part of a submission on the spot, and that work they genuinely wrote survives that conversation easily while work written for them does not. The consequence of the second falls on the student, not on whoever supplied the text.

sections.heading: Arabic as a first language, and the on-screen examination
paragraphs: Two things specific to this emirate are worth knowing. The first is that language and literature is not only an English course. Where a school offers Arabic as a first language, the same four criteria are applied to Arabic texts and taught in Arabic, and Arab students in UAE private schools are required to take Arabic as a first language alongside the licensed curriculum. In Dubai the KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students for Arabic as a first language, Islamic education and social studies, with combined classes prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and it requires teachers of Arabic and Islamic education to hold the relevant KHDA approval to teach those subjects. Abu Dhabi schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, so confirm the local detail with your school.

This matters for tutoring because families sometimes assume a first-language Arabic problem and an English essay problem are unrelated. They often are not. Criterion B and criterion D transfer across languages almost completely: a student who cannot plan an essay cannot plan one in either language, and a student who writes in one sentence shape does it in both. Fixing structure in one language frequently moves the level in the other, which makes it better value than it looks.

The second is the on-screen examination. Some Abu Dhabi schools enter MYP 5 candidates for the IB's externally set and marked on-screen papers, and language and literature is available among them. Where a school does, preparation shifts to timed analysis of unseen material, typed rather than handwritten, with sources read in a window instead of annotated in a margin. Strong writers on paper sometimes lose structure on screen simply because they cannot see the whole answer at once, and two or three rehearsals in the real format remove most of that penalty. Whether your school enters candidates is a school decision, so ask the coordinator rather than assuming; many excellent MYP schools do not.

process.title: Send one marked essay and the task sheet
process.description: The marked essay shows which strand lost the level; the task sheet names the required form and the criteria assessed. Between them the target is usually identifiable in ten minutes, and it is frequently criterion B, which almost no family predicts.

process.title: Sit the week-one timed analysis
process.description: A short unseen passage, a fixed time limit, no notes and no help, on a text the school is not assessing. It is kept, along with the conditions it was sat under, because this is the piece the week-six repeat gets compared against.

process.title: One session at no charge on real work
process.description: A fifty-minute session with a language and literature specialist at no charge, one per family, no card details taken. It runs on your child's own essay, and it ends with a named target strand rather than general encouragement about writing more.

process.title: Keep every draft, dated
process.description: First draft, annotated version, student rewrite, for each task across the term. The pattern worth reading is in the first drafts: when a later first draft already does what an earlier annotation had to ask for, the teaching has transferred.

process.title: Repeat the analysis at six weeks
process.description: Same passage, same time limit, same conditions. The two pieces side by side are the result, and they settle the question a term of positive sessions cannot. If there is no movement, we say so and look at whether the target, the tutor or the timetable is wrong.

whyPoints.title: A repeat, not a testimonial
whyPoints.description: Progress is measured by the same text analysed twice under identical conditions, six weeks apart, with both pieces kept. It is the one comparison that distinguishes a student who has improved from a tutor who has improved an essay, and it can go against us.

whyPoints.title: First drafts are the evidence
whyPoints.description: Every draft is kept and dated, and the pattern we read is in the first drafts rather than the final ones. If a later first draft already does what an earlier annotation had to ask for, something was learned. If only the final versions improve, something else was happening.

whyPoints.title: Strand-level diagnosis
whyPoints.description: Criterion A at 6 with criterion D at 3 is a different student from the reverse, and both come home with the same grade. Sessions are aimed at one named strand chosen from marked work, because a term spent on all four moves none of them.

whyPoints.title: Questions in the margin, never sentences
whyPoints.description: Drafts are annotated with questions the student answers in their own language, in the document, while the tutor watches. No sentence for a submission is ever supplied, which protects the student and is also the only way the record means anything.

whyPoints.title: Planning before prose
whyPoints.description: Criterion B moves faster from five sessions of planning essays without writing them than from twenty sessions of writing essays without planning them. It is an unpopular recommendation and it is the one that reliably works.

whyPoints.title: Oral work actually rehearsed
whyPoints.description: Two of criterion D's five strands concern speech, and oral tasks are the least prepared assessments in the subject. Recording a response, listening once and recording again produces a measurable improvement in a single session, and we use it rather than discussing it.

faqs.question: What is MYP language and literature marked on?
faqs.answer: Four criteria, each out of eight, applied by your child's own teacher. Criterion A is analysing: content, context, language, structure, technique and style, the effects of the writer's choices, opinions justified with examples and terminology, and comparison across texts. Criterion B is organizing: structure, coherence, referencing and formatting. Criterion C is producing text: thought and imagination, deliberate stylistic choices, relevant detail. Criterion D is using language: varied vocabulary and sentence structures, register, grammar and syntax, spelling and pronunciation. The four combine into the single 1-7 grade on the report, which is where the useful information disappears.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter's essay score a 4 when the writing is lovely?
faqs.answer: Because fluent writing is rewarded by criterion D and the essay is probably failing criterion A. The most common pattern we see in this emirate is a student who describes the text accurately, in order, in attractive prose, and then states that it is effective. Criterion A asks what the writer chose to do and what that does to a reader. A beautifully written retelling scores in the middle however good the sentences are. Ask for the four criterion levels separately rather than the grade, and the gap is usually obvious within a minute.

faqs.question: What is the actual difference between analysing a text and summarising it?
faqs.answer: Summary says what is in the text. Analysis says what the writer did and what it does to a reader. 'The narrator describes the room in detail' is summary. 'The narrator lists the room's objects without naming a single person, which delays the reader's sense that anyone lives there' is analysis, because it identifies a choice and names an effect. Students can produce the second sentence when asked directly and revert to the first when writing at length, so the fix is repetition on short passages rather than more discussion about long ones.

faqs.question: How do we know the tutoring changed the writer and not just one essay?
faqs.answer: By looking at first drafts rather than final ones. One heavily annotated essay proves a tutor can improve an essay. Three successive first drafts across a term, each stronger than the last, prove something about the student. Alongside that, the same unseen passage analysed in week one and again in week six under identical conditions, with no help, is the cleanest single measure available. Both pieces are kept. If the second is no stronger, the arrangement has not worked, and six weeks is early enough to change it.

faqs.question: Can we see a before-and-after of the same analysis?
faqs.answer: That is the design. In week one the student sits a timed analysis of a short unseen passage with no notes and no help, on a text the school is not assessing, and the conditions are written down. In week six the same passage is analysed again under the same conditions. Both pieces stay with you. Some families prefer to run the repeat themselves, which makes the comparison harder to dispute, and we are happy with that. A non-literary passage usually works better than a novel extract, because familiarity cannot flatter the second attempt.

faqs.question: Does grammar and spelling really carry its own criterion?
faqs.answer: Yes. Criterion D, using language, has five strands: varied vocabulary and sentence structures, register and style suited to the task, correct grammar, syntax and punctuation, spelling and legibility, and clear pronunciation with appropriate non-verbal communication in oral work. None of them requires insight and all of them require practice. The strand students lose without noticing is variety: a whole essay built from one sentence shape reads competently and sits in the middle. Rewriting the same idea five ways for ten minutes a session changes a writer's texture within a month.

faqs.question: How are oral tasks assessed in MYP language and literature?
faqs.answer: Through the same four criteria, with two of criterion D's strands specifically about clear pronunciation and appropriate non-verbal communication. Oral tasks are the least rehearsed assessments in the subject, so a student who writes at a 6 frequently speaks at a 4. The method that works is recording: a three-minute response recorded, listened to once and recorded again improves measurably on the second attempt. What students hear is usually pace, filler words and sentences that lose their grammar when the thought changes mid-clause, not pronunciation.

faqs.question: My son barely reads. Will that cap his criterion levels?
faqs.answer: It limits criterion A more than the others, because analysis improves with exposure to how texts are built, and a student who reads little has fewer patterns to recognise. It does not cap him. Criterion B and criterion D are mechanical and move with practice regardless of reading volume. The practical approach is to stop arguing about reading and start with short texts analysed closely: a single page, a newspaper column, a film scene. Students who learn to analyse something short often begin reading on their own afterwards, which is the reverse of the usual advice and works more often.

faqs.question: What is the on-screen language and literature examination like?
faqs.answer: Where a school enters MYP 5 candidates, it is externally set and marked, uses unseen material and is typed under timed conditions. That changes preparation: analysis of unfamiliar text against a clock matters far more than knowing a set text well, and sources are read in a window rather than annotated in a margin. Strong writers on paper sometimes lose structure on screen because they cannot see the whole answer at once. Two or three rehearsals in the real format remove most of the penalty. Whether your school enters candidates at all is a school decision, so ask the coordinator.

faqs.question: How many drafts should a tutor see before a task is submitted?
faqs.answer: Usually two, and the second should need less. A first draft written by the student alone, annotated with questions rather than corrections, then a rewrite that answers those questions. A third round is sometimes useful on a long piece and often a warning sign on a short one, because it suggests the student is editing towards someone else's idea of the essay rather than their own. The number matters less than the direction: each successive first draft across the term should need fewer of the same questions than the last one did.

faqs.question: Where is the line between feedback on a draft and writing it for him?
faqs.answer: Questions are feedback; sentences are not. 'You say this is effective, but effective at doing what, and for whom?' teaches the analysis strand without writing a word of it. 'This paragraph has three ideas in it, which one is it about?' teaches structure. Supplying the sentence that fixes the paragraph teaches nothing and leaves the student unable to defend their own work. The test is simple: could your child explain every sentence in the submitted piece if their teacher asked on the spot? Work they genuinely wrote passes that easily.

faqs.question: Is Arabic as a first language marked against the same criteria?
faqs.answer: Yes. Where a school offers Arabic as a first language, the same four criteria are applied to Arabic texts and taught in Arabic. Arab students in UAE private schools are required to take Arabic as a first language alongside the licensed curriculum, and in Dubai the KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in that subject, with teachers holding the relevant approval to teach it. Abu Dhabi schools are licensed by ADEK, so check the local detail with your school. Structure and language-use problems transfer between languages, so fixing one often moves both.

faqs.question: What is the difference between language and literature and language acquisition?
faqs.answer: Language and literature is for students working in the language at a near-native level, and it assesses literary and textual analysis. Language acquisition is for students learning an additional language, organised into phases and assessed on listening, reading, speaking and writing rather than on analysis of literature. Which course a student takes is a school placement decision based on their proficiency, not a parental choice, and schools reassess placement periodically. A student placed in the wrong one will show it quickly: either drowning in analysis or visibly unchallenged.

faqs.question: How long does it take to move a criterion A level?
faqs.answer: Four to eight sessions for one level, which is slower than parents hope and faster than they fear. Criterion A is a habit rather than a technique: the student has to stop describing and start identifying choices and effects, and that takes repetition on many short texts rather than lengthy explanation on a few long ones. Criterion B moves faster, in three to five sessions, because planning is mechanical. Criterion D's correctness strands can move in two. Anyone offering a level in a fortnight on criterion A is describing a transaction rather than teaching.

faqs.question: Does my child need to memorise literary terminology?
faqs.answer: Some, used rather than recited. Criterion A's third strand requires opinions justified using examples, explanations and terminology, so a student who cannot name a technique will struggle to explain its effect precisely. What is not rewarded is a term deployed as decoration in a sentence that would read the same without it. The useful approach is to learn fewer terms properly, each attached to an example the student found themselves, than to memorise a list. Twelve well-understood terms outperform forty half-known ones in every marked essay we see.

faqs.question: Will a language and literature tutor come to our home in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and visiting tutors are a service we provide only in India. UAE lessons are one to one, live over video, in Gulf Standard Time. For essay work the format matches the task: the draft sits on a shared screen with questions in the margin, the student answers them in the document while the tutor watches, and every version is saved rather than handed back on paper and lost. It also means the tutor is chosen for how well they teach criterion A, not for proximity.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-and-literature.closingHeading: One marked essay, one timed analysis, then decide
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-and-literature.closingBody: Two documents start this properly. Send one marked essay with the teacher's comments and the task sheet it was written for. Then have your child sit a short timed analysis of an unseen passage, with no help, and keep it. A specialist will read all three, name the single strand costing levels, and run one fifty-minute session at no charge on the essay itself. Six weeks later the same passage gets analysed again under the same conditions, and the two pieces side by side will tell you more than any amount of reassurance in between.

intro.heading: Price first, because that is what the search is really asking
paragraphs: Parents looking for an IB MYP mathematics tutor in Abu Dhabi almost always arrive with two questions and ask only one of them. The asked question is whether tutoring will help. The unasked one is what it costs, and most providers in this market answer neither: three of the six pages ranking for these searches publish no price at all, and two of the remaining ones quote United States dollars. So this page starts with dirhams, by year group, with the source of every figure named.

The published spread in the UAE market runs from about AED 33-65 an hour at the budget online end, through AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor working online, to AED 200-450 and above for an IB or IGCSE specialist. Bestimate's 2026 rate work puts a visiting tutor at AED 180-350, with some home tutors advertising up to AED 500 once travel is loaded in, and a named premium provider publishes AED 650. Converted to months, Bestimate's estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are roughly AED 240-600 at the budget tier, AED 600-1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist examination-year work.

What that spread hides is that MYP mathematics is not one product. A Year 7 student consolidating fractions, ratio and the beginnings of algebraic notation is a different purchase from a Year 11 on the extended route preparing for an on-screen examination and deciding whether Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is realistic in two years' time. The first needs patient consolidation and can sit comfortably at the mid band. The second needs someone who has marked criterion B investigations and knows the Diploma doors each route opens, and that person is at the specialist band for a reason.

Three local factors then move the number again. Travel is the largest: a tutor driving from the island to Al Shamkha, Al Samha or Al Falah prices the journey into the hour, and for mathematics that journey buys nothing a shared screen does not already provide. Timing is the second, because demand concentrates before each school's reporting rounds and before the on-screen examination window, and a family buying in those weeks is choosing from a thinner pool. Household structure is the third: two children in different MYP years is a different budget conversation from one, and it is one of the few places in this market where real savings exist.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For MYP mathematics that removes a cost rather than a capability. A shared screen with a writing surface shows working better than a notebook angled across a kitchen table, the session leaves a record, and the slot can move when a school bus from the island arrives late into Khalifa City. What you give up is a car in your driveway. What you gain is the ability to match on criterion B experience rather than on driving distance.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.programmesIntro: MYP mathematics sits in the middle of a ten-year arc, and what a tutoring hour should cost depends heavily on which end of that arc your child is at. The programmes below are described by what the mathematics is being assessed for, since that is what determines who can teach it and what they charge.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics is assessed against four criteria, each scored one to eight, with no percentages on the report. In MYP 4 and 5 the subject splits into standard and extended routes. Optional on-screen examinations are available in the final year. The criterion that distinguishes MYP mathematics from every national curriculum is criterion B, which requires a student to investigate a pattern and justify a general rule rather than apply a taught method.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts are spread between long-established schools on the island and fast-growing ones along the Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor. In newer cohorts a whole year group may be taught by one mathematics teacher, so a student who does not follow that teacher's approach to algebraic proof has nowhere else in the building to go, which is the commonest reason a family here starts paying for maths.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics divides into Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, each at Standard and Higher Level, with a twenty-mark exploration worth about a fifth of the subject grade. Which of those four combinations a student can realistically take is largely decided by what happened in MYP 4 and 5, which is why the extended route matters financially as well as academically.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates applying to engineering and medicine routes at UAE and overseas universities commonly need Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. A student arriving from the MYP standard route into that course is the single most expensive catch-up in the whole sequence, and it is avoidable two years earlier.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics is taught through inquiry with no criterion marking and no examinations. What matters for the years that follow is fluency and number sense: a Year 6 student who is still counting on fingers for multiplication facts will struggle with criterion A in MYP 2, not because the mathematics is hard but because the arithmetic is consuming all the attention.
programmes.countryNote: PYP provision in Abu Dhabi is distributed across community schools in Khalifa City, Al Reef, Al Falah and the newer mainland developments. Tutoring at this stage is cheap because any competent primary teacher can deliver it, and it is the best value in the whole sequence if a gap has already appeared.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: The alternative many Abu Dhabi families meet because a sibling or a previous school used it. IGCSE mathematics is examined by written papers with Core and Extended tiers at Cambridge, and Foundation and Higher tiers at Pearson, with syllabus codes such as 0580 and 4MA1. It rewards procedural fluency far more heavily than MYP criterion B does.
programmes.countryNote: Families moving a child between an IB and a British school mid-secondary in Abu Dhabi usually discover the difference through criterion B or through its absence. Cambridge runs June and November series and Pearson runs May/June and November, and both publish live timetables that should be read directly rather than restated.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.subjectsIntro: The grid below is the MYP mathematics content Abu Dhabi families most often pay to fix, with a note on what each topic actually costs in sessions. Topics are listed by the branch of mathematics rather than by year, because a Year 9 gap in proportional reasoning is a Year 7 topic that nobody closed.

subjects.name: Number: fractions, ratio and proportional reasoning
subjects.description: The most cost-effective thing to fix in the whole programme. A proportional reasoning gap resurfaces in similarity, in rates of change and in every real-life application task, so two or three hours spent here in Year 8 removes a recurring cost for the next four years.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation and notation
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging and the discipline of writing an equals sign that means something. Students lose criterion C marks here for presentation that looks careless but is actually conceptual: a line of working that does not follow from the one above it.

subjects.name: Linear and simultaneous equations
subjects.description: Well taught in most Abu Dhabi schools and rarely the real problem. Where it costs money is in the word-problem translation step, where a student who can solve the equation cannot form it from a described situation, which is criterion D territory.

subjects.name: Quadratics, factorising and the graph
subjects.description: The first topic where the extended route visibly separates from the standard one. Connecting the factorised form to the roots on a sketch is the skill that transfers directly into Diploma mathematics, and it is the one most often taught procedurally and understood shallowly.

subjects.name: Patterns, sequences and general rules
subjects.description: The heart of criterion B and the biggest single source of lost levels in MYP mathematics anywhere. A student has to find a pattern, express it as a general rule, test it, and then justify why it holds. Describing the pattern earns a low level however correct the answer is.

subjects.name: Geometry: angles, similarity and congruence
subjects.description: Reasoning with reasons is what is being assessed, not the final number. Abu Dhabi students who have come from systems that reward the answer alone routinely lose marks for omitting the justification, which is a writing habit rather than a mathematical gap.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and Pythagoras
subjects.description: Standard-route students meet right-angled trigonometry; extended students go into the sine and cosine rules and non-right-angled work. This is one of the two places where a late switch between routes costs real tutoring hours rather than a weekend of reading.

subjects.name: Statistics: representation and measures
subjects.description: Calculating a mean is not the assessment. Choosing an appropriate representation, interpreting a spread and saying what a dataset does not support is. Criterion D tasks lean heavily on this, and it is often the cheapest place to add levels quickly.

subjects.name: Probability, including conditional cases
subjects.description: Tree diagrams and two-way tables are usually fine; conditional reasoning is where extended students stall. A student who cannot say in words what a conditional probability means will not get a usable answer from a formula, however neatly it is recalled.

subjects.name: Functions, gradient and rate of change
subjects.description: The direct bridge into Diploma mathematics. Gradient as a rate, function notation and transformations of graphs are the topics an Analysis and Approaches teacher assumes are already in place, and the ones a standard-route student has met only lightly.

subjects.name: Real-life application tasks
subjects.description: Modelling a situation, choosing a method, and then evaluating how well the model fits reality. Students lose the top band by never questioning their own model. Ten minutes of teaching on the evaluation sentence moves more levels than an hour of extra practice questions.

subjects.name: On-screen examination technique
subjects.description: A distinct skill: reading a scenario on screen, working on paper, and entering answers in a form the interface accepts. Students who have only practised on paper lose time rather than marks, and time is what the paper is short of.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.regionsTitle: What maths tutoring costs across Abu Dhabi, by community
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.regionsIntro: Two things vary by where you live: what a visiting tutor would add for travel, and what time a session can realistically start once school transport is accounted for. Both show up in the bill, one as a rate and one as sessions that get cancelled.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Short journeys keep any travel loading low, so local in-home quotes here sit nearer the published middle of the band. The real constraint is co-curricular load, which pushes a usable maths slot past 7pm and makes a fixed visiting appointment fragile across a term.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment households with siblings sharing space, so the quiet surface matters more than the tutor's location. Families here commonly buy a weekend morning hour for investigation work and a short midweek review, which is cheaper than two evening hours that keep getting moved.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: School buses from the island frequently arrive after 4.30pm, so an advertised 4pm start is not a real option. A visiting tutor priced for a 4pm slot either waits or re-routes, and both end up in the rate. An online 6.30pm slot costs the same every week.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Dense MYP population feeding a small number of schools, which means reporting rounds and examination windows land on many households at once. Booking a term ahead rather than in the fortnight after a report is the single biggest saving available in this community.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Established island neighbourhoods with a mix of curricula on the same street, so sibling sets often span MYP and IGCSE mathematics. That is the household where one tutor covering two children at a combined rate is genuinely cheaper rather than theoretically cheaper.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Newer schools where an entire MYP year group may be taught by one mathematics teacher. Paying for a second explanation of algebraic proof is worth more here than in a school with four maths teachers and a departmental scheme that has settled.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Mainland villa communities with long drives to island schools and several children per household. Travel loading on a visiting tutor is at its highest here, which is where the gap between an online and an in-home rate becomes a monthly figure rather than a detail.

regions.name: Al Shamkha, Al Falah, Al Samha and Al Reef
regions.note: Distance governs everything. The local pool of tutors who have marked MYP criterion B investigations is thin, and the subset who will drive out in the evening is thinner. Matching online removes that constraint entirely and costs the same as it does on the island.

modes.description: The standard product: one hour a week tracking the school's scheme of work, with practice set between sessions. Appropriate where a student is broadly coping but losing levels on specific criteria. sections.heading: What an MYP mathematics hour costs in Abu Dhabi, by year group
paragraphs: No competitor page in this cluster publishes a rate table split by year group, which is strange, because it is the first thing that changes the number. A tutor consolidating Year 7 number work and a tutor preparing an extended Year 11 for an on-screen examination are not interchangeable, and pricing them identically is how families end up either overpaying for a straightforward job or underbuying for a hard one.

The bands below are assembled from published market figures and sorted by what each year group actually needs. Everything in the AED columns belongs to the provider named in the final column, at the date given. None of it is an IB Gram price list; our own figure comes from a consultation after a free first lesson, because quoting before anyone has seen a marked task would be a guess dressed up as a quote.

Read it as a floor and a ceiling rather than a price. The lower end assumes a competent generalist, which is adequate for MYP 1 to 3 consolidation and inadequate for criterion B investigation work in MYP 5. The upper end assumes someone who has marked against the four criteria and can tell you which descriptor band a piece of work currently sits in. For the middle years, paying the upper band is usually unnecessary. For extended mathematics in the final year, paying the lower one usually is. The point of splitting the table by year rather than by provider is that it lets a family place themselves in one row and stop comparing quotes that were never for the same job.

sections.heading: Why the final two years cost more than the first three
paragraphs: The jump is not inflation and it is not seniority for its own sake. Three things change in MYP 4 and 5 and each of them narrows the pool of people who can do the work, which is what actually sets a price in a market this size.

The first is the route split. Standard and extended mathematics diverge in the final two years, and extended content reaches into material that a general secondary tutor may not have taught since their own schooling. The second is criterion B at the top bands. Investigating a pattern and justifying a general rule is a genuine mathematical skill, and a tutor who has only ever taught procedures will coach a student to describe a pattern competently and cap them in the middle of the descriptor. The third is the Diploma shadow: a Year 11 conversation is partly about whether Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is realistic, which needs someone who has taught both.

That is why the specialist band exists and why paying it in Year 7 is usually a waste. A competent primary or lower-secondary mathematics teacher can close a proportional reasoning gap in three hours, and the same gap left until Year 10 will take six hours from someone charging twice as much. The cheapest mathematics tutoring any Abu Dhabi family will ever buy is the hour bought early, which is the opposite of how most households sequence the spend.

sections.heading: The standard or extended decision, and what it costs to take it late
paragraphs: This is the most financially consequential choice in MYP mathematics and it is usually made in a ten-minute conversation at an options evening. Standard and extended are not better and worse versions of the same course; they lead to different doors in the Diploma, and the door that closes is the expensive one to reopen.

In broad terms, a student heading for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level — which engineering, physics, economics and medicine routes at UAE and overseas universities commonly expect — wants the extended route and the algebraic depth it carries. A student heading for Applications and Interpretation, or for Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level, is well served by the standard route and will not be disadvantaged by it. The mistake is not choosing standard. The mistake is choosing standard by default and then discovering in DP1 that the intended degree wants the other course.

The table below sets out what each route covers, the Diploma door it opens, and what a late switch costs in tutoring hours. The figures in the last column are the realistic catch-up load, not a price: multiply by the specialist band from the first table in this page to get a number. The honest summary is that switching up during MYP 5 costs a term of sessions, and discovering the problem in DP1 costs considerably more than that, because the catch-up then competes with Diploma coursework and an Internal Assessment.

sections.heading: Four criteria, and what moving each one actually costs
paragraphs: An MYP mathematics report gives four numbers between one and eight and no percentage anywhere, which is why parents find it hard to know what they are buying. The useful translation is not into percentages. It is into which criterion is low and what kind of teaching moves it, because the four criteria cost very different amounts to shift.

Criterion A, knowing and understanding, is the cheapest to move and the one most tutoring sells itself on: more practice, fewer slips, better recall. Criterion C, communicating, is almost as cheap, because it is largely a set of habits about showing working and labelling a diagram. Criterion D, applying mathematics in real-life contexts, sits in the middle: the content is usually known and the missing piece is a sentence evaluating whether the model fits, which is teachable in a couple of sessions.

Criterion B, investigating patterns, is the expensive one. It asks a student to find a pattern, express a general rule, verify it, and justify why it holds. Practice questions do not move it; being made to justify, repeatedly, by someone who will not accept a description as a justification, does. That is a tutor's time rather than a worksheet, which is exactly why it costs more. If your child's report shows a 7 in A and a 4 in B, you now know both what the problem is and roughly what fixing it will cost. The same arithmetic works in reverse: a report with a low A and a strong B means the mathematics is understood and the arithmetic is leaking, which is the cheapest repair on the whole list.

sections.heading: What a monthly maths budget actually buys at each tier
paragraphs: Hourly rates are how this market quotes and monthly totals are how households budget, so the translation matters. Bestimate's 2026 work gives monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions of roughly AED 240-600 at the budget tier, AED 600-1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. Packages exist too: an AED 799 monthly rate for eight online sessions has been published in this market, as have in-home monthly rates of AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour visits.

The arithmetic on those packages repays a minute's attention. Eight online sessions at AED 799 a month works out at about a hundred dirhams a session, which is below the qualified-tutor band — so either the sessions are short, or shared, or delivered by a less experienced tutor. None of those is dishonest, and for Year 7 consolidation any of them may be fine. For criterion B work in Year 11 it is unlikely to be. The in-home monthly figures work out considerably higher per hour once the two-hour format is accounted for, and roughly a third of that premium is the car.

The pattern worth copying is to buy bounded rather than monthly. A six-session block on one named weakness, costed as a total, with a before-and-after task on the same criterion, tells you whether the money worked. A rolling monthly subscription does not, and it keeps charging whether or not the levels move. Where a monthly arrangement does make sense is a long run of consolidation in the middle years, where there is no single topic to bound.

sections.heading: The costs nobody quotes you
paragraphs: Four expenses sit outside the hourly rate and together they often exceed the difference between two providers' quotes. Naming them is more useful than shaving ten dirhams off an hour.

The first is cancelled sessions. A visiting tutor booked for 4pm in Khalifa City when the island school bus arrives at 4.40pm produces a term of half-length lessons or a term of rescheduling, and most arrangements charge for the slot rather than the minutes. The second is the exam-season surge. Demand concentrates before reporting rounds and before the on-screen examination window, and a family entering the market in those weeks is choosing from whoever has capacity. The third is sibling duplication: two children with two separately booked tutors covering overlapping content at different times is the commonest avoidable cost in Abu Dhabi's larger households.

The fourth is buying the wrong tier. Paying the specialist band for Year 8 number work is overpaying by roughly double; paying the budget band for extended criterion B work in Year 11 buys sessions that will not move the level, which is not a saving at all. The defence against all four is the same: a written plan with a session count, a slot that does not depend on traffic, and a diagnostic before anyone quotes a tier. A fifth cost is worth naming because families rarely see it as a cost at all: the term spent on the wrong criterion. Six sessions of extra practice questions aimed at a student whose weakness is justification rather than accuracy will produce a politely unchanged report, and the money is gone whether or not anyone admits what happened.

sections.heading: Tutoring in the context of an Abu Dhabi school bill
paragraphs: Tutoring is a second education expense sitting on top of a first, and the honest way to present a rate is against that background rather than in isolation. Private school fee regulation in Abu Dhabi sits with ADEK, which the UAE government portal describes as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, and fee increases are a regulated process rather than a school's own decision.

For comparison, the clearest recent published figure anywhere in the UAE comes from Dubai: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in that emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Dubai's own sector numbers for 2024-25 give useful scale: 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen curricula, with International Baccalaureate provision accounting for seven per cent of students. Those are Dubai figures and should not be read as Abu Dhabi policy; they are offered as the published context that exists.

Set against a full school fee, a bounded six-session block to fix proportional reasoning is a small number. Set against the same fee, a rolling specialist subscription from September to June is not. That is the actual budgeting question, and it is better answered by deciding what you are trying to fix than by comparing hourly rates between providers whose products are not the same thing.

sections.heading: Online, in-home and group maths lessons compared on price and on outcome
paragraphs: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Rather than leave that as a limitation, here is the comparison on the merits, including the one column where a group class genuinely wins.

For mathematics specifically the online case is unusually strong, because the whole subject is a shared writing surface. A tutor and a student working on the same digital page see each other's working line by line, the session leaves a record a parent can look at, and a graph can be plotted, transformed and re-plotted faster than it can be drawn. None of that is a compromise against a notebook on a kitchen table. What online removes is the travel loading in the rate — the gap between Bestimate's AED 180-350 in-home band and the AED 150-300 qualified online band is substantially the car — and the rigidity of a slot built around a driving route.

Group classes are cheaper per student and that is a real advantage for one specific job: drilling procedural fluency in criterion A content, where watching other students make mistakes is useful. They are close to useless for criterion B, because justification has to be prised out of one student at a time and a group lets the quiet ones hide. So the rational purchase for many Abu Dhabi families is a group class for consolidation and a small number of one-to-one hours for investigation work, rather than one or the other.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies: the other hours in the week
paragraphs: A maths budget in an Abu Dhabi household rarely exists alone, because mandatory UAE subjects run alongside the international curriculum and they take time out of the same week. The federal position, as the UAE government portal states it, is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind every emirate's requirement.

The most detailed published statement of how it works in practice comes from Dubai's regulator rather than Abu Dhabi's. KHDA's mandatory subjects guidance requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with implementation from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. It requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. It also calculates instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit and advises that any mandatory subject lesson should last at least twenty-five minutes.

Those are Dubai requirements and should not be reported as ADEK's. The reason they matter to a maths budget in Abu Dhabi is arithmetic: mandatory subjects occupy timetable hours, and a student who needs support in Arabic as well as mathematics has two expenses competing for the same evenings. Deciding which one to fund first is a real decision, and the honest answer is usually the one where a bounded block of hours produces a measurable change, which for most families is mathematics.

sections.heading: Verifying who you pay, in Abu Dhabi specifically
paragraphs: Two checks cost nothing and both are worth making before money moves. The first is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which introduced private tuition work permits. The UAE government portal states the permit is granted free of charge for two years, and lists eligible applicants as including teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a MoHRE permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so any specific figure quoted to you is unverified and should be ignored. MoHRE's own service page is 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing'.

The second is the conflict-of-interest check. Press reporting of ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with teachers tutoring outside school hours required to hold the MoHRE permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That should be verified against ADEK's current policy document before being relied upon as exact wording. The practical reading is clear: your child's own mathematics teacher, who also assigns the criterion levels on the report, is the wrong person to pay.

For completeness: IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge or Pearson, and operates no premises in the UAE. An operation with premises and staff in Dubai would require a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, a specific authorisation we do not hold and do not claim. What is on offer here is one-to-one teaching time delivered online, priced after a diagnostic.

process.title: Send the report, not a description
process.description: Four criterion numbers between one and eight tell a tutor more than a paragraph about how your child feels about maths. Add the year group and whether they are on the standard or extended route, and a sensible tier and hour estimate can be given before any money is discussed.

process.title: A free first lesson that reads the criteria
process.description: The first session sets a short diagnostic task covering all four criteria, marks it, and returns a written read: which criterion is holding the total down and what kind of teaching moves it. If the answer is that your child needs three hours rather than a term, you will be told that.

process.title: Pick a shape and get a total
process.description: A bounded topic block, a weekly consolidation hour, a sibling arrangement or a pre-examination intensive are different products at different prices. You get a session count and a total in writing before starting, along with the criterion the block is aimed at.

process.title: Re-run the same criterion task at the review point
process.description: Six weeks in, the same style of task is set again and marked against the same criterion. That is the measurement, not a sense that sessions are going well. A before-and-after on one criterion is the only honest way to tell whether the money worked.

process.title: Stop, or change tier
process.description: If the criterion has moved, the block ends. If it has not, the fix is usually a different tutor or a different criterion rather than more hours at the same rate. Rematching carries no penalty, and we would rather make that change than renew a block that is not working.

whyPoints.title: The rates are published, by year group
whyPoints.description: Hourly and monthly bands split by MYP year and by route, with every figure attributed to whoever published it. Three of the six pages ranking for these searches publish no price at all. An Abu Dhabi household budgets in dirhams per month and should be shown dirhams per month.

whyPoints.title: We cost by criterion, not by hour
whyPoints.description: A low criterion A is two to four hours of work; a low criterion B is eight to twelve with a specialist. Telling you which one your child's report shows, and what each costs, is more useful than any rate comparison and it is the thing nothing else on this search does.

whyPoints.title: No travel loading on a shared screen
whyPoints.description: Mathematics is a writing surface, and a digital one works better than a notebook turned sideways. Lessons are online, so a family in Al Shamkha pays the same as a family on Saadiyat Island and gets the same choice of tutor.

whyPoints.title: Bounded blocks with a stopping condition
whyPoints.description: A six-session block aimed at one named weakness, with a before-and-after task on the same criterion and a total agreed in advance. A rolling monthly arrangement keeps charging whether or not the levels move; a bounded block cannot.

whyPoints.title: The delivery model is stated, not implied
whyPoints.description: One-to-one lessons online on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram runs no home visits anywhere in the UAE and holds no accreditation from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Saying so plainly on a page that targets a local search is the point.

whyPoints.title: Honest about where group classes win
whyPoints.description: A small group is cheaper per student and better for drilling procedural fluency. It is close to useless for criterion B investigation work. We will tell you to use both rather than pretend one-to-one is the answer to everything your child needs.

faqs.question: What does an MYP mathematics tutor charge per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: It depends on the year group more than on anything else. Published UAE market figures put a qualified online subject tutor at AED 150-300 an hour and an IB or IGCSE specialist at AED 200-450 or more, with a budget online tier from around AED 33-65 and a named premium provider publishing AED 650. A visiting tutor runs AED 180-350 per Bestimate's 2026 work, with some advertising to AED 500 once travel is included. For MYP 1 to 3 consolidation the lower-middle of that range is adequate. For extended mathematics in Year 11 it is not.

faqs.question: Does MYP maths tutoring cost less for a Year 7 than for a Year 11?
faqs.answer: It should, and if a provider quotes you the same rate for both, ask what changes. A Year 7 hour consolidating number fluency and early algebra can be delivered well by a competent lower-secondary mathematics teacher. A Year 11 extended hour needs someone who has marked criterion B investigations against the descriptors and who can also advise on whether Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is realistic. That is a smaller pool and a higher band. The practical consequence is that the cheapest maths tutoring a family ever buys is the hour bought in Year 8 rather than Year 10.

faqs.question: Is a monthly package better value than paying by the hour for maths?
faqs.answer: Do the division before deciding. An AED 799 monthly rate for eight online sessions, which has been published in this market, works out at roughly a hundred dirhams a session — below the qualified-tutor band, so expect shorter sessions, a shared format or a less experienced tutor. For Year 7 consolidation that may be perfectly fine. For criterion B work it is unlikely to be. In-home monthly rates of AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour visits price higher per hour, and a meaningful share of that is travel. A bounded block with a fixed total usually beats both.

faqs.question: My daughter is at a 5 in maths. What does moving her to a 7 actually cost?
faqs.answer: That depends entirely on which of the four criteria is holding the total down, which is why the report matters more than the grade. If she is strong on criterion A and weak on criterion B, the work is investigation and justification: eight to twelve hours with someone who refuses to accept a described pattern as a justified rule. If the weakness is criterion C, it is presentation habits and takes two or three hours. A profile with one low criterion and three strong ones is the cheapest to fix. An evenly low profile is slower and more honest about needing a term.

faqs.question: Should we pay for extended mathematics support or keep our son on the standard route?
faqs.answer: Decide by the degree, not by the current grade. If he is heading for engineering, physics, economics or medicine, those routes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and the extended route is the comfortable path into it. If he is heading elsewhere, the standard route is a perfectly respectable choice and he will not be disadvantaged. The expensive outcome is choosing standard by default and discovering in DP1 that the intended degree wanted the other course. That conversation belongs at the end of MYP 3, not at the end of MYP 5.

faqs.question: What does it cost to switch from standard to extended mathematics in MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Realistically twenty to thirty hours of catch-up, concentrated on algebraic manipulation, non-right-angled trigonometry and functions as rates of change. At the specialist band of AED 200-450 an hour that is a substantial number, which is precisely why the decision belongs two years earlier. Switching during MYP 4 is far cheaper because the content gap is smaller and there is a year to absorb it. Discovering the problem in DP1 is the worst case, because the catch-up then competes with six Diploma subjects and an Internal Assessment for the same evenings.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both of my children if they are in different MYP years?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, and it is the most reliable way to reduce a tutoring bill in Abu Dhabi's larger households without reducing the teaching. The arrangement is consecutive one-to-one hours rather than a shared lesson, with one tutor holding both children's assessment calendars, and a combined rate agreed at the consultation. The saving comes from overlapping preparation and a contiguous slot. It stops working when the age gap is wide or the routes differ: a Year 7 and an extended Year 11 need genuinely different specialists, and pairing them saves money by lowering quality.

faqs.question: Is a small group maths class cheaper enough to be worth it?
faqs.answer: For some of the work, yes. A group of two to four is cheaper per student and genuinely good for drilling criterion A procedural fluency, partly because watching other students make mistakes is instructive. It is close to useless for criterion B, where justification has to be prised out of one student at a time and a group gives the quiet ones somewhere to hide. The rational purchase for many families is both: a group class for fluency and a handful of one-to-one hours for investigation technique. Buying only one of the two is the common mistake.

faqs.question: Does the price go up closer to the on-screen examinations?
faqs.answer: Effective prices do, because availability falls. Demand across Abu Dhabi concentrates in the weeks after reporting rounds and before the examination window, and because the large cohorts in the Al Raha and Khalifa City corridor run on similar calendars those spikes arrive together. A family entering the market then is choosing from whoever has capacity rather than from the right specialist. The same support booked a term earlier costs less in hours as well as in rate, because there is time for the student to practise between sessions rather than cram alongside them.

faqs.question: Why is there no in-home maths tutor option in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Because IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and every country page on the site says so. For mathematics that costs you very little. A shared digital writing surface shows working line by line better than a notebook turned sideways, the session leaves a record, and graphs can be drawn and transformed in seconds. What it removes is the travel loading inside the in-home rate and the rigidity of a slot built around a driving route through Khalifa City at half past four.

faqs.question: Do MYP criterion levels convert into a percentage I can track at home?
faqs.answer: Not reliably, and trying to is a common source of confusion. Each of the four criteria is scored one to eight, giving a maximum total of thirty-two, which the school then maps to a subject grade of one to seven using published boundaries. The boundaries are not a simple percentage conversion and a single criterion can hold an otherwise strong profile down. What you can track at home is far more useful: the individual criterion numbers across successive reports. A 4 moving to a 6 in criterion B is a real, visible change in a way that a percentage never is.

faqs.question: What share of a household education budget should maths tutoring take?
faqs.answer: Less than most families end up spending, and the saving comes from shape rather than rate. A bounded six-session block aimed at one named criterion is a small figure next to a school fee. A rolling specialist subscription from September to June is not, and it will keep charging whether the levels move or not. The useful discipline is to name the weakness, buy a block to fix it, re-test the same criterion, and then stop. If a provider cannot tell you what the block is aimed at, you are buying hours rather than a result.

faqs.question: Does my child need Arabic support alongside maths, and what does that add?
faqs.answer: Possibly, because mandatory UAE subjects run alongside the international curriculum. The federal position is that private schools must cover Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies whatever curriculum they are licensed for. The most detailed published guidance is Dubai's: KHDA requires those subjects in all its private schools, with separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies. Verify Abu Dhabi's requirements with ADEK and your school. Budget-wise the two compete for the same evenings, and the one to fund first is the one where a bounded block produces a measurable change.

faqs.question: Is my child's own maths teacher at an Abu Dhabi school allowed to tutor her for a fee?
faqs.answer: Treat that as a problem rather than a shortcut. Press reporting of ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the permit-holder's own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document. Beyond compliance there is an obvious conflict: the person assigning the criterion levels on the report should not also be paid to raise them.

faqs.question: How do I check a maths tutor is permitted to work in the UAE before paying?
faqs.answer: Ask directly, and ask early. Private tutoring here is regulated under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which introduced private tuition work permits. The government portal states the permit is granted free of charge for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. Tutoring without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, although no fine schedule is published, so disregard any figure quoted to you. MoHRE's service page, 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', is the official route.

faqs.question: Six weeks of sessions and the maths grade has not moved. Do we stop paying?
faqs.answer: Stop paying for the same thing, yes. Before stopping altogether, check two things. First, has the criterion the block was aimed at moved, even if the overall grade has not? A 4 to a 6 in criterion B with a flat subject grade is progress that a single report hides. Second, was the block aimed at the right criterion at all, which is why a before-and-after task on the same criterion matters. If the targeted criterion is genuinely flat after six sessions, the answer is a different tutor or a different tier, not more hours at the same rate.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.closingHeading: Send the four numbers and get a price
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.closingBody: If you are pricing an IB MYP mathematics tutor in Abu Dhabi, the quickest route to a real answer is to send the four criterion numbers from your child's last report, the year group, and whether they are on the standard or extended route. The first lesson is free and ends in a written read of which criterion is holding the total down and what moving it will cost in hours. Where three hours will do it, you will be told three hours. Lessons are one-to-one and online on Gulf Standard Time, for families from Saadiyat Island and Al Reem to Khalifa City, Al Raha and Al Shamkha, with no travel priced into the rate.

intro.heading: Why nobody publishes an MYP price, and what the numbers are
paragraphs: Three of the six best-ranked tutoring pages for this market publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, a currency no Abu Dhabi family transacts in. One agency's own list of frequently asked questions includes the question of what tutoring costs and then declines to answer it. The effect is that a parent trying to budget for Middle Years support has to collect quotes one at a time and has no way to tell whether a number is normal. This page starts with the numbers instead.

The published positions, read in October 2026, run as follows. At the budget end of online tutoring, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 per hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65. In the qualified-teacher band, Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. TutorChase quotes around AED 270. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 survey puts IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, and home tutors at AED 200 to 500. BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor. Monthly packages seen in this market include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work.

Those are market rates published by other providers, not an IB Gram price list, and they are quoted here because a parent cannot make a sensible decision without them. What IB Gram charges comes out of a consultation, because the honest answer depends on the subject group, the year, the number of sessions and whether the work is weekly or a short block. The free trial lesson comes first either way, one per student, with no card required.

The more useful part of the page is what moves a Middle Years number up or down, because it is not the same set of variables that moves a Diploma one. An MYP hour is generally priced below a Diploma hour, and for good reasons: the content is less specialised and the tutor pool is wider. There are three specific cases where that logic reverses in Abu Dhabi, and they are the ones where families get a quote they were not expecting. Language Acquisition in a particular phase, Design with its documentation-heavy assessment model, and the final-year Personal Project all draw on a much narrower pool than MYP Mathematics does.

Finally, a unit of measurement that is more honest than AED per hour. The Middle Years Programme is marked in criterion levels, four per subject, each from 0 to 8, and a level only moves when the school next marks a task assessing that criterion. That means the number of assessment opportunities in a term, not the number of hours bought, is what caps how fast progress can appear. Pricing a term of tutoring against the criterion you are trying to shift tells you whether the spend is proportionate. Pricing it against hours tells you almost nothing.
