process.title: Send a marked investigation and the four levels
process.description: One marked science task plus the four criterion numbers from the last report is enough to say which strand is losing the marks. A description of how science is going is not, because it reports how the lessons feel rather than what the marking says.

process.title: A free first lesson that produces a baseline
process.description: The first session sets a short task touching all four criteria, marks it against the descriptors, and returns four levels with the losing strand named on each. That baseline is what makes week eight measurable. A first session spent teaching feels better and costs the ability to measure anything.

process.title: Target the lowest criterion, which is usually C
process.description: The grade comes from the total, so the lowest criterion is holding it down. In Abu Dhabi that is most often processing and evaluating. Sessions are aimed at it explicitly, using data from your child's own school practicals rather than worked examples, and the target is written down.

process.title: Work between sessions, dated and kept
process.description: Attempts made alone between sessions are where the learning consolidates, and unsuccessful attempts are more useful than none. They go in the folder with dates on them. A student who produces nothing between sessions is buying a weekly demonstration, and we will say so rather than continue quietly.

process.title: Re-mark a comparable task at week eight
process.description: A fresh task of similar demand, marked on the same criterion and strand, placed beside the week-one baseline. That comparison is the measurement. Where the level has not moved, the diagnosis was wrong and the response is a change of target or tutor, not more hours.

whyPoints.title: The evidence comes back in writing
whyPoints.description: A marked task after every session with the losing criterion and strand named, plus a dated note of what moved. A parent with no scientific training can check that in five minutes, which is the whole point of reporting it that way rather than describing the sessions.

whyPoints.title: Criterion C taught on your child's own data
whyPoints.description: The marks in MYP sciences are mostly lost after the experiment, at a desk. Sessions work on the actual dataset from the actual school practical, because processing a worked example teaches the example and processing their own data teaches the skill.

whyPoints.title: A baseline before any teaching
whyPoints.description: The first session diagnoses rather than teaches, so that week eight has something to be compared against. It is a less satisfying first hour and it is the difference between measuring progress and having an opinion about it.

whyPoints.title: Criterion D is not ignored
whyPoints.description: Reflecting on the impacts of science carries the same weight as the other three criteria and is taught almost nowhere. Two or three sessions on structure and source use, using local Abu Dhabi material, is usually the cheapest level on the whole report.

whyPoints.description: Practical work belongs at school, with the equipment and the supervision. We will not pretend to substitute for it, and where a school's provision is thin the advice is to raise it with the school rather than improvise with kitchen equipment that teaches penalised habits.

faqs.question: What should a marked MYP science task tell me as a parent?
faqs.answer: Three things, and none of them requires you to understand the science. It should name the criterion and the strand inside it where the level was lost, so the comment is tied to a descriptor rather than being a general remark. It should separate a content error from a technique error, because those need opposite responses. And it should leave you able to say in one sentence what the next task must do differently. If it does not, ask for the strand to be named. That is an entirely reasonable request and any tutor marking to the descriptors can answer it.

faqs.question: Which of the four sciences criteria is my child most likely losing levels on?
faqs.answer: Criterion C, processing and evaluating, by a wide margin, and especially its evaluation strand. Students collect good data from a well-run school practical and then lose marks at four separate points afterwards: a table without units in the headers, a graph with the independent variable on the wrong axis or joined dot-to-dot, a conclusion that restates the hypothesis instead of answering the question with the data, and an evaluation listing generic weaknesses rather than one specific flaw in this method. Every one of those is a convention rather than a concept, which makes criterion C both the largest loss and the fastest repair.

faqs.question: He scores 7 for knowing and understanding and 4 for processing. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It means his content knowledge is strong and nobody has taught him the conventions of a scientific write-up, which is an extremely common and very fixable profile. It also means revision is the wrong purchase: he already knows the science, so more revision will produce a long evening and an unchanged report. The work is four to six sessions on processing and evaluating, using data from his own school practicals, with each attempt marked against the strand rather than against an answer. Expect the table and graph strands to move first and the evaluation strand to take longer.

faqs.question: How do you teach practical science if the lessons are online?
faqs.answer: The practical work happens at school, in a laboratory, with equipment and supervision, and nothing should substitute for that. What a session covers is everything around it. Before the investigation: hypothesis, variables, method and safety, which is the whole of criterion B and needs no apparatus. After it: table, graph, conclusion and evaluation, which is the whole of criterion C and happens at a desk. Content and the criterion D discussion are screen work by nature. So nearly all the recoverable marks in MYP sciences are accessible without a laboratory, which surprises most families.

faqs.question: What does a top-band hypothesis look like in MYP Sciences?
faqs.answer: It has three parts: the relationship expected, the scientific reasoning that generates that expectation, and ideally the shape the relationship should take. "The rate of reaction will increase as temperature rises, because particles gain kinetic energy and collide more often with enough energy to react, so the rate should rise non-linearly" is a top-band statement. "It will be faster if it is hotter" is a prediction and sits in the middle band however correct it proves. Nothing in the better version needs knowledge the student lacks, which is why this strand moves quickly once it is pointed out.

faqs.question: Does my daughter need to discuss uncertainty and precision in an MYP write-up?
faqs.answer: Not with the formal error propagation a Diploma investigation expects, but the habits start here and the marks reward them. Recording to the precision the instrument allows, keeping that precision consistent through a calculation, and not quoting a result to more significant figures than the measurements support are all criterion C expectations. The commonest loss is a burette or thermometer reading taken to one decimal place and then a final answer presented to four, which signals to a marker that the student does not understand what their own data can support. Ten minutes of teaching protects that mark for years.

faqs.question: Why does her conclusion lose marks when the data are right?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly because the conclusion restates the hypothesis rather than answering the question using the data. "My hypothesis was correct" is not a conclusion. A conclusion describes the trend the data actually show, quantifies it where possible, relates it back to the scientific reasoning in the hypothesis, and says whether the data support that reasoning. It is a different sentence doing a different job, and it is one of the quickest strands in the subject to fix because the thinking is already there and only the writing convention is missing.

faqs.question: What is criterion D and why has nobody mentioned it before?
faqs.answer: Reflecting on the impacts of science: applying scientific understanding to a real problem, discussing the consequences of using science to address it, and documenting sources properly. It carries the same weight as the other three criteria and in most schools it is assessed once or twice a year and taught almost never, which is why it rarely comes up. That makes it the cheapest level available to most students, because the task is largely a writing structure applied to science they already know. Two or three sessions typically moves it, and Abu Dhabi supplies excellent local material.

faqs.question: How long before a science report shows any movement?
faqs.answer: Eight weeks is a realistic horizon for criterion C and criterion D, about right for criterion B habits, and short for criterion A content repair, which takes a term. The important thing is that movement is measured rather than sensed, which means a baseline task marked in week one and a comparable task marked in week eight on the same criterion and strand. Without the baseline there is nothing to compare against and the week-four conversation becomes an exchange of impressions. Setting the horizon and the measurement at the start prevents that entirely.

faqs.question: Should we treat Biology, Chemistry and Physics separately in MYP 4?
faqs.answer: For content, yes, since they split in most Abu Dhabi schools at that point. For assessment technique, no, and this is the useful insight. The four criteria are the same across all three sciences, and criterion C processing skills transfer completely. A student weak on evaluation is weak on it in all three subjects, so one block of work fixes it everywhere at once. That is far better value than three separate content programmes, and it is also what the Diploma investigation will mark regardless of which science they eventually choose.

faqs.question: What should be in the folder after four weeks of science sessions?
faqs.answer: A baseline task from week one with four marked levels and the losing strand named on each. A rewritten hypothesis and variable list for a real school task. A processed dataset from one of your child's own practicals, with units in the table headers and a correctly axed graph. And dated attempts made alone between sessions, including the unsuccessful ones. If the processed data are from a worked example rather than from your child's own practical, the teaching is happening on somebody else's numbers, and that is worth raising.

faqs.question: Does an integrated sciences course disadvantage my child for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Less than families fear, provided criterion C is secure. Some Abu Dhabi schools keep an integrated course longer than others, which means slightly less depth in each discipline at the point of choosing Diploma sciences. That content gap is real and closable. What is not easily closable late is the processing and evaluation skill, and that is what the Diploma scientific investigation actually marks. A student leaving an integrated course with strong criterion C is better placed than one leaving a discrete course with strong content and no idea how to evaluate a method.

faqs.question: How does an interdisciplinary unit involving science get marked?
faqs.answer: Against its own criteria rather than against the four sciences criteria, which is why it appears as a separate line on the report and causes a predictable amount of confusion. What it rewards is synthesis: using understanding from two or more subjects to produce something neither could produce alone, plus a reflection on how combining them changed the outcome. A good science section and a good humanities section stapled together does not meet the criteria, because nothing was synthesised. Reading the unit's own criteria when they come home is worth more than any content support.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the science element of the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: With the science, yes; with the project, only within limits. A tutor can teach scientific content the student needs, explain a technique, question a plan and give feedback on work the student has produced. What a tutor must not do is supply the idea, the method or the writing, because the project is assessed as the student's own work and there is a supervisor's record of its development. The safe and useful boundary is that the student should be able to explain every decision in the project aloud, without notes, to anyone who asks.

faqs.question: His science teacher changed mid-year and his levels dropped. Does that explain it?
faqs.answer: Partly, and it is worth separating two effects. A new teacher may mark the same work slightly differently, particularly on the judgement strands of criteria C and D, which can move a level without anything changing in the student. A new teacher may also set different kinds of task, and a student strong on recall will score lower if the balance shifts towards investigation. Ask to see two marked tasks, one from each teacher, and look at which criterion moved. If it is C or D, it is probably task balance rather than a decline.

faqs.question: Must an online science tutor hold a UAE tutoring permit?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which introduced private tuition work permits, and individuals offering private tutoring without a MoHRE permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. The government portal records the permit as free of charge for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. No fine schedule is published, so disregard any amount quoted to you. Ask any tutor directly, and check MoHRE's own service page for the official route.

Each has marked student work against the published criteria and can look at a task your child has already had back from school and tell you which descriptor band it sits in and why.

intro.heading: Why a good Spanish speaker can still sit at a 5
paragraphs: Parents in Abu Dhabi come to MYP Spanish support with a specific confusion. The child talks happily in class, the teacher says they are confident, and the report says 5. Nothing in that picture is contradictory once you know how the subject is marked. MYP Language Acquisition is not graded on how willing a student is to speak. It is graded against four criteria, each worth 8 marks, and a student can be strong on two of them and weak on two of them and land exactly in the middle.

The four are specific. Criterion A is comprehending spoken and visual text - listening, essentially, including what a student can take from an image or a video they have not seen before. Criterion B is comprehending written and visual text, which is reading, and reading unfamiliar text in particular. Criterion C is communicating in response to spoken, written and visual text, which is what a student produces when they have been given something to respond to. Criterion D is using language in spoken and written form, which is accuracy, range and register. The school converts the profile across all four into a subject grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries.

In Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts, two of those four do most of the damage. Criterion B marks fall away when a student can decode every word in a text and still cannot say what the writer wanted the reader to conclude. That is a reading-strategy problem that looks like a vocabulary problem, and buying more vocabulary does not fix it. Criterion D marks fall away when the ideas are there and the grammar collapses under time pressure - ser and estar chosen by instinct, preterite where the imperfect belongs, agreement lost in the third sentence of a paragraph.

Phase matters as much as criterion. Language Acquisition runs across six phases, and a student placed one phase above their real working level will produce exactly the profile described above: cheerful oral work, reasonable comprehension of familiar material, and a criterion D score that will not move. Abu Dhabi schools place students into phases on arrival, often quickly, and a transfer in from a British or Indian curriculum school is the commonest way a mismatch gets locked in for a year.

This page is built to be diagnostic rather than persuasive. It sets out what each criterion actually measures, what a student can realistically do at each phase, the eight grammatical errors that recur in Abu Dhabi Spanish cohorts, what an ePortfolio counts as evidence, and where the academic-honesty line sits in a subject where a translation tool can produce a paragraph in two seconds. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India.
bullets: Criteria A and B are comprehension; C and D are production - a 5 usually means a split profile
Criterion B is a reading-strategy problem far more often than a vocabulary problem
Criterion D is where accuracy under time pressure shows, and where drilling beats discussion
A phase placed one level too high produces a confident speaker with a stuck grade
Ask your MYP coordinator for the phase on record and the last criterion profile

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.programmesIntro: Spanish runs through three IB programmes with a different assessment model in each, and the MYP phase a student leaves with decides which Diploma door is open. The map below is written around what each stage is marked on.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The programme in the URL. Spanish sits inside Language Acquisition across six phases, assessed against criteria A to D at 8 marks each. Tasks are set by the school rather than an external board for most students, which means the descriptors - not a past paper - are the thing to work from. A student's criterion profile is more informative than their subject grade, because it tells you which half of the subject is weak.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP schools run Spanish alongside mandatory Arabic, which compresses the weekly timetable more than families expect. Schools in the Khalifa City and Raha corridor carry the largest MYP cohorts in the emirate, and phase placement there is done at speed during an intake week - which is when a mismatch most often goes unnoticed until the first report.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Spanish continues as Language B at SL or HL, or as Language ab initio at SL for near-beginners. Language B is assessed on productive, receptive and interactive skills, with an individual oral and written tasks; ab initio covers a defined set of themes for students with little or no prior study. The phase reached at the end of MYP 5 effectively decides which of the three is available, and ab initio is closed to a student with real prior study.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma language cohorts in Abu Dhabi are small, and a school may run Spanish B SL in a single class or not at all in a given year. Families discover this at option-choice time in MYP 5, two years after the decision that mattered - which is the phase trajectory through MYP 3 and 4.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Spanish in the PYP is an additional language inside transdisciplinary units, with no phase label and no criterion marking. Assessment is formative and school-designed. Support at this stage is about oral confidence and sound-to-spelling mapping, which is genuinely useful preparation for criterion A later, because Spanish spelling is regular in a way English is not and a child who learns that early reads faster forever.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi primary sections introduce Spanish from Year 3 or 4, and a child who moves schools inside the emirate can lose two years of it. That gap is the usual reason a Year 7 student is placed in Phase 1 while a classmate from the same school sits in Phase 3.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme includes a language development component evidenced through a portfolio rather than an examination, and Spanish can sit inside it. The evidence requirement is lighter than Language B, but it is still evidence - recorded tasks, reflections and samples - so support focuses on building a defensible portfolio rather than on exam technique.
programmes.countryNote: Few Abu Dhabi schools run the Career-related Programme, so most readers of this page will not need it. It appears here because parents comparing language routes are occasionally told the CP portfolio is equivalent to Language B, and it is assessed on different things.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.subjectsIntro: A criterion profile in one subject usually repeats in another, because MYP criteria reward the same habits across the programme. The grid below names what each subject is actually marked on, so you can see whether the problem is Spanish or is a thinking habit showing up in Spanish.

subjects.name: Spanish - Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Criteria A to D at 8 marks each. The characteristic Abu Dhabi profile is strong A and C with weak B and D: a confident speaker who cannot infer from unfamiliar text and loses accuracy under timed conditions. Both halves are fixable, by different methods.

subjects.name: French - Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Same criteria, same phases. Students taking both Spanish and French confuse verb endings long before they confuse vocabulary, and the fix is to teach the two systems against each other rather than separately.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio and Language B
subjects.description: The Diploma continuation. Assessed on receptive, productive and interactive skills with an individual oral. The phase a student reaches in MYP 5 is what makes HL realistic, SL sensible, or ab initio the only honest option.

subjects.name: English - Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text, using language. A student who retells rather than analyses in English will usually do the same in Spanish criterion C, because it is one habit expressed in two languages.

subjects.name: Arabic - Language Acquisition and first language
subjects.description: A mandatory subject in UAE private schools with separate provision for Arab and non-Arab students and set school material. It competes directly with Spanish for weekly study time, which is why sequencing matters more than volume.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, thinking critically. Source-inference work here is the same skill as Spanish criterion B, and progress in one transfers measurably to the other.

subjects.name: Mathematics - Standard and Extended
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, applying maths in real-life contexts. Communication marks are lost for unjustified steps, the same way criterion C marks are lost for unsupported assertions.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating among the four criteria. Evaluation is the weak strand in most cohorts, and students who cannot evaluate a method rarely evaluate their own Spanish writing either.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, evaluating, evidenced through a design folder. Process documentation carries the marks, which is the same lesson the Language Acquisition ePortfolio teaches.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Investigating, planning, taking action, reflecting. It runs in the same year as the heaviest Spanish assessment load, and a student who has learned to keep a process journal for Spanish evidence finds it markedly easier.

sections.heading: What each of the four criteria actually measures
paragraphs: Each criterion in MYP Language Acquisition carries 8 marks, and each is assessed through a different kind of task. Knowing which task belongs to which criterion is what lets a parent read a report rather than guess at it. The table below maps the four, names the task types Abu Dhabi schools typically use, says where marks are lost, and states what a session can actually change.

Criterion A, comprehending spoken and visual text, is assessed on listening or audiovisual material with questions that go beyond retrieval. Students lose marks here by answering what they heard rather than what was asked, and by missing the inference questions entirely because they have run out of time replaying the earlier ones. The fix is a listening routine with a fixed order of operations, not more listening.

Criterion B, comprehending written and visual text, is where the largest share of unexplained grade loss sits. The tasks use text the student has not seen, and the questions ask for purpose, audience, tone and implication. A student with good vocabulary and no reading strategy will answer the literal questions and leave the inference questions blank or vague. Criterion C, communicating in response to text, is production with a prompt attached: students who write well in general but ignore the audience and purpose stated in the task cap themselves at the middle bands. Criterion D, using language in spoken and written form, is accuracy, range and register - and it is the criterion that responds to drilling rather than discussion.

Read a report by criterion, not by subject grade. A profile of 7, 4, 6, 4 and a profile of 5, 5, 5, 5 produce a similar subject grade and require completely different work. The first is a comprehension-and-accuracy problem in a fluent speaker. The second is a student who is below the descriptor everywhere and probably in the wrong phase.

sections.heading: Phase 1 to Phase 6: what a Spanish learner can realistically do
paragraphs: Phase is the single most consequential administrative fact about a Language Acquisition student, and most parents never see it written down. The six phases describe a progression from recognising familiar language to interpreting unfamiliar text and producing extended writing for a defined purpose. A school chooses the phase, teaches to its descriptors, and marks against them - so a student in the wrong phase is being measured with the wrong ruler.

The symptoms of a phase set too high are consistent. The student participates, understands the teacher, and scores respectably on criteria A and C where context carries them. Criterion B collapses, because the texts assume a reading range they do not have. Criterion D sits at 3 or 4 permanently, because the accuracy demanded belongs to a later stage of learning. The report reads as a plateau, and no amount of extra vocabulary shifts it.

A phase set too low is less common and easier to spot: the student is bored, scores 7s, and learns nothing new for a year. That matters for the Diploma, because a student parked below their level in MYP 4 and 5 may arrive at option choices without the range for Spanish B HL, and may be ineligible for ab initio precisely because they have studied Spanish for years.

The table below is a practical translation of the phase progression. It is a planning tool, not a substitute for the published descriptors - ask your MYP coordinator which phase is on record for your child and which descriptors the school is marking against, and compare them against what you see at home.

sections.heading: The eight errors that cost Abu Dhabi students Spanish marks
paragraphs: Criterion D is the most diagnosable part of the subject, because the errors repeat. Across MYP Spanish cohorts the same eight patterns account for the great majority of accuracy loss, and seven of them are drillable in a term. Naming them is more useful than any general advice about practising more.

Ser and estar is the first and the most persistent, because English collapses both into one verb and students choose by instinct rather than rule. The second is preterite against imperfect: students who know both forms still narrate in a single tense, which reads as a beginner error even when the vocabulary is advanced. Third is the subjunctive trigger - not the forms, which most students can produce, but recognising the clause that requires it. Fourth is gender and number agreement, which usually survives the first two sentences of a piece and then degrades.

The remaining four are quieter but equally costly. Por and para, where students learn a list of uses and never a principle. False friends with English, which produce confident, wrong sentences that a reader notices immediately. Written accents, where a missing mark changes a tense or a meaning rather than merely looking untidy. And register - the tú and usted decision, plus the gap between how a student speaks in class and the formality a task demands of them.

What a session does with this list is not lecture it. The working method is a short piece of timed production, marked against the descriptor, with every error logged by category. After three weeks the log shows which two of the eight patterns are actually costing marks for that student, and the remaining sessions drill those two. An error log is the single most effective document in language tutoring and almost nobody keeps one.

sections.heading: Criterion B: decoding is not comprehending
paragraphs: If one section of this page is worth acting on, it is this one. Criterion B carries 8 marks and it is where Abu Dhabi MYP Spanish students lose most of the grade they cannot explain. The reason is a mismatch between how the subject is taught and how it is assessed. Teaching builds vocabulary and structures on familiar themes. Assessment hands over a text the student has never seen and asks what the writer is trying to achieve.

The symptom is recognisable at home. Give your child a short Spanish article and they will translate it for you reasonably well, then be unable to say who it was written for or what it wanted the reader to do. That is not a vocabulary deficit. It is the absence of a reading routine, and students who have one outperform students with larger vocabularies on this criterion consistently.

The routine itself is unglamorous and takes about four weeks to become automatic. Read the questions before the text, so attention has somewhere to go. First pass for topic and text type only - is this an advert, a blog, a news report, a letter, and what does that type usually want? Second pass for the specific items. Then, for each inference question, find the exact phrase in the text that licenses the answer and underline it, because an inference without textual evidence is a guess and marks accordingly.

Progress is measurable within a term, which is why it is a good first target. One short unfamiliar text a week, worked through the routine, with the student forced to point at the licensing phrase each time. Ten texts in, the routine holds under timed conditions. That is a criterion B movement of two or three marks for most students, which on a four-criterion profile is often the difference between a 5 and a 6.

sections.heading: The oral task and what a recording is actually marked on
paragraphs: Spoken Spanish is assessed under criteria C and D, and the task is usually recorded or conducted live with the teacher. Students and parents both assume the oral rewards fluency, by which they usually mean speed and confidence. The descriptors reward something narrower: whether the student addresses the stimulus and the stated purpose, and whether the language is accurate and appropriate in register.

That gap explains a common outcome. A student who speaks quickly, fills pauses in English, and talks around the stimulus rather than about it will score below a slower student who answers the prompt, repairs their own errors, and stays in Spanish. The first sounds better to a parent listening from the next room. The second scores better.

Three things are worth rehearsing explicitly. Repair strategies in Spanish rather than in English - a student who can say that they meant something else, or ask for a moment, keeps the register intact where an English filler breaks it. Register itself, because tú and usted is a marked choice and the wrong one is visible immediately. And the opening thirty seconds, which set the examiner's expectation and are the easiest part of the task to prepare without rehearsing a script, which the descriptors penalise.

The method that works is recording the student, marking the recording against the descriptor, and annotating a transcript so they can see the loss points rather than being told about them. Most students have never heard themselves speak Spanish. The first time they do, with a descriptor next to it, is usually the most productive twenty minutes of a term.
bullets: The descriptors reward addressing the stimulus, not speaking quickly
English fillers break register; Spanish repair strategies preserve it
The tú and usted choice is marked and immediately visible
Rehearse the task type, not a script - memorised answers are penalised
Mark a recording against the descriptor and annotate the transcript

sections.heading: The ePortfolio and what counts as evidence
paragraphs: Where an Abu Dhabi school enters MYP eAssessment, Language Acquisition is evidenced through an ePortfolio rather than a sat examination paper. Not every school takes that route, and the components a school enters vary, so the first thing to establish is which route your child is actually on - the MYP coordinator can confirm it in a sentence, and planning without that answer wastes a term.

Where a portfolio is the assessment, the implications for support are substantial. The work is the student's own, produced over months, selected and refined rather than performed once. That rewards consistency and record-keeping, and it punishes students who produce strong single pieces and keep no account of how they got there. Support therefore looks less like exam coaching and more like a structured habit of drafting, feedback and revision across the year.

It also moves the academic-honesty line into sharper focus, because a portfolio is produced at home where a translation tool, a generative model and a Spanish-speaking relative are all within reach. The rule is the same as anywhere in the IB: the work submitted must be the student's own, and a tutor teaches, reviews and gives feedback on it. A tutor who hands back a corrected version to be copied has not helped the student and has created a malpractice exposure for them.

What legitimate support looks like in practice is specific. Reading a draft and commenting against the criterion without rewriting the sentences. Marking an error log so the student makes the correction themselves. Teaching the structure a text type needs, then watching the student apply it to their own topic. Asking why a tense was chosen rather than changing it. The work stays the student's; the teaching is what is purchased.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when a translator is one tap away
paragraphs: Language subjects carry an academic-honesty problem that maths does not. A paragraph of fluent Spanish is thirty seconds away on any phone, and the output is now good enough that a teacher often cannot be certain. Abu Dhabi parents ask about this more than about any other aspect of the subject, usually because a teacher has raised a concern about work that was genuinely the student's.

The IB position is clear in principle: work submitted for assessment must be the student's own, and misrepresenting someone else's work - or a machine's - as your own is malpractice. The consequence falls on the student, which is why this matters more than the convenience of a shortcut. The practical difficulty is that a student using a translator for a single unfamiliar word is doing something different from a student generating a paragraph, and the line between them has to be taught rather than assumed.

A workable rule for home use, and the one we teach, is that tools may be used to check something the student has already produced, never to produce it. Look up a word, by all means. Run a finished sentence past a dictionary to confirm a gender. Do not type an English paragraph in and copy out the Spanish, because the student learns nothing, the register will be wrong for the task, and the accuracy will be inconsistent with their classwork in a way that is visible.

There is a related question specific to Abu Dhabi's households. A Spanish-speaking parent or helper at home is an asset for criteria A and C and a liability for criterion D, because a fluent speaker correcting a draft produces writing the student cannot reproduce under timed conditions. The honest use of a native speaker at home is conversation and listening practice. The dishonest use is editing. Keep the two apart and the help is genuinely valuable.
bullets: Submitted work must be the student's own - the consequence falls on the student
Tools may check what the student produced, never produce it for them
A fluent relative editing drafts inflates criterion D and hides the real level
Conversation and listening practice at home is useful and entirely legitimate
A tutor teaches, reviews and gives feedback; a tutor never supplies assessed work

sections.heading: What the first session establishes, and what it does not
paragraphs: A first session is a diagnosis. It is one free trial lesson per student, booked without card details, with nothing payable before or after it and no obligation to continue. What it produces is a written note, and the note answers three questions a report card does not.

First, which phase the student is genuinely working in, judged against what they can do with an unfamiliar short text rather than against what they say about their Spanish. Where that differs from the phase on record at school, we say so and explain what evidence it rests on, because that conversation belongs with the MYP coordinator and a parent needs something concrete to take into it.

Second, which criterion to target first. A split profile - strong A and C, weak B and D - gets a different plan from a flat profile. The note names one criterion, the task type to work on, and what evidence of movement will look like by a stated date, so that six weeks later there is something to check rather than a feeling.

Third, what the honest commitment is. For criterion B, 45 minutes a week plus one short text between sessions is usually enough. For criterion D, the useful shape is more marking than talking - short corrected pieces several times a week - and that is a different arrangement. If the honest answer is that your child is in the right phase, doing fine, and needs no tutoring, the note says that too. Where no MYP Spanish specialist is free for the slot you need, we tell you rather than substituting a generalist and charging for a specialist.
bullets: One free trial lesson per student, no card details, nothing payable
A phase judgement based on performance with unfamiliar text
One named criterion, one task type, and a date to check against
An honest commitment estimate - and an honest no, where that is the answer
A plain statement when no specialist is available for your slot

process.title: Send a marked Spanish task and the criterion profile
process.description: The most useful documents are a recent marked piece of work and the criterion breakdown from the last report. Those two together show whether the gap is comprehension or production, which decides everything about the plan that follows.

process.title: Free trial lesson, used to check the phase
process.description: One lesson, one student, no card details and nothing payable. The tutor works the student through a short unfamiliar text and a timed written piece, which is how a phase is judged honestly rather than from a conversation.

process.title: One criterion named, with evidence of movement defined
process.description: You receive a written note naming the criterion to work on first, the task type it will be worked through, and what movement should look like by a stated date. One criterion at a time is slower to promise and faster to deliver.

process.title: Weekly session plus production between sessions
process.description: Sessions run 45 or 60 minutes on Gulf Standard Time around the Abu Dhabi school run. Between them the student submits short written work or a recording, which comes back marked against the descriptor with the errors logged by category.

process.title: Reassess, retarget or stop
process.description: After six weeks the error log and the marked tasks show whether the criterion has moved. If it has, the next criterion is named. If the work is done, the block ends - a tutoring arrangement that cannot say when it should finish is not a plan.

whyPoints.title: Marked against the descriptor, not impressionistically
whyPoints.description: Written work and recordings come back with the criterion letter, the band and the reason - the same way a school department marks. A parent can take that note into a conversation with the MYP coordinator and it will hold up.

whyPoints.title: Phase checked before anything else
whyPoints.description: A student in the wrong phase is being measured with the wrong ruler, and no amount of tutoring fixes that. The trial lesson exists to judge the phase against performance on unfamiliar text, and to say so plainly when it looks misplaced.

whyPoints.title: An error log, kept by category
whyPoints.description: Criterion D moves when the same mistake stops recurring, which requires counting it. The log shows which two of the eight recurring Spanish error patterns are actually costing this student marks, and the sessions drill those two.

whyPoints.title: One criterion at a time, with a date on it
whyPoints.description: Plans that target everything move nothing. Each block names a single criterion, a task type and a date by which movement should be visible in marked work, so the arrangement can be judged rather than felt.

whyPoints.title: The academic-honesty line taught, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Tools may check what a student has produced and never produce it for them. A tutor teaches, reviews and gives feedback on the student's own work - we do not supply assessed work, and we explain to students why the risk of that falls on them.

whyPoints.title: Online one-to-one, with the limits stated
whyPoints.description: Lessons run over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India - and where no Spanish specialist is free for your slot, we say so.

faqs.question: How is MYP Spanish actually graded in an Abu Dhabi school?
faqs.answer: Against four published criteria, each worth 8 marks: comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to text, and using language in spoken and written form. The school marks tasks against descriptor bands for your child's phase, then converts the profile into a subject grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries. Ask for the criterion breakdown rather than the grade, because a profile of 7, 4, 6, 4 and a flat profile of 5, 5, 5, 5 look similar on a report and need completely different work. The breakdown is the document that tells you what to do.

faqs.question: Why does my child speak Spanish confidently but still score a 5?
faqs.answer: Because confidence is rewarded under two criteria and penalised by neither, while the grade is an average across four. A fluent speaker typically scores well on criterion A, where context carries them, and on criterion C, where they have something to say. The grade then sits in the middle because criterion B asks them to infer purpose and audience from text they have never seen, and criterion D asks for accuracy under time pressure. Both of those are trainable, by different methods: a reading routine for B, and short corrected production with an error log for D.

faqs.question: Which Spanish grammar errors cost the most marks at MYP level?
faqs.answer: Eight patterns account for most criterion D loss. Ser against estar, chosen by instinct because English merges them. Preterite against imperfect, where students narrate in a single tense. Subjunctive triggers recognised too late rather than forms unknown. Gender and number agreement degrading after the first two sentences. Por and para learned as a list rather than a principle. False friends with English. Written accents that change a tense or a meaning. And register, including the tú and usted decision. An error log kept for three weeks will usually show that only two of the eight are actually costing your child marks.

faqs.question: How is the Spanish oral task marked, and does speaking fast help?
faqs.answer: Speaking fast does not help and often hurts. The spoken task is assessed under criteria C and D, which reward addressing the stimulus and the stated purpose, and using accurate language in an appropriate register. A student who talks quickly, fills pauses in English and talks around the prompt will score below a slower student who answers it, repairs their own errors in Spanish and holds the register. The productive method is to record the student, mark the recording against the descriptor, and annotate a transcript so they can see the loss points instead of being told about them.

faqs.question: What goes into a Language Acquisition ePortfolio for Spanish?
faqs.answer: Where a school enters MYP eAssessment, Language Acquisition is evidenced through a portfolio of the student's own work produced over months rather than a single sat paper. The components a school enters vary and not every Abu Dhabi school takes that route, so confirm with the MYP coordinator which route your child is on before planning around it. Where it applies, support looks like a structured habit of drafting, criterion-referenced feedback and revision across the year. It rewards consistency and record-keeping, and it punishes students who produce strong single pieces and keep no account of their process.

faqs.question: Does a missing accent in Spanish writing actually lose marks?
faqs.answer: It can, because in Spanish an accent is not decoration. It distinguishes tenses and meanings, so a missing or misplaced mark can change what the sentence says rather than merely how it looks. Under criterion D, which assesses accuracy and range, repeated accent errors read as a control problem. The practical fix is narrow and quick: a student only needs the small set of contrasts that recur in their own writing, found from an error log rather than from a textbook list. Most students fix this in two or three weeks once someone has shown them which pairs matter for them.

faqs.question: Can my child use a translation app for Spanish homework?
faqs.answer: The rule we teach is that a tool may check something the student has already produced, never produce it for them. Looking up a word or confirming a gender on a finished sentence is reasonable. Typing an English paragraph in and copying out the Spanish is not: the student learns nothing, the register is usually wrong for the task, and the accuracy will be inconsistent with their classwork in a way teachers notice. Work submitted for assessment must be the student's own, and the consequence of misrepresenting a machine's output as their own falls on the student.

faqs.question: My child started Spanish in MYP 3 - which phase should they be in?
faqs.answer: A genuine beginner starting in MYP 3 would normally be placed in Phase 1 or 2, working on familiar topics with heavy support, and would progress towards Phase 3 by the end of MYP 4 with consistent study. The risk in a late start is placement into a continuer group for timetabling reasons rather than for level, which produces permanent criterion D scores of 3 or 4 and a student who concludes they are bad at languages. Ask the MYP coordinator which phase is on record and which descriptors are being used, then compare that against what your child can do with an unfamiliar short text.

faqs.question: Is Phase 3 Spanish at the end of MYP 5 enough for Diploma Spanish B?
faqs.answer: Phase 3 at the end of MYP 5 makes Spanish B at SL realistic and HL difficult. Phase 4 makes SL secure and HL achievable with work. Phase 5 makes HL realistic. The decision that matters is taken earlier than families expect, because phase progression is cumulative: the trajectory through MYP 3 and 4 is what determines where a student finishes. A student who has studied Spanish for years is also generally ineligible for ab initio, which is designed for near-beginners, so parking below level in MYP 4 narrows rather than preserves the options.

faqs.question: What exactly does criterion D measure in spoken Spanish?
faqs.answer: Accuracy, range and register in speech - whether the grammar holds up in real time, whether the vocabulary reaches beyond the rehearsed, and whether the formality suits the task and the audience. It is not a measure of volume or speed. The commonest losses are tense control slipping once the student is improvising, agreement errors appearing after the first few sentences, English fillers breaking the register, and a tú or usted choice that does not match the situation described in the prompt. All four are visible on a recording and none of them are visible in a conversation nobody recorded.

faqs.question: The Spanish report says 5 - what is missing for a 7?
faqs.answer: Almost always two things, and they are rarely vocabulary. The first is inference under criterion B: the ability to read a text never seen before and state what it wants the reader to think or do, with the licensing phrase identified. The second is accuracy under time pressure under criterion D, where the gap between what a student knows and what they produce in twenty minutes is widest. Ask for the criterion breakdown and look at which two numbers are lowest. A two-mark movement on each of two criteria is usually what separates a 5 from a 6 or 7.

faqs.question: Do Abu Dhabi schools teach Spanish from Spain or from Latin America?
faqs.answer: Both are taught and both are acceptable in assessment - the descriptors assess comprehension, communication and accurate use of language, not a single national variety. What matters is consistency within a piece of work, because mixing varieties mid-paragraph reads as a control problem under criterion D. It is worth asking your child's department which variety its materials use, so a tutor works with the same one and the student is not corrected in two directions at once. Vocabulary differences are the visible part; the pronoun and past-tense usage differences matter more for writing.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark Spanish work the same way my child's department does?
faqs.answer: Where the tutor works from the published criteria and the phase descriptors the school is using, yes - and that is the point of asking which phase is on record before anything else. What a tutor cannot do is predict a school's internal grade boundaries, which schools set for their own tasks. What they can do is say which descriptor band a piece of work sits in, name the specific feature keeping it there, and mark the next piece the same way so movement is visible. That consistency is more useful to a student than a number.

faqs.question: Is it too late to fix Spanish accuracy in the final MYP year?
faqs.answer: Accuracy is the most improvable part of the subject late on, which makes MYP 5 a better year for criterion D work than for criterion B work. Short corrected production several times a week, with an error log, moves tense control and agreement within a term because those are habits rather than knowledge gaps. Inference under criterion B improves more slowly and is better started in MYP 3 or 4. The constraint in MYP 5 is the calendar rather than the subject: the Personal Project runs in the same year and competes for the same evenings, so the plan has to be realistic about hours.

faqs.question: Does a Spanish-speaking parent at home help or hurt the grade?
faqs.answer: It helps criteria A and C and can quietly damage criterion D. Conversation and listening practice with a fluent speaker at home is valuable and entirely legitimate - it builds exactly the comprehension and confidence the first two criteria reward. Editing drafts is the problem: writing corrected by a fluent adult produces work the student cannot reproduce under timed conditions, which inflates the apparent level, hides the real one and leaves the student unprepared. Keep the two uses apart, and a Spanish-speaking household is one of the strongest assets a MYP language student can have.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the criterion breakdown, not the grade
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.closingBody: A subject grade tells you there is a problem. The criterion breakdown tells you which one. Send a recent marked Spanish task and the last criterion profile, and the free trial lesson - one lesson, one student, no card details, nothing payable - will produce a written phase judgement, one named criterion to target first, and a date by which movement should be visible in marked work. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school run, with short written or recorded work marked between them.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach the standard mathematics route as a course in its own right rather than as a lighter version of something else. That means the full standard syllabus, criterion-marked task technique, and an honest view of which Diploma mathematics courses follow from it. Tell us the year and the four criterion levels from the last report.

intro.heading: Standard is a route, not a ranking
paragraphs: At the start of MYP 4, mathematics in an IB school divides. Half a year group continues on what the programme calls standard mathematics and the other half moves onto extended. Many Abu Dhabi families read that split as setting, hear the word standard, and conclude their child has been placed in the lower group. That reading causes a specific and avoidable kind of damage: a student who believes they are in the weak set stops trying to reach the top descriptor bands, and a 7 that was available quietly becomes a 5.

The accurate reading is different. Standard mathematics covers the core of the MYP mathematics framework and is assessed against exactly the same four criteria as extended, each scored one to eight, with the same maximum total and the same grade scale running to 7. Extended adds breadth and algebraic depth on top of the core; it does not replace it with harder versions of the same ideas. A student on standard who understands proportional reasoning deeply and can justify a general rule is doing better mathematics than a student on extended who has memorised the cosine rule and cannot say when it applies.

What follows from that is the point of this page. If standard is a route rather than a ranking, then tutoring on it should look like teaching a course properly rather than like remediation. The work is to secure the standard syllabus, raise the criterion levels that are low, and get the student to the top descriptor bands that the standard route genuinely offers. Nothing about that requires pretending the extended content is coming. It requires knowing the standard syllabus precisely and knowing where its own difficulty sits.

There is a second honest conversation, and it is about the Diploma. The route a student finishes MYP on shapes which of the four Diploma mathematics courses are comfortable two years later. Applications and Interpretation at both levels, and Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level, are reachable from the standard route without heroics. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is a real stretch from it, and families whose child is aiming at engineering or physics should know that in MYP 4 rather than in DP1. Saying so is not an argument for moving routes. It is an argument for making the choice with the information.

A note on how any of this is delivered. IB Gram's tutoring for UAE families is one-to-one and online, over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For mathematics the online format is a genuine advantage, because a shared digital writing surface shows a student's working line by line, keeps a record of it, and lets a graph be redrawn in seconds. Matching without a driving radius also means a family in Al Shamkha or Al Samha chooses from the same tutors as a family on Saadiyat Island.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.programmesIntro: The standard route sits inside a longer sequence, and its job is to leave a student able to do the next thing. The programmes below are described by what they expect a student to arrive already able to do, which is the test that matters when choosing a route.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics runs as a single course through MYP 1 to 3 and then divides into standard and extended for MYP 4 and 5. Both routes are assessed against knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts, each scored one to eight. Both can reach a subject grade of 7. The optional on-screen examination in the final year is available on either route.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts span long-established island schools and fast-growing ones along the Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor. In several newer schools the route decision is taken by the mathematics department on the basis of MYP 3 criterion levels, with limited scope to appeal, which makes the MYP 3 year quietly decisive for a family with a Diploma plan in mind.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Four mathematics options: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, each at Standard or Higher Level. Each carries a twenty-mark exploration worth about a fifth of the subject grade. The content assumption at entry is not the same across the four, which is the whole reason the MYP route matters.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools generally offer at least three of the four combinations, and Applications and Interpretation has grown as a sensible destination for students from the standard route who still want substantial mathematics. Where a school offers only two combinations, the route decision in MYP 4 constrains the Diploma choice more tightly than the family expects.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics is taught through inquiry with no criterion levels. What it leaves behind is number sense: a student who is fluent with fractions, place value and multiplicative reasoning arrives in MYP 1 able to spend attention on the mathematics rather than on the arithmetic underneath it.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi families often transfer between systems during the primary years, and a child arriving into MYP 1 from a curriculum that emphasised procedure over reasoning meets criterion B for the first time with no preparation for it. That is the gap that shows up again at the route decision three years later.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: The parallel the standard route most resembles in level, though not in assessment style. Cambridge mathematics 0580 is tiered Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 is tiered Foundation and Higher. Both are examined by written papers with no criterion marking and no investigation component, which is the real difference a transferring student feels.
programmes.countryNote: Because Abu Dhabi has large British-curriculum cohorts alongside IB ones, families compare the two constantly. The practical point is that an IGCSE Higher or Extended tier student transferring into MYP standard will find the content familiar and the criterion B expectations entirely new.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.subjectsIntro: The grid below is the standard mathematics syllabus as a student meets it, with the difficulty that actually sits inside each strand. Where extended goes further, that is noted, so the shape of the route is visible rather than implied.

subjects.name: Number and the four operations in context
subjects.description: Integers, fractions, decimals, percentages and the discipline of choosing an operation from a described situation. The difficulty here is not calculation but selection: a student who can divide perfectly often cannot tell from a worded context that division is what the situation wants.

subjects.name: Ratio, proportion and rates
subjects.description: The strand that quietly determines a standard-route grade. Direct and inverse proportion, scale, unit rates and percentage change recur in geometry, in statistics and in every real-life application task, so a weakness here is paid for four times over.

subjects.name: Algebraic expressions and linear equations
subjects.description: Simplifying, substituting, expanding single brackets, solving linear and simultaneous equations. Standard treats quadratic work lightly where extended treats it as central. The standard-route difficulty is forming an equation from words rather than solving one that is given.

subjects.name: Sequences and general rules
subjects.description: Linear and simple non-linear sequences, expressed as a general rule in terms of position. This is where the standard route's criterion B tasks live, and where a student can reach the top descriptor band without any extended content at all, provided they justify rather than describe.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and straight-line graphs
subjects.description: Plotting, gradient, intercepts and interpreting a line in context. Standard asks what the gradient means in the situation modelled; extended goes on into transformations and non-linear function families. Reading a gradient as a rate is the transferable skill.

subjects.name: Geometry: angles, polygons and reasoning
subjects.description: Angle facts, properties of shapes, similarity and congruence, with reasons stated. The assessment is the reasoning rather than the answer, and standard-route students lose levels on criterion C by producing the right number with no justification attached.

subjects.name: Mensuration: perimeter, area, surface area and volume
subjects.description: Compound shapes, prisms, cylinders and conversion between units. Reliably taught and reliably examined, and one of the few strands where sustained practice does genuinely move criterion A levels quickly.

subjects.name: Right-angled trigonometry and Pythagoras
subjects.levels: Standard route · extended adds sine and cosine rules
subjects.description: Standard covers right-angled triangles thoroughly and stops there. Extended continues into non-right-angled cases. A standard-route student who is secure on right angles and on labelling has everything the route asks for.

subjects.name: Statistics: collecting, representing, interpreting
subjects.description: Choosing a representation, calculating measures of centre and spread, and saying what a dataset does and does not support. Criterion D tasks lean on this heavily, and the missing step is almost always the interpretive sentence rather than the calculation.

subjects.name: Probability of single and combined events
subjects.levels: Standard route · extended adds conditional cases
subjects.description: Sample spaces, tree diagrams and two-way tables, with independent and mutually exclusive events. Standard stops before conditional probability. Students lose marks by computing correctly and then stating a conclusion the probability does not support.

subjects.name: Real-life modelling tasks
subjects.description: Taking a situation, choosing a mathematical model, applying it and then evaluating how well it fits. The top descriptor band requires the evaluation, and it is the single most commonly omitted sentence in standard-route work across every school.

subjects.name: On-screen examination technique
subjects.description: Reading a scenario on screen, working on paper, and entering a response in an acceptable form. Standard-route candidates sit a paper pitched at the standard syllabus, so the technique matters more than extra content: lost time, not lost knowledge, is the usual cost.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.regionsIntro: What differs between Abu Dhabi communities on this page is not price but circumstance: how a school handles the route decision, how often families transfer between curricula, and how much of the week is already committed before an evening session can happen.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Established schools with large year groups, so the route decision is usually made on several terms of criterion evidence rather than one test. Students here often have heavy co-curricular commitments, so the realistic session is late evening or weekend rather than straight after school.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A high proportion of mid-year arrivals from other systems, which is the group most likely to be placed on standard on arrival and most likely to be misread as struggling. A diagnostic across all four criteria is worth more here than extra practice on whatever the class is currently doing.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long bus journeys from island schools mean a student is often home after half past four and tired. For standard-route work that argues for shorter, more frequent sessions on specific criteria rather than a single long weekly hour that ends in diminishing returns.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Dense MYP population feeding a handful of schools, so route decisions and reporting rounds happen simultaneously across many households. Families here often compare their child's placement with a neighbour's, which is where the standard-is-the-lower-set misreading spreads fastest.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Mixed-curriculum streets where a standard-route MYP student has friends sitting IGCSE Higher tier. The comparison is unhelpful because the assessment styles differ, and explaining that difference to the student is sometimes the most useful thing a first session does.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Newer cohorts where the mathematics department may be small and the route decision correspondingly blunt. A standard placement here is more likely to be provisional than permanent, so securing the core and documenting criterion levels is the practical route to a review.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large mainland households with several children at different stages. Standard-route work benefits from a predictable slot that does not depend on a car being free, which is the ordinary constraint in a household running three school runs.

regions.name: Al Shamkha, Al Falah and Al Reef
regions.note: Thin local supply of tutors who have marked MYP criterion tasks, as opposed to tutors who can teach the content. Since the standard route's difficulty sits in criterion B and D technique rather than in the content, that distinction matters more here than anywhere.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.modesIntro: Standard-route support divides by what is actually wrong, and the four shapes below are genuinely different pieces of teaching rather than different durations of the same one.

modes.title: Securing the core
modes.description: For a student whose criterion A levels are low because earlier content never settled. The work is ratio, proportion, algebraic notation and mensuration, taught until they are automatic. This is the most productive thing available on the standard route, because almost every lost level elsewhere traces back to an unsecured core topic rather than to the topic being assessed.

Short, frequent practice with marking at the start of each session

modes.title: Criterion B investigation technique
modes.description: The standard route's top band is reached through justification, not through harder content. Sessions take a sequence or a geometric pattern, require a general rule, and then refuse to accept the rule until the student has verified it and said why it holds. It is slow work and it is the difference between a 5 and a 7 on this route.

modes.title: Criterion D application and the evaluation sentence
modes.description: The cheapest level on the standard route. Students model a situation competently and then stop, never saying how well the model fits or what it ignores. Teaching that final paragraph takes two or three sessions and moves criterion D immediately, because the mathematics was already there.

modes.title: Route review preparation
modes.description: For families who believe a standard placement was made on thin evidence and want a review at the end of MYP 4. It is an honest ask, not a guaranteed outcome, and the school decides.

sections.heading: What standard mathematics actually is, answered literally
paragraphs: Standard mathematics is the core route of MYP mathematics in years four and five of the programme, running alongside extended mathematics rather than beneath it. It uses the same four assessment criteria, the same one-to-eight level scale, the same thirty-two-point total and the same subject grades one to seven. A student on standard can be awarded a 7. The route determines the breadth of content, not the ceiling of achievement.

The content difference is best described as depth in algebra and reach in a few named topics. Extended carries the full quadratic treatment, non-right-angled trigonometry, function transformations and conditional probability. Standard covers linear algebra thoroughly, right-angled trigonometry thoroughly, single-event and combined probability, and the whole of number, ratio, geometry, mensuration and statistics. Framed that way it is obvious that standard is not a reduced syllabus so much as a differently bounded one.

Why the misreading persists is worth naming, because it affects outcomes. Schools often make the route decision at the end of MYP 3 using criterion levels, and a letter home that says a child has been placed on standard reads to a parent exactly like a setting decision. The student then hears it the same way. From that point, the realistic ceiling in their own mind drops, effort on the top descriptor bands stops, and the self-fulfilling version of the misreading arrives in the next report. A tutor's first job on this route is frequently to undo that, which takes one honest conversation and a task the student succeeds at.
bullets: Same four criteria, same one-to-eight levels, same grade ceiling of 7
Extended adds depth in algebra and reach in four named topics
The route is a content boundary, not an ability label
Undoing the lower-set reading is often the first useful session

sections.heading: The standard syllabus beside extended, strand by strand
paragraphs: Families deciding about routes, or wondering what a standard-route student has not met, are rarely shown the two syllabuses side by side. The comparison below is the practical version: what standard covers, where extended goes further, and what the difference means for a student sitting a criterion-marked task.

Read down the middle column first. Everything there is content a standard-route student is expected to handle at the top descriptor bands, which is the thing most worth remembering. A 7 on standard requires complete security across that column plus genuine justification on criterion B, and that is a demanding combination. It is not reached by drifting.

Read the right-hand column second, and only with a purpose. If your child is heading for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, those rows are the gap and it is worth knowing its size. If they are not, those rows are simply other people's syllabus and chasing them steals time from the standard core, which is where the available levels actually are. The commonest wasted tutoring on this route is extended content taught to a student who has not secured ratio. One further use for the comparison is conversational. A standard-route student who has heard from a friend on extended that they are doing the cosine rule often concludes that they are being given less mathematics. Showing them the middle column, and pointing out that criterion B at the top band is available on everything in it, is a more honest answer than reassurance and it changes how the next task gets attempted.

sections.heading: The four criteria read for a standard-route student
paragraphs: A criterion-marked report gives four numbers and no explanation, and the explanation is where the useful information lives. What follows is each criterion described by the step a standard-route student typically does not take, because that step is the whole difference between the level they have and the level above it.

Criterion A rewards applying procedures accurately in both familiar and unfamiliar situations, and the word unfamiliar is doing the work. A student who is fluent on exercises and freezes on a rearranged question is sitting in the middle bands by design, not by accident. Criterion C rewards notation, terminology and a logical line of working, which sounds cosmetic and is not: a solution where line three does not follow from line two is marked down whether or not the final answer is right.

Criterion B is the route's real opportunity. It asks a student to find a pattern, express it as a general rule, verify the rule and justify why it holds. A standard-route student who gets to justification is in the top bands using only standard content. Most do not, because describing the pattern feels like the answer. Criterion D asks for a model, applied and then evaluated, and the evaluation is the sentence nobody writes. Both of those are technique rather than content, which is exactly why a standard-route student has as much access to the top of the scale as anybody. The practical reading of a four-number report, then, is to look for the gap between the highest and the lowest level rather than at the average. A profile of 7, 4, 7, 5 is not a student who is averagely good at mathematics; it is a strong mathematician who has never been taught to justify or evaluate, and the two low numbers are the cheapest to move.

sections.heading: Where standard-route levels are actually lost
paragraphs: Four failure modes account for most of the lost levels on this route, and all four are diagnosable from a single piece of marked work. None of them is about the student being bad at mathematics, which is the diagnosis families fear and the one that is almost never correct.

The first is arithmetic leakage: a correct method undermined by a slip in fractions, negatives or place value. It costs criterion A marks and it compounds, because a wrong intermediate value makes the rest of the solution unverifiable. The second is the word-problem translation gap, where a student who can solve an equation cannot form one from a described situation. That is criterion D as much as criterion A, and it responds to practice on forming rather than solving.

The third is the justification stop, already described, and it is the largest single cause of a capped criterion B. The fourth is presentation that hides thinking: unlabelled diagrams, no units, steps omitted because they felt obvious. Criterion C is explicitly about this, and it is the fastest level on the whole route to recover, because the mathematics is already correct and only the record of it is missing. A student who starts writing units and labelling axes gains a level in a fortnight. Worth adding that none of the four shows up as a topic name on a report, which is why parents so often conclude that the problem is the current unit of work. It is almost never the current unit. A marked task from any point in the year will display the same four signatures, and that is what makes a single piece of marked work worth more to a diagnosis than a term of verbal updates from anyone.

sections.heading: From standard mathematics into the Diploma: which doors stay open
paragraphs: This is the conversation that should happen in MYP 4 and usually happens in DP1. The four Diploma mathematics courses make different assumptions about what a student arrives able to do, and the standard route leaves some of them comfortable and one of them hard.

Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level follows naturally and is a sound destination. Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is reachable with work, and it is a serious mathematics course rather than a soft option; it carries statistics and modelling that many degree routes genuinely want. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level is reachable with a bridging effort concentrated on quadratics and function behaviour. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is the hard one, because it assumes the algebraic fluency that extended mathematics was building.

What to do with that information depends entirely on the degree, not on pride. If a student is aiming at engineering, physics or certain economics and medicine routes at UAE or overseas universities, Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is commonly expected and the gap from standard should be planned for deliberately. If they are not, then Applications and Interpretation is not a consolation prize and treating it as one causes families to force a student into a course they will struggle in. The table below states the gap honestly in each direction. One more practical point: Abu Dhabi schools do not all offer all four combinations, and a school running only two will constrain the choice further. Ask the Diploma coordinator which combinations run in practice rather than which appear in the prospectus, because a course that attracts four candidates in a given year sometimes does not run at all, and that is a fact worth having before the MYP 4 route decision is made rather than after.
