sections.heading: The six subject groups, and which courses Abu Dhabi families actually book
paragraphs: A Diploma student chooses one course from each of six groups, with three taken at Higher Level, and the enquiry pattern in this emirate is heavily concentrated. Group 5 Mathematics generates more requests than all the other groups combined, which is unsurprising: it is compulsory, it has two distinct courses, and it is where a weak foundation becomes visible fastest. Group 4 sciences come next, led by Chemistry, then Group 3 Economics and Business Management, then Group 1 English A.

Groups 2 and 6 generate fewer requests and are much harder to fill. A Standard Level French or Spanish student with an oral four weeks away is a common and urgent enquiry; a Higher Level Arabic B student or a Visual Arts candidate is a rare one, and the specialist may not exist in a UAE time zone at all. That asymmetry is worth knowing before a family builds a plan around finding someone locally.

There is a second pattern worth naming. Requests cluster around the components that are assessed late and taught early. The scientific investigation, the Mathematics exploration, the Extended Essay and the Higher Level English essay are all introduced in DP1 and completed under pressure in DP2, which is precisely why they arrive as emergencies. A family that books a single-component block on one of them in DP1, when nobody feels any urgency at all, is buying the cheapest useful hours in the whole programme, and buying them at the only point when a tutor has room to teach the skill rather than rescue a draft.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches against Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: This is the most consequential choice a Diploma student makes and the one most often made for the wrong reason. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic, proof-oriented course. Applications and Interpretation is statistical, modelling-led and assumes a graphing calculator in nearly every question. They are not easier and harder versions of the same syllabus, and a student who dislikes algebra does not automatically belong on Applications, where regression, hypothesis testing and financial mathematics make their own demands.

The weighting structures are identical, which hides the difference. At Standard Level both courses set two papers at 40 per cent each plus the exploration at 20. At Higher Level both set three papers, at 30, 30 and 20 per cent, plus the exploration at 20. So a family comparing the two on paper sees the same architecture and concludes the courses are similar, which they are not. The difference is entirely in what the questions ask for.

Where it matters most is university entry, and this is where honest advice has to be specific rather than general. Engineering, physics, mathematics and several economics degrees typically expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, while many other courses accept either. The only safe method is to read the published entry requirements for the specific programme at the specific university, including Khalifa University, United Arab Emirates University, Zayed University and NYU Abu Dhabi for students staying in the emirate. Nothing on this page should be treated as a substitute for that, and no tutor should present a course choice as a requirement when the university's own page is a click away.

sections.heading: The sciences after the 2023 guide, and where the 24 investigation marks sit
paragraphs: The Diploma sciences were reorganised for first examinations in 2025, and the change matters for anyone buying tuition. The internal assessment is now a single scientific investigation marked out of 24 across four criteria: research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation, each worth six. It carries 20 per cent of the final grade at both Standard and Higher Level. Paper 1 is in two parts, multiple choice and data-based, at 36 per cent; Paper 2 is at 44 per cent.

The practical consequence is that a quarter of the available marks sit in two criteria most students treat as an afterthought. Conclusion and evaluation together are worth 12 of the 24, and they are the parts written last, usually late at night, usually thinly. A draft that describes a limitation without saying what it does to the result has written an evaluation that scores in the bottom band while reading perfectly acceptably. That is a thirty-minute fix with an outside reader and almost never gets one.

On the written papers, the pattern is just as consistent. Data-based questions in Paper 1B are answered from memory rather than from the data supplied. Extended responses in Paper 2 assert a correct principle and skip the derivation the mark scheme pays for. Command terms are read as synonyms when they are not. None of these is a content gap, and all of them are visible in one marked paper. Confirm the current weightings with your school's Diploma coordinator, because the guides are revised and a stale figure is worse than none.

sections.heading: The orals: the most coachable component in the Diploma
paragraphs: Every Group 1 and Group 2 student sits an individual oral, and it is the single most improvable assessment in the Diploma for a reason nobody says out loud: it is rehearsable. A written paper is sat once under conditions nobody can simulate exactly. An oral is a performance of a known length on prepared material, and performances improve with rehearsal in a way that recall does not.

In English A: Language and Literature the individual oral is worth 30 per cent at Standard Level and 20 per cent at Higher Level, which makes it the largest single component at Standard Level. Students routinely prepare it for a fortnight. The components they prepare for months are worth less. In Group 2 languages the oral carries a comparable share and is where fluency, not vocabulary, decides the band, which is exactly what rehearsal addresses.

Rehearsing over video has a specific advantage: the session can be recorded and the student can hear themselves, which is uncomfortable and extremely effective. Most students have never heard their own oral. The first time they do, they notice the filler, the under-length answers and the three points they meant to make and did not, without any of it needing to be pointed out. Three rehearsals with playback, spread across a fortnight, change a band more reliably than any amount of additional reading. The one caution is timing. An oral rehearsed six weeks out and then left alone goes stale, and an oral rehearsed the night before is a recital rather than a performance. A fortnight of spaced rehearsal, finishing two or three days before the assessment, is the window that produces the best bands.

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level: what the extra content actually is
paragraphs: Families often ask whether a student should drop a subject from Higher to Standard Level, and the answer depends on what the difference is in that specific course, because it varies. In some courses Higher Level adds an extra paper. In others it adds content threaded through the existing papers. In English A it adds a separate written essay. Treating Higher Level as a general intensity setting is how the decision gets made badly.

The level change also has consequences beyond workload. A Diploma requires three subjects at Higher Level, so dropping one means raising another. University entry requirements are frequently expressed at Higher Level for the subject most relevant to the degree, so a student intending to read engineering who drops Mathematics to Standard Level may have closed a door that is difficult to reopen. Those are the questions to settle before the timetable change, and they belong to the school's Diploma coordinator rather than to a tutor.

Where tutoring genuinely helps is in establishing whether the Higher Level course is beyond the student or merely behind. Those look identical from a report grade and completely different on a marked paper. A student who scores respectably on Higher Level questions from taught topics and badly on anything from the first term is behind, which is fixable. A student who finds the taught material itself out of reach under time is in a different position, and an honest tutor says so rather than selling two more terms of sessions.

sections.heading: Where Diploma marks are lost, group by group
paragraphs: After enough marked papers the pattern is monotonous, which is good news: monotonous problems are teachable. Across every group, the largest single category of lost marks is a correct idea expressed in a shape the mark scheme does not reward. The second largest is time. Content genuinely never met is a distant third, and it is the only one of the three that most families assume is the problem.

The table below is the diagnostic shortlist a first session works through. It is deliberately concrete, because a general instruction to read the question more carefully has never improved anybody's mark. Telling a Biology student that the word explain requires a because, and then marking four answers until the because appears without prompting, does.

One subject-group note worth adding. In Group 5 the losses are mechanical: method omitted, so partial credit is unavailable. In Group 4 they are evaluative: a limitation named with no consequence attached. In Group 3 they are judgemental: an evaluation that lists and never chooses. In Group 1 they are structural: an argument asserted and never sustained. Four different problems, four different remedies, and a tutor who treats them all as read the question more carefully is not going to move any of them. There is also an order worth respecting. Fixing the mechanical losses first produces visible mark movement inside a month and buys the student enough confidence to tackle the evaluative and structural problems, which take a term. Starting with the hardest category, which is what a keen tutor instinctively does, leaves a student working hard on the slowest-moving part of their own script while the easy marks continue to leak away in every paper they sit.

sections.heading: The honesty line across the investigation, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge
paragraphs: A page organised around assessment components has to be clear about which of them a tutor may touch and how. The rule is the same across all of them: a tutor teaches the skill the component assesses, explains what the criteria reward and how many marks each carries, reads what the student has produced, and writes down what the criteria would credit and refuse. The student then revises it, in their own words, with their own judgements and their own data.

What is never acceptable is authoring, supplying or editing assessed work to completion. This is a live issue in this market rather than a theoretical one: at least one site ranking for these searches sells finished Internal Assessments. Under IB rules that is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student's own certification rather than on the vendor. A deadline is not a reason to buy one, and no tutor who values a student's diploma will come near it.

Two operational consequences follow. Feedback is written rather than spoken, so a supervisor, a coordinator or a parent can see exactly what was said and when. And board materials are referenced and linked rather than reproduced: subject guides, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB and are used on screen from the official source. Both of those make the support auditable, which is the point. If a Diploma coordinator asked how a student was helped, the answer should be a document rather than a memory.

sections.heading: How private tuition reaches an Abu Dhabi student
paragraphs: One-to-one, over live video, at a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time. The session uses a shared whiteboard, a document camera or phone stand so handwritten working is visible in both directions, and the real past paper annotated live rather than a retyped version. Sessions are recorded, which matters particularly for Group 2 orals and for Mathematics working a student will want to revisit.

IB Gram does not send tutors into homes anywhere in the United Arab Emirates. Visiting a student's address is a service we run only in India. On a page about subject and level matching, that constraint is the argument rather than the apology: the number of people who can teach Higher Level Further Mathematics, hold a valid tutoring permit and reach a specific Abu Dhabi community by 18:00 is frequently zero, while the number who teach the course is not.

Coverage is stated before anything is paid. Mathematics at both levels and in both courses, the three sciences, English A and Economics start within a week in normal conditions. Business Management at Higher Level, French and Spanish are usually available with a little more notice. Arabic B at Higher Level, Further Mathematics, Design Technology, Music and Visual Arts are genuinely thin, and where nothing suitable is free you are told so and offered a later slot, a wait, or nothing rather than a generalist described as a specialist. Where a specialist sits in another time zone, the session times that implies are stated plainly before you decide, because a tutor three hours west means a 21:00 start in Abu Dhabi and that is a real constraint on a school night rather than a detail.

sections.heading: Choosing a private tutor: six questions worth asking
paragraphs: Most families assess a tutor on qualifications and rapport, both of which matter and neither of which predicts much on their own. The six questions below are more diagnostic, and a tutor who answers all of them well is almost always worth booking regardless of where they studied.

Which course and level do you teach, and can you name the components and their weightings? A specialist answers immediately. Where do students lose marks in this course? A good answer is specific to components, not general advice about revision. What will exist after four weeks that I can look at? The right answer is a marked script, an error log and a written note. How do you handle my child's internal assessment? The right answer draws the line at annotation. What happens if this is not working? The right answer involves a review against evidence. And do you hold a private tuition work permit?

That last one is worth asking of anybody. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and those tutoring without it are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no figure should be quoted to you. Asking the question also tells you something about how seriously the person on the other end takes the arrangement.

process.title: Send the course title and level exactly as the school entered them
process.description: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL is a different request from Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches SL, and a family that writes maths tutor will get a coin toss. The school's entry record or statement of entry is the only reliable source, and it takes a minute to check.

process.title: Name the component, if you know it
process.description: Paper 3, the HL essay, the investigation's evaluation criterion, an individual oral. A component-level request produces a far better tutor match and a far shorter diagnostic than a general description of the subject being difficult, and it is usually knowable from the last piece of marked work.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the specialist
process.description: A real lesson on real content with the person who would teach the course, booked without card details. It is also where the course and level get confirmed out loud, which catches the mismatches that a form does not. If the match is wrong, this is the cheap place to find out.

process.title: A timed component diagnostic
process.description: Session one is timed questions from the actual component, marked against the published mark scheme while the student watches. The output is an error log classified by topic and command term. Teaching that starts before this exists is aimed at a described problem rather than a measured one.

process.title: Fortnightly marked work and a term review
process.description: Timed questions every second session, marked and returned with a one-page note. At the end of a term the first diagnostic sits beside the latest comparable one. Where little has moved, the useful responses are a different tutor, a different approach, or stopping, and we will say which we think applies.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the course, not the subject
whyPoints.description: Higher Level and Standard Level are different courses, and the two Mathematics courses are not difficulty settings of one syllabus. Tutors are matched from the school's own entry record, and the first session confirms it out loud, because a competent tutor teaching slightly the wrong course is the most expensive failure in this market.

whyPoints.title: Weightings known before teaching starts
whyPoints.description: A tutor who cannot name the components and their shares is not yet a specialist in that course. Knowing that the investigation's conclusion and evaluation carry 12 of its 24 marks, or that the individual oral is 30 per cent at Standard Level, changes where a term's hours go.

whyPoints.title: Component blocks quoted as finite
whyPoints.description: Paper 3 technique, an HL essay, an oral rehearsal or an evaluation criterion are defined pieces of work with an end date. They are quoted that way rather than converted into an open-ended weekly commitment, and they are the highest return per hour available in the Diploma.

whyPoints.title: Honest about fit, including upwards
whyPoints.description: Sometimes the marked paper shows a student is behind on a Higher Level course, which is fixable. Sometimes it shows the course is out of reach under time, which is a different conversation and belongs with the Diploma coordinator. Selling two more terms instead of having it is the easy option and the wrong one.

whyPoints.title: The assessed-work line stated in advance
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and annotates; the student writes. Nothing assessed is authored, supplied or edited to completion, and feedback is written so a coordinator could audit it. In a market where completed Internal Assessments are openly on sale, that is a substantive difference.

whyPoints.title: Scarce courses named as scarce
whyPoints.description: Arabic B at Higher Level, Further Mathematics, Design Technology, Music and Visual Arts are thin in UAE evening hours and you are told so before paying. A generalist presented as a specialist in those courses produces a cancelled arrangement in week three and a wasted month in between.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether we ask for a maths tutor or name the exact course?
faqs.answer: It matters more than almost anything else on this page. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented with a non-calculator paper; Applications and Interpretation is statistical, modelling-led and assumes a graphing calculator throughout. A tutor strong in one can teach the other's topics and quietly teach them the wrong way, which produces correct sessions and no mark movement. The weighting structures are identical at each level, which hides the difference. Send the course title and level exactly as your child's school entered them, from the statement of entry rather than from memory, and the match stops being a coin toss.

faqs.question: What share of a DP science grade does the investigation carry now?
faqs.answer: Twenty per cent at both Standard and Higher Level, marked out of 24 across four criteria worth six marks each: research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. The useful consequence is that conclusion and evaluation together carry 12 of those 24, and they are the parts students write last and thinnest. An evaluation that names a limitation without stating what it does to the result reads perfectly well and scores in the bottom band. Confirm the current structure with your school's Diploma coordinator, since the science guides changed for first examinations in 2025 and are revised between cohorts.

faqs.question: My son is on Chemistry HL and sinking. Should he drop to Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Settle one question first: is he behind, or is the course beyond him? Those look identical on a report grade and completely different on a marked paper. A student who scores respectably on Paper 2 questions from topics taught in the first year, and badly on everything recent, is behind, which is fixable in a term. A student who finds the taught material itself out of reach under time is in a different position. One timed diagnostic distinguishes them. The decision itself belongs with the Diploma coordinator, because dropping a Higher Level subject means raising another and may affect university entry requirements.

faqs.question: Which Mathematics course do UAE universities expect for engineering?
faqs.answer: Engineering and physical-science degrees commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, but the only safe answer is the one published by the specific programme. Read the entry requirements on the university's own page: Khalifa University, United Arab Emirates University, Zayed University and NYU Abu Dhabi all publish theirs, and they do not all say the same thing. No tutor should present a course choice as a hard requirement when the university's own page is one click away, and no page should imply that tutoring is needed to satisfy an admissions rule.

faqs.question: How much of the English A grade is the individual oral worth?
faqs.answer: In Language and Literature it is 30 per cent at Standard Level and 20 per cent at Higher Level, which makes it the largest single component at Standard Level. Most students prepare it for about a fortnight. It is also the most improvable assessment in the Diploma, because unlike a written paper it is a rehearsable performance on prepared material. Three rehearsals with playback across two weeks change a band more reliably than additional reading does, and recorded video sessions help here specifically: most students have never heard their own oral, and the first time they do they fix half of it unprompted.

faqs.question: What does Paper 3 at Higher Level actually test?
faqs.answer: In both Mathematics courses Paper 3 is two extended problem-solving questions worth 20 per cent of the grade, and it is where Higher Level candidates most often run out of time rather than ideas. Each question builds across several parts, so an early error propagates, and students who have practised only short exam questions have never experienced a problem that develops over twenty minutes. It is the clearest case on this page for a single-component block: four to eight sessions on sustained problems, six to ten weeks before the examination, rather than general course revision.

faqs.question: Why do marks go missing on content my daughter clearly understands?
faqs.answer: Because the mark scheme pays for a shape rather than for the idea, and the shapes are not interchangeable. In Mathematics, method not written down means a slip in the last line costs every mark instead of one. In the sciences, a correct principle asserted without the derivation scores half. In Economics, an evaluation that balances considerations without choosing cannot reach the top band. In English, an argument asserted and never sustained reads fluently and scores descriptively. All four are visible in one marked paper and none of them is a knowledge problem, which is why the first session is a paper rather than a conversation.

faqs.question: Can a single tutor cover two Diploma subjects for the same student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth being careful about when. Mathematics and Physics is a genuine pairing: the overlap in algebraic technique is real and a strong tutor in both saves a slot. Chemistry and Biology is a weaker pairing than it looks, because the assessment demands differ more than the content suggests. Economics and Business Management is usually a false economy. The honest test is whether the tutor can name the components and weightings of both courses without checking. If they can, the pairing is real; if they hesitate on the second, you are buying one specialist and one generalist.

faqs.question: How scarce are tutors for less common Diploma courses in the emirate?
faqs.answer: Genuinely scarce, and this is disclosed before booking rather than discovered later. Mathematics in both courses and at both levels, the three sciences, English A and Economics are reliably available in UAE evening hours and usually start within a week. Business Management at Higher Level, French and Spanish need a little more notice. Arabic B at Higher Level, Further Mathematics, Design Technology, Music and Visual Arts are thin, and sometimes the honest answer is that nothing suitable is free. No competitor page in this market discloses a coverage limit at all, which is a choice rather than an oversight.

faqs.question: Will a tutor help my daughter with her Mathematics exploration?
faqs.answer: Within a boundary that is worth stating precisely. A tutor will explain what the five criteria reward and how the 20 marks are allocated, discuss whether a proposed question is developable, teach the mathematics the question needs, read a draft your daughter has written and write down what the criteria would credit and refuse. She then revises it herself, in her own words. What never happens is authoring, supplying or editing assessed work to completion. At least one site ranking for these searches sells finished Internal Assessments, which is malpractice under IB rules and risks her own certification.

faqs.question: Is it better to start in DP1 or wait until the components get closer?
faqs.answer: DP1, and the reason is cost rather than virtue. The components that arrive as emergencies in DP2, including the scientific investigation, the Mathematics exploration, the Extended Essay and the Higher Level English essay, are all introduced in DP1 when nobody feels any urgency. A four-session block on one of them in DP1 does the work of three times as many hours bought in a panic in November of DP2, because there is room to teach the skill rather than to triage a draft. The hours bought early are the cheapest useful hours in the whole programme.

faqs.question: What should I ask a prospective tutor before booking anything?
faqs.answer: Six things. Which course and level do you teach, and what are its components and weightings? Where do students lose marks in this specific course? What will exist after four weeks that I can look at? How do you handle an internal assessment draft? What happens if this is not working? And do you hold a private tuition work permit? A specialist answers the first two immediately and specifically. A generalist offers advice about revision technique. The permit question is worth asking of anybody, since private tutoring in the UAE requires one under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023.

faqs.question: Does my child's tutor need a UAE work permit for private lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, whose service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing and lists a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so be cautious of any amount quoted to you.

faqs.question: How is a video session supposed to work for handwritten mathematics?
faqs.answer: Through a second camera pointed at the page, which sounds improvised and works better than sitting beside someone. A phone on a cheap stand, or a tablet with a stylus, lets the tutor watch the working as it is produced rather than inspect a finished answer. That is the whole point for Group 5 and for Physics, where the marks sit in the method. The real past paper is annotated live on a shared screen, and the session is recorded, so a worked solution from October is still available in April. Nothing on that equipment list costs more than one in-home session at market rate.

faqs.question: Are the weightings on this page definitely current for my child's cohort?
faqs.answer: Treat them as a working guide and confirm them with your school's Diploma coordinator. IB subject guides are revised between cohorts, and the sciences changed shape for first examinations in 2025, so a figure that was right for one year group can be wrong for the next. No IB examination or results date appears anywhere on this page, because the organisation's own site blocks automated checking and an unverified date published across a site is worse than no date at all. Where this site quotes Cambridge or Pearson dates elsewhere, they come from those boards' own published key dates.

abu-dhabi/ib-private-tutor.closingHeading: Name the course, then the component
abu-dhabi/ib-private-tutor.closingBody: The single most useful thing you can send is the course title and level exactly as the school entered them, plus the component the last piece of marked work went wrong on. With those two facts a shortlist comes back the same day, and the free trial lesson is a real lesson with the specialist rather than a call with a coordinator. Session one is timed questions from that component, marked against the published mark scheme while your child watches. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, recorded, and the coverage position for your course is stated before anything is paid for.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work in the primary phase: early reading, number fluency, written sentence construction and the research skills a unit of inquiry demands. Each one has taught inside an IB PYP classroom or has trained in the programme, and each works one-to-one over video with your child's own books on screen.

intro.heading: What a PYP tutor should be able to show you after six weeks
paragraphs: A parent in Al Reem Island or Khalifa City types IB PYP home tutor in Abu Dhabi into Google for a reason that is rarely about homework. The school report says your child is meeting expectations. The parent-teacher conference lasted eleven minutes and ended warmly. And yet the reading at bedtime is slower than it was last year, the times tables still need fingers, and nobody has given you a number you can hold on to. The Primary Years Programme is designed that way on purpose - it reports against learning outcomes rather than ranking children - which is excellent practice and completely unhelpful if you are trying to work out whether to pay for help.

So this page is built around evidence rather than reassurance. Every claim a tutor makes about a primary child can be checked against something physical: a running record of a page read aloud, a timed set of number facts, two pieces of writing three weeks apart with the same task and the same marking criteria, a short list of the research steps your child took in their last unit of inquiry. If a tutor cannot produce those, the only thing being measured is your invoice.

The second thing this page does is answer the home-tutoring question honestly, because the search term says home tutor. Visiting primary tutors are a real and sizeable market in Abu Dhabi. Published market rates run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour once travel is priced in, against AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified online tutor, and the gap is almost entirely the drive. For a Khalifa City or Al Raha household, a tutor coming from the island after 16:00 has a commute that is neither short nor predictable, and the family pays for it twice - once in the rate, once in the ten minutes at the start of the lesson when a six-year-old is being peeled away from whatever they were doing.

IB Gram does not send a tutor to your address anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India. In Abu Dhabi the lesson happens over live video, one child and one tutor, with the child's own exercise book under a camera or scanned and annotated on screen. That is not a compromise dressed up as a feature. It means a family in Al Reef can work with a tutor who has actually taught PYP phonics and PYP number, rather than whichever adult is willing to drive out to Al Reef on a Tuesday, and it means a 40-minute session can start at 16:15 while a young child is still awake enough to use it.

What follows is the detail: what the PYP assesses and how, what good evidence looks like week by week, where primary reading and number quietly break, what the Exhibition in the final year is and what a tutor may and may not touch, how Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies sit alongside the programme under federal rules, and how a 35-minute online lesson for a young child is actually run. Read the report-reading section at the end before your next conference; it is the cheapest thing on this page.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The Primary Years Programme is not one undifferentiated block. What a tutor works on in FS2 has almost nothing in common with what a Year 6 child needs in the months before the Exhibition. These are the four bands Abu Dhabi primary families ask about, and what support looks like inside each.

programmes.name: PYP Early Years
programmes.description: Play-based inquiry, oral language, early phonics and number sense. Children are learning that print carries meaning, that quantity can be counted and compared, and that a question can be asked of an adult. There is no written assessment worth the name; progress is read from observation, photographs and what a child can say about their own work.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi families often arrive in FS2 from three different systems in three years, because of moves between emirates and between countries. A child who did a phonics-first English nursery and a child who did a play-based one will sound equally fluent and decode very differently. One short baseline session usually settles which of the two you have.

programmes.name: PYP Years 1 to 3
programmes.description: The decoding years. Phonics moves to fluency, fluency to comprehension, and number moves from counting to place value and the four operations. This is where a gap is cheapest to fix and easiest to miss, because a child who reads haltingly but accurately still looks like a reader to a parent listening at bedtime.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi this band collides with the start of Arabic as an additional language for non-Arab pupils, which federal regulation requires private schools to teach. A child managing English decoding and a second script in the same term is carrying a genuine load, and the English work often stalls first.

programmes.name: PYP Years 4 to 6
programmes.description: Reading to learn rather than learning to read. Multi-step word problems, fractions, data handling, extended writing with paragraphs that do separate jobs, and research skills inside units of inquiry. Children who coasted on fluent decoding and quick recall start to find that neither is sufficient.
programmes.countryNote: This is the band that generates most of the tutoring enquiries from Khalifa City, Al Raha Gardens and Yas Island, and the trigger is almost always a Year 4 or Year 5 report that mentions problem solving or written explanation for the first time.

programmes.name: The PYP Exhibition year
programmes.description: A collaborative, student-led inquiry presented to the school community, drawing together the programme's key concepts and the approaches-to-learning skills. It is the first time many children own a piece of work end to end: choosing a line of inquiry, planning it, gathering information, and standing up to explain it.
programmes.countryNote: Exhibition term is also the term Abu Dhabi families are deciding on MYP entry or a move to a British Year 7, so the calendar is crowded. Support here is process coaching - questioning, planning, source checking, rehearsal - and nothing else.

programmes.name: The step into MYP
programmes.description: Subject teachers instead of one class teacher, eight subject groups, criterion-related assessment with letters and descriptors, and a timetable that moves. The academic content is rarely the problem. Self-management is: knowing what is due, where it is written down, and what the criteria actually ask for.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi schools run the PYP and the MYP on one site and several do not, so some children change campus and programme in the same September. A short block across the summer aimed at organisation rather than content is usually a better buy than subject tutoring in term one.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary tutoring is usually sold as English and maths. That is too coarse to be useful. Below are the strands Abu Dhabi PYP families actually ask for, with what each one assesses and the point at which it tends to break.

subjects.name: Early reading and phonics
subjects.description: Grapheme-phoneme correspondence, blending, segmenting and the irregular high-frequency words English refuses to make regular. Breaks when a child has memorised enough words to sound fluent on familiar text and cannot decode an unfamiliar one. A running record on a cold page exposes it in four minutes.

subjects.name: Reading comprehension and inference
subjects.description: Retrieval, inference, vocabulary in context, and the difference between what a text says and what it implies. Marks and comments are lost on inference questions, where children answer the question they expected rather than the one asked. Fixed by teaching the question types, not by reading more.

subjects.name: Writing: sentence and paragraph construction
subjects.description: Subordination, punctuation that carries meaning, paragraphing that does a job, and vocabulary choice. Most primary writing problems in Abu Dhabi classrooms are sentence-level, not idea-level: the child has plenty to say and no reliable way to end a sentence.

subjects.name: Number: place value and the four operations
subjects.description: Counting, place value, written methods and recall of number facts. The gap that matters is automaticity. A child who calculates 7 x 8 correctly but slowly has no working memory left for the word problem wrapped around it, which is why Year 4 word problems feel sudden.

subjects.name: Fractions, decimals and proportional reasoning
subjects.description: Equivalence, comparison, operations with fractions, and the link to decimals and percentages. The single largest source of upper-primary maths anxiety, usually because equivalence was taught as a procedure rather than as a picture a child can draw.

subjects.name: Multi-step problem solving
subjects.description: Reading a problem, identifying what is being asked, choosing operations in order, and checking plausibility. Children lose it at the first step rather than the arithmetic. A session here is mostly annotation and talk, with surprisingly little calculating.

subjects.name: Science within units of inquiry
subjects.description: Living things, materials, forces, earth and space, handled through the transdisciplinary themes rather than as a timetabled subject. Support is about questioning, fair testing, recording observation and explaining a result in writing - the skills that transfer to MYP sciences.

subjects.name: Research and information skills
subjects.description: Framing a question, finding sources that answer it, judging whether a source is worth using, taking notes without copying, and crediting what was used. This is the backbone of the Exhibition and the skill most often missing when a child's project looks copied.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Script, sound-letter mapping, high-frequency vocabulary and the spoken forms used in class. Federal regulation requires private schools to teach Arabic language, so this is not optional enrichment. Non-Arab pupils most often stall at reading unvowelled text.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Standard Arabic reading and writing for Arab pupils, which runs on a different curriculum and at a different pace from the additional-language route. Children who speak a dialect at home and meet Standard Arabic only at school are the usual case.

subjects.name: Self-management and organisation
subjects.description: Recording what is due, breaking a task into steps, starting without a prompt, and checking work before it goes in. Treated in the PYP as an approaches-to-learning skill, which means it is taught and can be taught again. The highest-value target in the year before MYP.

subjects.name: Spoken English and presentation
subjects.description: Explaining a process aloud, answering a question in a full sentence, and presenting work to a group. Rehearsed directly before the Exhibition and before any class presentation, with recording and playback rather than advice.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi primary families are spread across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the newer mainland communities, and the practical constraint is almost always the school bus and what time it drops. These are the communities we are asked about most, with the detail that changes a session plan.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense towers with several British and international primaries within a short radius. Buses drop early, so a 15:45 or 16:00 start is realistic and an exhausted 18:00 session is avoidable for a Year 1 or Year 2 child.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Villa and low-rise housing around a small cluster of well-known primaries. Parents here most often ask for reading and early writing support, and often for two siblings in consecutive 35-minute slots rather than one long hour.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Large villa community with a long bus run for children attending island schools. A 16:30 start is safer than 16:00. This is where upper-primary maths and problem-solving enquiries cluster most heavily.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Family housing feeding a mix of British and IB primaries, with after-school clubs running to 16:30 twice a week. Families here commonly book one weekday session and one Friday or weekend morning.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Bateen
regions.note: Established island neighbourhoods close to several long-standing schools, so bus journeys are short and children arrive home comparatively fresh. Arabic support requests are proportionally higher in this cluster.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Newer schools and a young primary population, with a high proportion of families who moved emirate or country within the last two years. Baseline reading and number checks matter more here than anywhere else in the emirate.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Mainland villas a long drive from the island, which is exactly where a visiting tutor's travel premium bites hardest and where online delivery changes the arithmetic most. Evening slots after 17:00 are the norm.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large mixed residential districts with children travelling to schools across the emirate. Session timing varies household by household, so we set the slot after the first week rather than before it.

regions.name: Masdar City and Al Falah
regions.note: Smaller, newer communities where the local primary options are limited and some children commute considerable distances. Short, twice-weekly sessions survive a long bus ride better than one long weekly lesson.

schoolClusters.city: The island: Al Bateen, Al Mushrif and Al Khalidiyah
schoolClusters.note: Long-established primaries within short bus journeys of each other, which is why this cluster generates requests for early-morning weekend sessions as often as weekday ones. abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.modesIntro: Primary sessions are short by design. A 60-minute lesson is a secondary format, and buying one for a six-year-old mostly buys you fifteen minutes of a tired child. These are the three shapes that work, all delivered one-to-one over live video.

modes.title: Weekly 40-minute one-to-one
modes.description: The default for Year 3 upwards. Long enough to revisit last week's target, teach one new thing and set a short practice task; short enough that the child is still thinking at the end. The parent gets a two-line note naming the target and what to practise before the next session.

modes.title: Twice-weekly 30-minute reading block
modes.description: The format for FS2 to Year 2 and for any older child whose decoding is the bottleneck. Early reading responds to frequency rather than duration, so two short sessions beat one long one. Each session includes a cold read, a taught point and a re-read of the same text.

Explicit phonics teaching rather than general reading practice

modes.title: Holiday or half-term catch-up block
modes.description: Four to six sessions across a school break, aimed at one named gap: place value before Year 4, fractions before Year 5, paragraphing before Year 6, or organisation before MYP entry. Bought as a block with a stated start and finish rather than an open-ended arrangement.

modes.title: Sibling pair sessions
modes.description: Two children in the same household, consecutive slots rather than a shared screen. Siblings two or more years apart need different content and different pacing, and sharing a lesson usually means one of them is waiting. Consecutive 30-minute slots keep the evening to one hour in total.

sections.heading: What a search for a PYP home tutor in Abu Dhabi is usually asking for
paragraphs: The literal answer first. A PYP home tutor is a tutor who works with a child enrolled in the IB Primary Years Programme, one-to-one, outside school hours. In Abu Dhabi that service exists in two shapes: someone who drives to the family's address, and someone who teaches over live video. Published market rates for the first run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel folded in; the second sits around AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor, with budget online providers advertising from AED 45. IB Gram works in the second shape only. We do not run home visits in the UAE, and the page says so here rather than in a footnote.

The reason parents type home tutor rather than online tutor is rarely a strong preference for a stranger in the sitting room. It is a proxy for three things: one-to-one attention, someone who will actually look at the child's own books, and a time that fits around a school bus. All three are deliverable over video, and the third is deliverable better, because nobody is driving from Al Bateen to Al Reef at 16:30. The one thing a visiting tutor genuinely offers that video does not is physical presence with a very young child, and that is handled by a parent being in the room rather than by paying for a commute.

Where the two formats really differ is the pool. A family in Al Reef choosing an in-home tutor is choosing from the adults willing to make that drive on a Tuesday afternoon. The same family choosing online is choosing from everyone who can teach PYP number fluency. For a mainstream Year 2 reading problem the pool size may not matter much. For Arabic as an additional language, for a child with English as a second language, or for upper-primary proportional reasoning taught the way the PYP teaches it, the pool is the whole decision.

sections.heading: The PYP sets no exams, so what counts as evidence?
paragraphs: In the Diploma Programme a parent can read a mock grade and argue about it. The PYP gives you descriptors against learning outcomes, a portfolio, and a conference. That is pedagogically sound and it leaves a paying parent with nothing to measure. So the first thing a PYP tutor should do is manufacture measurable evidence, from the first session, and hand it to you dated.

There are four kinds worth having. A running record: the child reads an unfamiliar page aloud, the tutor marks every error and self-correction, and you get an accuracy rate and a reading band. A number-facts check: a fixed set of facts, timed, repeated identically every three weeks, so recall speed is visible rather than inferred. A dated writing sample: the same task type, the same criteria, three weeks apart, with the criteria annotated on both. And a short log of what the child could and could not do unaided in their last unit of inquiry.

None of this replaces the school's own assessment, and it is not an attempt to grade a programme that deliberately does not grade. It is a tutor's working record, which exists so that the decision to continue or stop paying is made on something other than a feeling. The table below sets out what should exist at each point in a twelve-week plan, and who produces it. If a tutor cannot name the artefact for week four before week one starts, the plan is not a plan.

sections.heading: Reading: the measure that quietly decides everything else
paragraphs: Primary reading has two separate engines and they fail separately. Decoding is the mechanical conversion of print to sound. Comprehension is making meaning from what has been decoded. A child can have a serious decoding problem and sound like a competent reader on a familiar book, because memory is doing the work. The same child meets an unseen text in Year 4 and the floor disappears. This is the most common misdiagnosis in primary tutoring, and it is why the first session should always involve a cold page.

A running record settles it in four minutes. The child reads roughly a hundred words of unfamiliar text aloud; the tutor marks substitutions, omissions, insertions and self-corrections; accuracy comes out as a percentage and errors get sorted into types. A child substituting visually similar words has a decoding problem. A child reading accurately and fluently but unable to say what happened has a comprehension problem. A child reading accurately, slowly, with no expression, has a fluency problem, and fluency is the bridge: slow decoding consumes the working memory that comprehension needs.

The teaching that follows is different in each case and should look different in the lesson. Decoding gets explicit, sequenced phonics with real decodable text, not more library books. Fluency gets repeated reading of the same passage until it sounds like speech, which children find oddly satisfying and parents find strange. Comprehension gets question types taught by name - retrieval, inference, vocabulary in context, author's choice - because most comprehension marks in upper primary are lost to answering a question the child expected rather than the one printed. Inference in particular is a teachable skill, not a quality of mind, and twenty minutes a week on it changes upper-primary reading comments within a term.
bullets: A cold, unfamiliar page in session one, or the diagnosis is a guess
Error types matter more than the error count: substitution, omission, self-correction

sections.heading: Number fluency, and why Year 4 word problems feel sudden
paragraphs: Parents in Khalifa City and Al Raha Gardens tend to call in Year 4 or Year 5, and the trigger is usually a report comment about problem solving. The problem is almost never problem solving. It is that recall of number facts has not become automatic, so every multi-step question spends the child's working memory on arithmetic and leaves nothing for the structure of the problem. Fix automaticity and a chunk of the problem-solving comment resolves itself without anybody teaching problem solving.

The diagnostic is simple and repeatable. A fixed set of number facts, timed, same set every three weeks. Not a worksheet of eighty questions, which measures endurance; a short set that measures speed. Alongside it, one multi-step word problem read aloud with the child annotating rather than calculating: underline what is being asked, circle the numbers that matter, write the order of operations before touching one. Watching where a child stops is the whole diagnosis, and it is usually step one.

The sequence of real breakpoints is predictable. Place value in Year 2 and Year 3, because everything written depends on it. Multiplication and division facts in Year 3 and Year 4. Fraction equivalence in Year 4, which is the single largest source of upper-primary maths anxiety and is usually a victim of being taught as a procedure before it was ever drawn. Proportional reasoning in Year 5 and Year 6, which is the direct ancestor of the ratio and percentage work that decides IGCSE and MYP maths sets later. A tutor who can name which of these is missing, and show you the check that proves it, is worth more than one who covers the week's homework.

sections.heading: Writing in the PYP: sentence level before structure
paragraphs: Most primary writing feedback in Abu Dhabi reports is about structure and ideas, and most primary writing problems are about sentences. A Year 4 child who writes one enormous breathless sentence per paragraph does not have an idea problem; they have no reliable way to end a sentence. Teaching a paragraph plan to that child is a waste of a session, because the plan will be written in the same unpunctuated prose it was supposed to organise.

The order that works is narrow and dull and effective. First, sentence boundaries: the child writes four sentences about one picture and reads them aloud, hearing where each stops. Then subordination: one taught connective at a time, used until it is boring. Then punctuation that carries meaning rather than decoration - commas separating clauses, not sprinkled by instinct. Only then paragraphing, taught as jobs rather than lengths: this paragraph introduces, this one gives evidence, this one explains. Vocabulary last, because an ambitious word in a broken sentence loses more than it gains.

Evidence here is easier than parents expect. Two pieces of writing on the same task type, three weeks apart, with the school's own criteria annotated on both. The second piece should show the taught feature appearing without a prompt. If a child uses the taught connective only when reminded, the feature has not been learned, and that is useful information rather than failure. The PYP's own assessment practice - portfolios, conferences, dated samples - is unusually well suited to this, because the school is already collecting exactly the artefacts a tutor should be comparing.
bullets: Sentence boundaries before paragraph plans, every time
One connective taught at a time, used to the point of tedium
Same task type three weeks apart, with the school's criteria annotated on both
A taught feature only counts once it appears without a prompt

sections.heading: Units of inquiry and the Exhibition: what a tutor may and may not touch
paragraphs: The PYP organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes - who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet - and a small set of key concepts, including form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective and responsibility. Children work through units of inquiry rather than discrete timetabled subjects, which is why a parent asking what my child is studying in science often gets an answer about a unit instead of a topic. It is not evasion. Science genuinely sits inside the unit.

This matters for tutoring because the transferable skill is the inquiry process, not the unit content. A tutor who teaches your Year 5 child facts about migration has helped with one unit for three weeks. A tutor who teaches them to turn a theme into a researchable question, to find two sources that disagree, to take notes in their own words and to credit what they used, has given them the method for every unit after it, and for the MYP work that follows.

The Exhibition in the final PYP year is where this becomes visible and where the honesty line matters. The Exhibition is the child's work. A tutor may ask questions, help plan a timeline, teach note-taking, challenge a weak source, rehearse the presentation and give feedback on a draft the child wrote. A tutor may not supply the content, rewrite the child's text into adult prose, or hand over finished sections. The difference is obvious in the room and obvious to a teacher reading the result, and a project that suddenly reads like a thirty-year-old is worse than useless to the child who has to stand up and explain it.
bullets: Six transdisciplinary themes run through every PYP year, including the Exhibition year
Key concepts taught explicitly: form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective, responsibility
Tutoring targets the inquiry method, which transfers; unit facts do not
Exhibition support is questioning, planning, source checking and rehearsal - the words stay the child's

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the PYP in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must follow the Ministry of Education's general regulations. That federal baseline is the reason your child's IB primary timetable contains subjects the IB does not set. In Abu Dhabi the licensing and inspection of private schools sits with ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection outcomes.

For a primary family the practical consequence is timetable pressure, and it lands hardest on exactly the children who can least absorb it. A Year 2 pupil consolidating English decoding is simultaneously meeting a second script. A Year 5 pupil who arrived from a British school eighteen months ago is several years behind the Arabic pace of classmates who started in FS1. Neither is a failure of the child or the school; it is arithmetic. And it is almost always the English or maths work that visibly stalls, because that is where the parent is looking.

Tutoring here is worth buying for a specific reason rather than a general one. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different curricula at different paces, and a tutor for one is not a tutor for the other. For non-Arab pupils the usual stalling point is reading unvowelled text, which is a teachable decoding problem rather than a vocabulary problem. Content for these subjects is set and regulated, so a tutor's job is to teach the child to access what the school is already delivering, not to substitute a different syllabus for it.

sections.heading: How a 35-minute online lesson for a young child actually runs
paragraphs: Parents are reasonably sceptical that a six-year-old can learn over video, and the scepticism usually comes from having watched remote schooling in a large group. One-to-one is a different activity. There is nowhere to hide, the tutor can see the child's face and the child's page at the same time, and the lesson stops the moment attention goes. The practical requirements are small: a device on a table rather than a lap, the child's own exercise book and a pencil, a second camera or a phone propped over the page for younger children, and an adult within earshot.

The shape of a 35-minute primary session is fixed because young children need the same frame every week. Two or three minutes retrieving last week's target. Twelve to fifteen minutes on the single new thing. Eight minutes of the child working while the tutor watches and deliberately does not prompt, which is where independence is actually measured. Five minutes setting a short practice task. Then a two-line note to the parent naming the target and the practice. No session covers three things, because a child of seven will retain one.

Scheduling is where online delivery stops being a trade-off and starts being an advantage. School buses in Khalifa City, Al Reef and Mohammed Bin Zayed City drop at varying times, clubs run late twice a week, and nobody wants a tired child at 18:30. A video lesson can start at 16:15 and finish before dinner, and during Ramadan it can move to a late-morning weekend slot or a post-Iftar evening one without anyone recalculating a drive. Sessions can also follow a family that travels between Abu Dhabi and abroad, which a visiting tutor cannot.
bullets: Device on a table, child's own book, pencil, and an adult within earshot
One new thing per session - a seven-year-old will retain one
Eight unprompted minutes every lesson, because that is where independence shows
Slots can move for Ramadan, school buses, clubs and family travel

sections.heading: Reading the school report, and the conversation to have at the next conference
paragraphs: PYP reports describe what a child can do against learning outcomes, often with descriptors rather than grades, plus comments on approaches-to-learning skills and the learner profile. Parents from exam-based systems read meeting expectations as a pass mark and stop there. It is more useful to read the report as a set of claims, each of which has evidence sitting in a portfolio somewhere in the school, and to go to the conference asking to see two of them.

Three questions change a conference. First: can you show me a piece of unaided work from this term that demonstrates this comment? Unaided is the operative word, because supported work tells you what the child can do with an adult beside them. Second: what is the one thing that, if it improved, would move several of these comments at once? Teachers almost always know, and the answer is frequently reading fluency or self-management rather than the subject the parent was worried about. Third: what would you expect to see by the end of next term if this were going well?

Those three answers are also the correct brief for a tutor. Take them, name one target, build a baseline check in week one and repeat it in week four, and you have replaced a vague worry with something that can be falsified. If after six weeks the repeat check has not moved and the unaided work looks the same, that is a signal to change target or stop - and a tutor worth keeping will say so before you do. Progress in the PYP is not mysterious. It is just not reported as a number, so somebody has to produce one.
bullets: Ask to see unaided work, not supported work, for any comment you doubt
Ask which single improvement would move several comments at once
Ask what the teacher would expect to see by the end of next term
Turn those three answers into one tutoring target with a week-one baseline

process.title: Tell us the year group and the worry
process.description: Year group, school, and the sentence from the report or the conference that prompted the search. If there is a recent report or a photographed page of the child's work, send it. Two minutes of this removes a whole session of guessing later.

process.title: Free 30-minute trial lesson
process.description: The child works with the tutor on a cold task - an unfamiliar reading page, or a short number-facts check - while you listen in. There is no charge and no card details are taken. You end it with a named gap and the tutor's reasoning for it, in writing.

process.title: Agree one target and a baseline
process.description: One target for the block, with the exact check that will be repeated in week four written down before the first paid session. If a tutor cannot say now what evidence week four will produce, that is worth knowing before you pay rather than after.

process.title: Weekly sessions with a two-line note
process.description: Thirty to forty minutes, one-to-one over live video, at a slot set after the first week once the school bus and clubs are known. Every session ends with two lines to you: the target worked on, and the short practice task before next week.

process.title: Review at week four and week twelve
process.description: The identical baseline check is repeated at week four and the result sits beside the original, dated. At week twelve you get a one-page summary and a recommendation, which is sometimes to change target and sometimes to stop. Both are legitimate outcomes.

process.title: If the match is wrong, say so
process.description: Primary tutoring depends on a child liking the adult on the screen, and that is not predictable from a profile. Tell us in the first fortnight and we will change tutor rather than persuade you. A child who stops talking in session two has already given the answer.

whyPoints.title: Specialists in the primary phase, not secondary tutors scaled down
whyPoints.description: Early reading, phonics sequencing and number automaticity are their own disciplines. A capable DP Mathematics tutor is not automatically able to diagnose why a Year 3 child's column subtraction fails in the tens, and the two jobs need different training.

whyPoints.title: Evidence you can read, not reassurance
whyPoints.description: Running records with accuracy rates, timed number-facts checks repeated identically, dated writing samples annotated against the school's own criteria. The point is to make the decision to continue or stop a decision about data rather than about politeness.

whyPoints.title: A tutor pool that is not limited by a drive
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means a family in Al Reef or Al Falah chooses from everyone who can teach the thing their child needs, including Arabic as an additional language and English as a second language, rather than from the adults willing to make the journey.

whyPoints.title: Session lengths built for the age
whyPoints.description: Thirty to forty minutes for primary, twice-weekly short blocks for early reading, and consecutive slots for siblings instead of a shared screen. Buying a 60-minute lesson for a six-year-old buys fifteen minutes of a tired child and forty-five of goodwill.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits on the Exhibition and on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Support for the PYP Exhibition is questioning, planning, source checking, note-taking and rehearsal. The content and the words stay the child's own. We say what a tutor may not do as plainly as what they will, because the alternative is a project nobody can defend.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives a UAE school week
whyPoints.description: Slots are set after the first week, once the bus time and the club nights are known. Lessons move for Ramadan, for school breaks and for family travel between Abu Dhabi and abroad, because a video lesson has no commute to re-plan around.

faqs.question: My child is in PYP Year 3 in Abu Dhabi and there are no exams - how would I even know tutoring is working?
faqs.answer: By insisting on repeatable checks. A good tutor produces a baseline in week one that can be repeated exactly: a running record on an unfamiliar page with an accuracy rate, or a fixed timed set of number facts. The identical check is repeated at week four and week twelve and the results sit side by side, dated. Alongside that, ask for a piece of work the child completed unaided that they could not do in week one. Those three artefacts answer the question without relying on anyone's impression, including yours. If a tutor cannot name the week-four evidence before the first paid session, there is no plan to evaluate.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a PYP tutor to our villa in Khalifa City or Al Raha?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Lessons for Abu Dhabi families are delivered one-to-one over live video, with your child's own exercise book on screen and an adult within earshot for younger children. In practice this suits the Khalifa City and Al Raha school runs better than a visiting tutor would: nobody is driving from the island at 16:30, so a 40-minute session can start at 16:15 and finish before dinner. It also means you choose from every tutor who can teach what your child needs, rather than from those willing to make the drive.

faqs.question: What does a visiting primary tutor cost in Abu Dhabi compared with one-to-one online?
faqs.answer: Published market rates for in-home one-to-one run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 per hour with travel folded into the quote; Bestimate's 2026 rate table puts the common band at AED 180 to AED 350, with home tutors advertising up to AED 500. Qualified online one-to-one in the same market sits around AED 150 to AED 300, on Unitors' published rates, and budget online providers advertise from AED 33 to AED 65. Monthly packages seen in the market include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. All figures are other providers' published rates as at October 2026, not ours.

faqs.question: How long should a tutoring session be for a six-year-old?
faqs.answer: Thirty minutes, twice a week, is better than sixty minutes once. Early reading in particular responds to frequency rather than duration, because what is being built is automaticity and automaticity needs repetition spaced out. For children from about Year 3 upwards a single 40-minute weekly session works, with roughly fifteen minutes of teaching, eight minutes of unprompted independent work and five minutes setting a short practice task. A 60-minute primary lesson sounds like better value and usually is not: the last twenty minutes are spent managing a tired child rather than teaching one.

faqs.question: Is my child's slow reading a decoding problem or a comprehension problem?
faqs.answer: A running record on an unfamiliar page tells you in about four minutes, and it is worth doing before buying anything. The child reads roughly a hundred words aloud while the tutor marks substitutions, omissions and self-corrections. Substituting visually similar words points to decoding. Reading accurately and fluently but being unable to retell what happened points to comprehension. Reading accurately but slowly and flatly points to fluency, which matters because slow decoding uses up the working memory comprehension needs. The three cases need genuinely different teaching, so a tutor who starts with more library books rather than a cold page is guessing.

faqs.question: What is the PYP Exhibition and how much can a tutor help with it?
faqs.answer: The Exhibition is the student-led inquiry in the final PYP year, usually Year 6, presented to the school community and drawing together the programme's key concepts and approaches-to-learning skills. It is the child's own work. A tutor may ask questions that sharpen the line of inquiry, help build a timeline, teach note-taking in the child's own words, challenge a source that will not stand up, give feedback on a draft the child has written, and rehearse the presentation. A tutor may not supply the content, rewrite the text into adult prose, or hand over finished sections. A project that suddenly reads like an adult is worth nothing to a child who has to stand up and explain it.

faqs.question: Why does my Year 5 report mention problem solving when my child is fine at arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Usually because the arithmetic is correct but not automatic. If recalling 7 x 8 takes two seconds of effort, a four-step word problem spends the child's working memory on calculation and has nothing left for the structure of the question. The report sees an abandoned problem and calls it problem solving. The fix is in two parts: timed recall of multiplication and division facts until they are instant, and annotation practice where the child underlines what is asked, circles the numbers that matter and writes the order of operations before calculating anything. Watching where a child stops is the diagnosis, and it is normally step one.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates the Abu Dhabi school my child attends, and does it affect tutoring?
faqs.answer: Private schools in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain are regulated by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. Dubai schools fall under KHDA, Sharjah under the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah under its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah under the federal Ministry of Education. For tutoring the relevance is indirect but real: the regulator sets the framework your child's school reports within, and ADEK's professional-ethics rules restrict school staff from paid tutoring of pupils enrolled at their own school. IB Gram holds no accreditation from any of these bodies and claims none.

faqs.question: My child started Arabic two years late after moving to Abu Dhabi - can a tutor realistically close that?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the honest framing matters. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language under federal regulation, so a child arriving in Year 4 meets classmates who began in FS1. Nobody closes four years in a term. What a tutor can do is remove the specific blocker, which for most non-Arab pupils is reading unvowelled text rather than vocabulary. That is a decoding problem and it responds to explicit, sequenced teaching. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different curricula at different paces, so make sure you are buying the right one; a tutor for one is not automatically a tutor for the other.

faqs.question: Should I book one tutor for both of my primary children to save money?
faqs.answer: One tutor, yes. One shared session, usually not. Siblings two or more years apart need different content at different pacing, and a shared screen generally means one child works while the other waits, which you are paying for. Consecutive 30-minute slots with the same tutor keep the family commitment to a single hour in the evening while giving each child their own target, their own record and their own parent note. It also helps the tutor: a single adult who knows both children spots patterns across the household, like a shared gap in place value, that two separate tutors would each see half of.

faqs.question: What should I ask at the next parent-teacher conference before paying for anything?
faqs.answer: Three questions. Can you show me a piece of unaided work from this term that demonstrates this comment - unaided being the operative word, because supported work shows what the child does with an adult beside them. What is the single thing that, if it improved, would move several of these comments at once - teachers usually know, and the answer is often reading fluency or self-management rather than the subject you were worried about. And what would you expect to see by the end of next term if this were going well. Those three answers are also the correct brief for any tutor you then hire.

faqs.question: Does a young child actually concentrate on a video lesson, or is that wishful thinking?
faqs.answer: One-to-one video is a different activity from the large-group remote schooling most parents remember. There is nowhere to hide, the tutor sees the child's face and the child's page simultaneously, and the lesson adapts the moment attention drops. The practical conditions do matter: the device on a table rather than a lap, the child's own exercise book and pencil in front of them, a phone or second camera propped over the page for younger children, and an adult within earshot. Under those conditions a 30 to 40 minute primary session holds. Under the opposite conditions - a tablet on a sofa, nobody nearby - it does not, and no format would.

faqs.question: Is it too early to get help if my child is only in FS2?
faqs.answer: It is not too early to get a baseline, which is different from starting a long programme. Abu Dhabi primary families often arrive in FS2 having been through two or three different early-years approaches, and a child who attended a phonics-first nursery and one who attended a play-based nursery can sound identically fluent and decode completely differently. A single trial session on an unfamiliar text and a short oral-language task usually tells you whether anything needs doing. Frequently the answer is no, and that answer is free. Where something does need doing at this age, it is almost always short, cheap and far easier than the same gap in Year 4.

faqs.question: What happens to lessons during Ramadan, school breaks and summer travel?
faqs.answer: They move, because there is no commute to re-plan. During Ramadan families commonly shift a weekday session to a late-morning weekend slot or a post-Iftar evening one, and that is a scheduling conversation rather than a rebooking fee. Across school breaks many Abu Dhabi families take a short block of four to six sessions aimed at one named gap - place value before Year 4, fractions before Year 5, organisation before the move into MYP - with a baseline in the first session and the same check repeated in the last. If the family travels, sessions follow the family, which is the one thing a visiting tutor cannot do.

faqs.question: My child is moving from PYP Year 6 into MYP next year - what is actually worth tutoring?
faqs.answer: Self-management, in most cases, rather than subject content. The step into MYP brings subject teachers instead of one class teacher, eight subject groups, criterion-related assessment with letters and descriptors, and a timetable that moves during the week. Children rarely struggle with the academic material in term one; they struggle with knowing what is due, where it is recorded and what the criteria are asking for. A short block across the summer aimed at recording tasks, breaking work into steps, starting without a prompt and checking against criteria is usually a better purchase than subject tutoring, and it is cheaper.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start with a cold page and a baseline, not a package
abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingBody: If you are weighing up an IB PYP home tutor in Abu Dhabi, the first thing to buy is a diagnosis rather than a block of hours. Book the free 30-minute trial lesson: your child works on an unfamiliar reading page or a short timed number check, you listen in, and you finish with one named gap and the tutor's reasoning in writing. No charge and no card details. If the gap is real, we agree one target, write down the week-four check before the first paid session, and run 30 to 40 minute lessons one-to-one over live video at a slot that fits the school bus. If there is no gap worth paying for, we will tell you that too.
