intro.heading: Why a PYP parent cannot read the report card the way they expect to
paragraphs: A parent who sat GCSEs or CBSE boards reads a school report looking for a number. The Primary Years Programme does not give one. Reporting in the PYP is built around the learner profile, the approaches to learning, and a portfolio of work gathered across the year, and every IB World School designs its own format within that. So an Abu Dhabi parent can finish a parent-teacher conference having heard that their child is a thoughtful inquirer who is developing as a communicator, and still have no idea whether the child can read a Grade 4 text without stopping.

That is not a criticism of the programme. The PYP is deliberately built to assess thinking rather than recall, and the absence of an externally set paper before the Middle Years Programme is what lets a Grade 2 teacher spend three weeks on one unit of inquiry. It does mean the signal a parent needs arrives late. A child who is two years behind on decoding can sit happily in a well-run inquiry classroom for a long time, because the talk carries them. The gap surfaces when the reading load rises, usually in Grade 5 or in the first term of MYP Year 1.

This page is built around the fix for that: evidence. Every session a child does with an IB Gram tutor produces something you can look at. A running record with the error count and the self-correction rate. A page of writing with the teaching point circled. A set of six fraction questions with the two the child got wrong and the reason why. A reading age from a standardised passage, taken at the start and again eight weeks later. None of this replaces the school's own assessment, and none of it is an IB document. It exists so that the question "is my child actually moving?" has an answer you can hold.

Abu Dhabi makes the logistics particular. The emirate's private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which publishes its own inspection ratings for each school. Families are spread across the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, Saadiyat and Yas, and the newer mainland communities out towards Al Shamkha, and the school run between those is what decides whether a 4pm lesson is realistic. Online delivery removes that variable entirely: the lesson starts when the child sits down, not when a tutor finds parking.

One more thing specific to the UAE. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum in every private school in the country, because the federal rule is that a private school may choose its curriculum but must still teach those subjects and follow the Ministry's general regulations. For a non-Arab child in a PYP school, Arabic as an additional language is often the first subject where a parent sees a mark they do not like, and it is the one a tutor is asked about most often at primary level.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.programmesIntro: Primary Years sits at the bottom of a continuum, and the decisions a family makes in Grade 4 or 5 are really decisions about what comes next. These are the four routes an Abu Dhabi child in a PYP school realistically moves into, and what each one demands on arrival.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.ageRange: Ages 3-12 · FS1 to Grade 5 or Year 6
programmes.description: Six transdisciplinary themes, revisited each year through units of inquiry built on a central idea and lines of inquiry. Seven key concepts frame the questions asked: form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective and responsibility. Assessment is internal and portfolio-based. The final year ends with the Exhibition, a long collaborative inquiry the student presents to the school community. There is no IB-set examination at any point.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi, PYP schools sit alongside a majority of British and American curriculum schools, so a child who transfers in mid-primary often arrives from a system where they were given a level or a percentage. Expect a term of adjustment to being asked what you think rather than what the answer is. ADEK inspection reports give the primary phase its own judgement, which is the fastest way to see how a school's early years are rated.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each marked against four criteria labelled A to D, with every criterion scored out of 8 and converted to a subject grade from 1 to 7. The jump from PYP is less about content than about the criterion language: a Year 7 student who writes a good answer can still score low on Criterion C because they did not do what the command word asked. The Personal Project in the final year is the structural descendant of the Exhibition.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi schools run the full IB continuum, so a PYP child may move into MYP in the same building with the same timetable. The content continuity is real; the assessment shock is not softened by it. Families who have been through both usually say the useful term for tutoring is the second half of Grade 5, spent on note-making, source use and writing to a command word, rather than the first term of MYP spent catching up.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subject groups, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. Each subject carries an internally assessed component. Abu Dhabi schools sit the May session. The habits that decide a DP grade, reading a command term properly and sourcing a claim, are taught far earlier than DP1, which is the argument for treating primary research skills as foundational rather than optional.
programmes.countryNote: For an Abu Dhabi family, the Diploma matters at primary age for one practical reason: UAE Ministry of Education equivalency. The British-track requirements are published and specific, while no IB points threshold has been confirmed on a Ministry source, so any figure you see quoted for the IB should be checked against moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation channel before you plan around it.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: The route many PYP families switch to at the end of primary or middle school, because the Abu Dhabi school market is dominated by British curriculum provision. Cambridge syllabuses carry four-digit codes such as 0580 for Mathematics and 0625 for Physics; Pearson Edexcel uses codes like 4MA1 and 4PH1. Both sit terminal written papers, which is a different proposition from a portfolio.
programmes.countryNote: Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track asks for five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education not counted among the five, plus one A-Level at no less than E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. That is the sourced rule, and it is worth knowing in Grade 5 because it shapes which subjects a child must still be sitting five years later.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.subjectsIntro: At primary level the useful unit is not a subject but a skill that is either in place or missing. These are the ones Abu Dhabi families ask about, with what a session on each actually looks like.

subjects.name: Early reading and phonics
subjects.description: Letter-sound correspondence, blending, segmenting and the common exception words that phonics cannot explain. A session is short, fast and repetitive: decodable text, then a non-word check to see whether the child is decoding or guessing from pictures. The diagnostic that matters is whether errors are visual, phonic or contextual, because each needs a different fix.

subjects.name: Reading fluency and comprehension
subjects.description: Words correct per minute on an unseen passage, then the inference questions a fluent reader can still fail. Most primary comprehension marks in Abu Dhabi classrooms are lost on retrieval under time pressure and on questions asking why rather than what. Sessions use short texts read twice, with the second pass annotated for evidence.

subjects.name: Writing: structure and sentence control
subjects.description: Sentence demarcation, subordination, paragraph purpose and the difference between a description and an explanation. PYP writing tasks are usually embedded in a unit of inquiry, so the child is writing about photosynthesis while also learning to open a paragraph. Tutoring separates the two so the writing itself can be taught.

subjects.name: Number, place value and mental calculation
subjects.description: Counting, partitioning, bridging through ten, and the mental methods that make written methods survivable. A child who writes column addition correctly but counts on fingers for 8 plus 7 will stall in Grade 4. Sessions use a diagnostic set of twenty items to find which number bond is missing, then drill only that.

subjects.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
subjects.description: The single most common reason an Abu Dhabi primary parent books a tutor. The usual fault is that the child has learned fraction procedures without a model of what a fraction is, so equivalence works and comparison does not. Work starts with the bar model and returns to procedure only once comparison is secure.

subjects.name: Measurement, shape and data handling
subjects.description: Unit conversion, perimeter and area confusion, reading scales that do not increase in ones, and interpreting a graph rather than describing it. These topics turn up inside units of inquiry rather than as standalone chapters, which is why they are often the gaps nobody noticed until the Grade 5 year.

subjects.name: Science inquiry and fair testing
subjects.description: Variables, prediction, measurement and the difference between a result and a conclusion. Primary science marks are rarely about recall; they are about whether a child changed one thing at a time and can say why that mattered. Sessions build one short investigation at a time, planned, run and written up.

subjects.name: Research and note-making for units of inquiry
subjects.description: Finding a source, judging whether it is any good, taking notes in the child's own words and crediting where something came from. This is the approaches-to-learning strand that carries furthest: it is the same skill the MYP calls Criterion A and the Diploma calls academic honesty. Started in Grade 3, it is cheap to teach.

subjects.name: PYP Exhibition coaching
subjects.description: Narrowing a vague interest into an answerable question, building a plan with dates, choosing the action, and rehearsing the presentation. The tutor's role is process: asking the next question, reviewing the child's draft and giving feedback on it. The inquiry, the writing and the presentation are the student's own work throughout.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Script formation, vocabulary, listening and the spoken responses primary assessments ask for. Arabic runs alongside the licensed curriculum in every UAE private school, and for a non-Arab child in Abu Dhabi it is usually the first subject where the school report shows something a parent wants to act on. Sessions are oral-heavy and short.

subjects.name: English as an additional language
subjects.description: Academic vocabulary, the connectives that carry an explanation, and the listening load of an inquiry classroom taught entirely in English. A child can be socially fluent in the playground and still not follow a Grade 3 science lesson. Work targets the words the current unit of inquiry actually uses.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.modesIntro: Primary tutoring fails when it is scheduled like secondary tutoring. A ninety-minute block after a full school day does not work on a nine-year-old. These are the three shapes that do, and what each one is for.

modes.title: Weekly 45-minute one-to-one
modes.description: The default from Grade 3 upward. One skill per session, a short retrieval warm-up on last week's work, twenty-five minutes of new teaching, then five minutes setting the week's practice. Short enough that the child is still thinking at the end, long enough to finish something. The session note goes out the same evening with the work attached.

modes.title: Twice-weekly 30-minute sessions for early readers
modes.description: Reading in FS2 to Grade 2 responds to frequency, not duration. Two short sessions beat one long one because decoding is a motor habit before it is a comprehension skill. Each session is a decodable text, a non-word check and three minutes of writing. A running record is taken fortnightly so the error rate is a number rather than an impression.

modes.description: A six to ten week block running alongside the school's own Exhibition timeline, usually weekly with a longer session near the presentation. The work is scoping the question, building a dated plan, deciding the action, and rehearsing in front of someone who asks hard questions. The tutor reviews the student's drafts and gives feedback; the student writes every word of it.

sections.heading: What an IB PYP tutor actually does when there is no exam to revise for
paragraphs: An IB PYP tutor in Abu Dhabi teaches the underlying skill the unit of inquiry assumes a child already has. There is no Primary Years paper, so there is nothing to revise. What there is instead is a set of foundations that either hold or do not: decoding, fluency, number bonds, fraction sense, sentence control, note-making, and the ability to answer the question that was asked. A good primary session picks one of those, diagnoses it in the first ten minutes and then teaches it.

This is a different job from secondary tutoring and it is worth being blunt about the difference. A Diploma tutor works backwards from a mark scheme. A primary tutor works forwards from a diagnostic, because the thing that will eventually be marked is five years away. That changes the evidence a parent should expect. Instead of a predicted grade, you get an error rate, a words-correct-per-minute figure, a list of which twelve of twenty number facts are missing, and a piece of writing with the teaching point marked on it.

It also changes what tutoring should not do. Pre-teaching next week's unit of inquiry so the child looks prepared in class is a waste of a session, and it hides the gap rather than closing it. Doing the child's unit work with them is worse, because the whole point of an inquiry classroom is that the thinking is the assessment. The useful work sits underneath: if a Grade 4 child cannot skim a page for a fact, no amount of help with this term's topic will fix next term's.

The practical shape of that, for an Abu Dhabi family, is a weekly 45-minute online session with one named tutor, a diagnostic in week one, a repeat of the same diagnostic in week eight, and a short written note after each lesson. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, so there is no travel window to plan around and no limit on which tutor a family in Al Reef can work with.

sections.heading: The six transdisciplinary themes, and where primary students actually stall
paragraphs: Every PYP year revisits the same six transdisciplinary themes, which is why a parent can feel the curriculum is circling. It is: the themes are containers, and the content inside them deepens each year. What stays constant is the demand each theme makes on a child's skills, and that demand is where tutoring earns its place. A child does not struggle with "Sharing the planet" as a topic. They struggle because that theme asks them to read a data display and explain a cause, and one of those two is missing.

The table below maps each theme to the skill it leans on and the point at which primary students in Abu Dhabi classrooms commonly stall. It is drawn from the pattern of what families ask for rather than from any IB document, and it is useful for one specific purpose: when your child's class is three weeks into a unit and something is not working, it tells you which underlying skill to check first.

The seven key concepts, form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective and responsibility, are the question-generators that sit across all six themes. They are also the best diagnostic tool a parent has. Ask a Grade 4 child what causes something they have just studied. If the answer is a restatement of what happened rather than why, the gap is explanation, not knowledge, and that is a teachable thing with a specific method behind it.

One caution about using this table with a school. These are tutoring observations, not criteria, and no school should be asked to map its units against them. If you want the school's own view of where your child sits, ask for the portfolio and ask which approaches-to-learning strand the teacher would prioritise. That question gets a far more useful answer than asking how your child is doing.

sections.heading: Making progress visible when the programme does not give marks
paragraphs: This is the page's main argument, so here it is plainly. In a programme with no external assessment, the only way to know whether tutoring is working is to generate evidence on purpose and look at it on a schedule. Not a feeling that the child seems more confident. A measurement, taken the same way twice, eight weeks apart.

Each artefact below is something an IB Gram primary tutor produces as a by-product of teaching, not as extra admin. A running record happens because the child reads aloud. A diagnostic grid happens because the first session tests twenty number facts. An annotated writing sample happens because the tutor marks one teaching point rather than everything. The discipline is in keeping them comparable: same passage type, same twenty facts, same marking focus, so the second measurement means something.

What a parent does with these matters as much as having them. Three of them are worth bringing to a parent-teacher conference, because they turn a vague conversation into a specific one. Walking in and saying that your child reads 74 words per minute on an unseen Grade 3 passage with four self-corrections changes the meeting. The teacher will have their own data; the point is that you now have something to compare it against and a reason to ask whether the two agree.

There is a limit worth stating. None of this is an IB assessment, and none of it predicts anything about MYP or Diploma grades. It is a measure of whether a specific skill moved in eight weeks. That is a small claim, and small claims that are actually true are more use to a parent than large ones that are not.

sections.heading: Reading, fixed in the order it has to be fixed
paragraphs: Reading problems at primary age almost always get treated at the wrong level. A Grade 3 child who cannot answer inference questions gets comprehension worksheets, when the real issue is that decoding is still costing so much working memory that nothing is left for meaning. The order is not negotiable: letter-sound knowledge, then blending, then fluency, then comprehension, then inference. Teaching the fourth before the second is holds is how a child spends two years in intervention without moving.

The screening that sorts this takes about twelve minutes. A child reads a short unseen passage aloud while the tutor marks errors and self-corrections, then reads a handful of non-words. Non-words matter because they cannot be guessed from context or pictures. A child who reads real words at a good rate and collapses on non-words is compensating, and compensation runs out somewhere around Grade 4 when the vocabulary stops being predictable.

From there the work is specific. Phonic errors get a scripted sequence, drilled briefly and often. Visual errors, where the child reads a word that looks similar, get slowed-down tracking work. Contextual errors, where the child substitutes a word that makes sense but is not on the page, are often a sign of a fluent guesser and need accuracy pressure rather than more practice. Each one is a different plan, which is why the diagnostic comes before any teaching.

Comprehension then gets taught as a procedure rather than a quality. Find the question type. Go back to the text. Underline the words you are using. Answer with those words plus a reason. For a child in an inquiry classroom reading a lot of non-fiction, that procedure transfers directly into unit work, which is the other reason primary reading is the highest-value thing a tutor can fix: it is the only skill that improves every other subject at the same time.
bullets: Non-word screening separates genuine decoding from skilled guessing
Error type, not error count, decides which method is used
Fluency is measured on unseen text, never on a passage the child has practised
Comprehension is taught as a four-step procedure, not as a reading habit

sections.heading: The PYP Exhibition, counted backwards from the showcase
paragraphs: The Exhibition is the final PYP year's long collaborative inquiry, presented to the school community. Each school sets its own brief and its own dates, so no two Abu Dhabi schools run it identically. What is consistent is where it goes wrong, and that is almost always at the start: the question is too wide, so the research sprawls, so the plan slips, so the last fortnight becomes a panic about the display board rather than the thinking.

The backwards count below is the structure that holds it together. It is written against a generic ten-week brief; your school's dates will differ and the school's brief always wins. Use it to ask your child one question each week, which is the whole of a parent's job here: not what have you found, but is your plan still right.

The academic-honesty boundary needs saying out loud on an Exhibition page, because this is where families get it wrong with good intentions. A tutor may ask questions, teach how to take notes, explain how to credit a source, review a draft the student has written and give feedback on it. A tutor may not write any part of it, dictate it, redraft it to completion, or build the presentation. The same rule runs all the way up the IB: the Exhibition, the Personal Project, the Internal Assessment and the Extended Essay are all the student's own work, and the habit of keeping that line clean is easier to build at age ten than at seventeen.

One practical note on the presentation. Rehearsing in front of a tutor over video has an accidental advantage: the child can be recorded and watch themselves back, which does more for delivery in one viewing than a term of being told to speak up. Two rehearsals with real questions, a week apart, is usually enough.

sections.heading: What primary tutoring costs in the Abu Dhabi market
paragraphs: Primary tutoring sits at the lower end of the UAE market, because it rarely needs a subject specialist. The published market bands give a usable picture. Budget online provision runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits around AED 150 to 300, with Unitors quoting IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits, travel included, run roughly AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate's 2026 rate table putting the band at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors asking AED 200 to 500.

Those are market figures published by the providers named, not IB Gram prices. For a primary child the relevant observation is that the premium bands exist for subject scarcity, and primary reading or Grade 4 maths is not scarce. A family paying specialist rates for early literacy is paying for something the market does not require. The things worth paying more for at primary age are consistency of tutor, short frequent sessions rather than long infrequent ones, and written evidence after each lesson.

The in-home premium deserves a specific note on a primary page. A home visit at primary level typically carries a minimum booking, often two hours, because the travel does not pay for itself on a 45-minute lesson. That is exactly the wrong shape for a nine-year-old: two hours after school is past the point of useful attention. The economics of in-home delivery push towards session lengths that primary children cannot sustain, which is a structural argument for online delivery rather than a marketing one.

Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session give a planning anchor: roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work. Monthly packages seen in the market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. IB Gram's own position is a free trial lesson first and a consultation that quotes against the actual subject and frequency, rather than a published rate card that would be wrong for most families.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the Primary Years Programme
paragraphs: Every private school in the UAE teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside whatever international curriculum it is licensed to deliver. The federal position is that a private school is not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement, and it applies in Abu Dhabi as it does in Dubai.

In practice this means a PYP classroom runs two assessment cultures at once. The units of inquiry are assessed internally against the programme's own framework; the mandatory subjects are taught to a prescribed syllabus with its own expectations and, for Arabic, its own language of instruction rules. A parent who has only read about the PYP is sometimes surprised to find the first mark that worries them comes from a subject the PYP does not contain.

For a non-Arab child, Arabic as an additional language is where most primary tutoring requests land. The work is unglamorous and effective: script formation, high-frequency vocabulary, listening, and the short spoken responses primary assessments ask for. Frequency beats duration, as with reading, so two 30-minute sessions a week outperform one hour. Progress is visible quickly at this age, which is also why it is worth starting in Grade 2 or 3 rather than waiting for a report that says there is a problem.

One important boundary. For the mandatory UAE subjects, schools are required to teach the prescribed content, and using different or additional material without prior Ministry permission is not permitted. A tutor's job on these subjects is to teach the child the content the school is already delivering: vocabulary, script, comprehension and oral confidence. It is not to supply an alternative syllabus, and any tutoring offer that promises its own Arabic or Islamic Education curriculum is describing something a school could not use.
bullets: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies run alongside the PYP in every UAE private school
Arabic as an additional language is the most requested mandatory-subject support at primary level
Two 30-minute sessions a week beat one 60-minute session for language work

sections.heading: ADEK, inspection reports and reading the primary phase judgement
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi's private schools are overseen by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is the single most useful source a primary parent in Abu Dhabi has and the one almost nobody uses. Of the competitor tutoring pages reviewed for this project, not one named it. Inspection reports are published per school, which means a family choosing between two PYP schools can read an independent judgement rather than a prospectus.

The detail that matters for a primary family is that inspection reports give phase-level judgements, not just a single overall rating. A school can be strong in secondary and weaker in its early years, or the reverse, and the overall band hides that. If you are choosing a school for a five-year-old, the primary phase judgement and the specific comments on teaching and assessment in the early years are worth more than the headline.

ADEK also sets professional-ethics expectations for school staff. Press reporting on the Abu Dhabi rules describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and notes that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That is press-reported rather than quoted from the current policy document, so verify it against ADEK's own published policy before relying on it. The practical consequence is simple and worth knowing: if your child's class teacher offers private lessons, that is a question to raise, not an opportunity to take.

None of this makes IB Gram an ADEK matter. IB Gram is not inspected, licensed or accredited by ADEK or by any UAE authority, holds no educational services permit, and operates no centre or office in the emirate. The regulators are named here because knowing what they govern is useful to a parent, not because any of them endorses this service.

sections.heading: From PYP to MYP: the gap that shows up in the first term of Year 7
paragraphs: The transition out of the Primary Years Programme is where the absence of marks finally becomes visible. A Grade 5 child who has been described as a developing communicator arrives in MYP Year 1, meets a task marked against four criteria out of 8 each, and gets a 3 on Criterion C for a piece of work that would have been praised the year before. Nothing has gone wrong with the child. The assessment has changed from a description of growth to a judgement against a descriptor.

Three skills carry most of the weight in that first term. Reading a command word and doing exactly what it asks, rather than writing everything known about the topic. Making notes from a source in the child's own words, with the source recorded. Structuring an answer so each paragraph does one job. All three are teachable in Grade 5, in the second half of the year, in about eight to ten sessions. All three are painful to teach in MYP Year 1 while the student is also being graded on them.

Families moving out of the PYP to a British curriculum school instead face a different gap, and the Abu Dhabi school market makes this the more common route. Year 7 in a British school assumes a child can take a test, revise for it, and work from a textbook. A child from an inquiry classroom may never have revised in their life, because there has been nothing to revise for. Revision is a skill, not a character trait, and the first six weeks of Year 7 is a poor time to discover it is missing.

The honest version of the recommendation: if your child is in the final PYP year and you are planning any transition, the highest-value tutoring is not subject content. It is note-making, command words, paragraph structure and how to prepare for a test. That is a short block, it is cheap at primary rates, and it removes most of what families later describe as the transition being hard.

process.title: Tell us the skill, not just the subject
process.description: The useful first message is specific: Grade 4, fractions, can do the procedure but cannot compare two fractions. Or Grade 2, reading, guesses from pictures. That is enough to match a tutor who has taught that exact thing rather than a generalist who covers primary.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the diagnostic done in it
process.description: The trial is a real session, not a sales call. The tutor runs the twelve-minute reading screen or the twenty-item number-fact grid, teaches one thing, and sends you the result. You see the starting measurement before you decide anything. No card details are taken to book it.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Primary tutoring works on routine. One tutor, one slot, same day each week, set around your school run rather than around a tutor's driving time. Families in Al Reef and Khalifa City usually take a later slot; island families take an earlier one.

process.title: A session note every week and a measurement every eight
process.description: After each lesson you get what was taught, what the child got wrong and a five-minute daily practice. At week eight the week-one diagnostic is repeated identically, so the comparison is real. If the number has not moved, the plan changes rather than continuing.

process.title: A term summary you can take to the school
process.description: Each term you get two skills that moved, one that did not, and the evidence behind both. Bring it to the parent-teacher conference and ask whether the school's own assessment agrees. Where the two disagree is the most informative conversation available to a primary parent.

whyPoints.title: Subject match beats proximity
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means a family in Al Shamkha works with a tutor chosen for having taught early reading or Grade 5 fractions, rather than whoever is within a twenty-minute drive. At primary level the specialism that matters is the skill, and the pool for that skill is far larger than one emirate.

whyPoints.title: Session lengths that suit the age
whyPoints.description: Thirty minutes twice a week for an early reader, 45 minutes once a week from Grade 3. In-home delivery pushes towards two-hour minimums because travel has to be paid for; online delivery has no such pressure, so the lesson can be the length the child can actually sustain.

whyPoints.title: Evidence rather than reassurance
whyPoints.description: A running record, a diagnostic grid and an annotated writing sample after every third session. The claim being made is small and checkable: this specific skill moved this much in eight weeks. Nobody is predicting an MYP grade from a Grade 3 reading score.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on the student's own work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, review and give feedback. They do not write, redraft to completion or produce any part of an Exhibition, a Personal Project, an Internal Assessment or an Extended Essay. Building that habit at primary age is the cheapest academic-honesty insurance a family can buy.

whyPoints.title: Permit transparency
whyPoints.description: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and carries a code of conduct. We will tell you a tutor's permit position rather than leaving you to assume it.

whyPoints.title: Honest coverage limits
whyPoints.description: If no UAE-based tutor covers a niche primary need in the slot you want, we say so and offer the alternative, which may be a tutor based outside the UAE teaching in your time zone. Disclosing a coverage limit is more useful than quietly filling the slot with whoever is free.

faqs.question: Does my child need a tutor if the PYP has no exams?
faqs.answer: Not because of exams, no. The reason primary tutoring is worth considering is that the skills a PYP classroom assumes, decoding, fluency, number bonds, fraction sense and note-making, are either in place or not, and an inquiry classroom can mask a gap for a long time because the talk carries the child. A tutor's job at this age is to test those foundations, name which one is missing and teach it. If the diagnostic comes back clean, you have paid for one session and learned something useful. That is a reasonable outcome.

faqs.question: What does an IB PYP tutor actually teach in a 45-minute session?
faqs.answer: One skill. A typical session opens with a five-minute retrieval check on last week's work, spends about twenty-five minutes teaching the target skill with the child working rather than watching, then sets a five-to-ten-minute daily practice for the week. Nothing from the school's current unit of inquiry is pre-taught, because that hides the gap instead of closing it. You receive a note the same evening listing what was taught, what the child got wrong and the practice set. Every third session that note arrives with a marked piece of the child's writing attached.

faqs.question: How do I know my Grade 3 child is behind if the report card has no grades?
faqs.answer: Ask for two things the school already has: the portfolio, and which approaches-to-learning strand the teacher would prioritise next. Then get an independent measurement. A twelve-minute reading screen gives words correct per minute on an unseen passage plus an error type, and a twenty-item number-fact grid shows which facts are missing and how long recall takes. Those are numbers you can compare eight weeks later. The useful conversation with a school is not whether your child is doing well, which invites a reassuring answer, but whether the school's assessment agrees with an independent measurement.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child prepare for the PYP Exhibition?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor can help narrow a vague interest into an answerable question, teach how to judge a source, show how to take notes in the child's own words, review a draft the student has written and give feedback on it, and run rehearsals with hard questions. A tutor cannot write any part of it, dictate it, redraft it to completion or build the presentation. The Exhibition is the student's own work, as the Personal Project, the Internal Assessment and the Extended Essay are later, and keeping that line clean at age ten is a habit that pays off at seventeen.

faqs.question: How long should an online lesson be for a seven-year-old?
faqs.answer: Thirty minutes, twice a week, rather than an hour once. Reading and number facts at that age respond to frequency because they are closer to motor habits than to understanding, so short and often beats long and rare. From Grade 3 upward, 45 minutes once a week works for most children, with a longer session only near something specific like an Exhibition presentation. An in-home visit usually carries a minimum booking of around two hours because the travel has to pay for itself, and two hours after a full school day is well past the point of useful attention for a primary child.

faqs.question: Will an online tutor hold a young child's attention?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on how the session is run, not on the format. What works at primary age is a shared screen the child writes on rather than watches, short turns, frequent switching between talking and doing, and a session short enough to end while the child is still engaged. What fails is a tutor talking for twenty minutes. Practically, the setup matters: headphones, a fixed place the child sits each week, and a parent nearby for the first two sessions. Al Reem Island families in apartments usually find the quiet corner is the thing worth solving first.

faqs.question: My child moved from a British primary school to a PYP school in Abu Dhabi. What changes?
faqs.answer: The assessment culture, mainly. A British primary report gives you levels or percentages; PYP reporting is built on the learner profile, approaches to learning and a portfolio, and each school designs its own format within that. Children usually need a term to adjust to being asked what they think rather than what the answer is. The content gap is normally small; the habits gap is not. The two things worth checking early are whether the child can take notes from a source and whether they can explain a cause rather than retell an event, since both are assumed in an inquiry classroom.

faqs.question: Does the PYP cover Arabic and Islamic Education in Abu Dhabi schools?
faqs.answer: Those subjects run alongside the PYP rather than inside it. UAE private schools may choose their international curriculum, but they must still teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies and follow the Ministry's general regulations. So a PYP classroom in Abu Dhabi operates two assessment cultures at once: internal inquiry assessment, and prescribed mandatory-subject teaching with its own expectations. For non-Arab children, Arabic as an additional language is where most primary tutoring requests land, and it is often the first subject where a parent sees a mark they want to act on.

faqs.question: What does a PYP tutor send me after each lesson?
faqs.answer: A short note with three lines: what was taught, what the child got wrong, and the five-to-ten-minute daily practice for the week. Every third session it arrives with a piece of the child's writing marked for one teaching point rather than for every error, because marking everything teaches nothing. Fortnightly you also get a running record showing words correct per minute, error type and self-correction count. At week eight the week-one diagnostic is repeated identically so the comparison is genuine rather than impressionistic, and each term you get a summary of what moved and what did not.

faqs.question: When should we start tutoring before the move to MYP?
faqs.answer: The second half of the final PYP year is the right window, and the work is not subject content. Three skills carry most of the weight in the first term of MYP Year 1: reading a command word and doing exactly what it asks, making notes from a source in the child's own words with the source recorded, and structuring a paragraph so it does one job. Those take roughly eight to ten sessions at primary rates. Taught in Grade 5 they are cheap; taught in MYP Year 1 they are being learned while they are also being graded.

faqs.question: How much does primary tutoring cost per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market bands put budget online provision at roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, while a qualified subject tutor online sits around AED 150 to 300. In-home one-to-one, travel included, runs roughly AED 180 to 500 on Bestimate's 2026 table and from independent home tutors. Those are the providers' own published figures, not IB Gram's. Primary work rarely needs the specialist bands above AED 300, which exist for subject scarcity rather than for early literacy or Grade 4 maths.

faqs.question: Do private tutors working with Abu Dhabi families need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service is listed as private tutor licensing with a two-working-day completion time, applied for through its app, website and e-services. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

faqs.question: Can the same tutor cover both maths and reading for my child?
faqs.answer: Often yes at primary level, and that is usually the better arrangement. Below MYP the specialism that matters is the skill rather than the subject, and a tutor who diagnoses reading well can generally run a number-fact grid too. What we would not do is stretch one tutor across both when the diagnostic shows two serious gaps, because 45 minutes split in half teaches neither properly. In that case the honest answer is two sessions, or one skill now and the other next term, and we will say which we think matters more.

faqs.question: Can lessons be scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school run and after-school clubs?
faqs.answer: That is the main scheduling constraint at primary age and it is the reason slots differ so much by community. Saadiyat and Al Bateen families, with short pick-ups, often take 3:30pm or 4pm. Khalifa City and Al Reef families, where a bus route can take forty minutes each way, generally need 5pm or a weekend morning. Because lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, there is no travel window to fit around, so the slot is set by your child's day. Families travelling in summer keep the same tutor and shift the time to their current zone.

faqs.question: Is it a problem that my child's class teacher also offers private lessons?
faqs.answer: It is at least a question worth asking. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and notes that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That reporting is secondary, so check it against ADEK's current published policy rather than treating this answer as authoritative. The general principle is sound: the person assessing your child should not also be paid to prepare them.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.closingHeading: Start with a measurement, not a promise
abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.closingBody: The problem a PYP parent in Abu Dhabi has is not a shortage of encouragement. It is the absence of a number. So begin with one: a twelve-minute reading screen or a twenty-item number-fact grid, run inside a free trial lesson with no card details taken, and sent to you with the result written out. If the diagnostic is clean, you have spent one session and learned your child is fine. If it is not, you know exactly which skill is missing, how it will be taught, and what the same measurement should look like eight weeks later. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, timed to your school run rather than to a tutor's drive across the emirate.

abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are priced on subject depth and level rather than on a single platform rate. Each names the IB subject group and level they teach, which is the variable that moves a quote more than anything else in this emirate.

intro.heading: The price is knowable, and most of this market hides it
paragraphs: Of the six strongest pages ranking for IB tutoring queries in this market, three publish no price at all. One of the three asks the price in its own list of frequently asked questions and then declines to answer it. The two that do publish quote in US dollars, a currency Abu Dhabi families neither earn nor spend. That is the state of pricing transparency you are shopping in, and it is why most parents arrive at a first call with no idea whether AED 200 an hour is cheap or extortionate.

It is neither; it is the middle of the market. Published rates across the UAE run roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour for a budget or university-student tutor, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel inside the rate, and AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB, IGCSE or A Level specialist. One premium provider publishes AED 650. Those figures are read from provider pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table in October 2026, and they are the market rather than an IB Gram price list.

The headline band is the least interesting part, though. What a parent actually needs is the list of things that move a quote, because that is what you can negotiate, plan around or decide to pay for deliberately. Subject scarcity moves it. Level moves it: a Higher Level Diploma subject is not priced like a Middle Years one. Session length moves the per-hour figure. The month you book in moves availability and therefore the effective rate. Whether the hours include marking between sessions moves it substantially, and is the single most common omission from a cheap quote.

Abu Dhabi has its own pressures on all of this. The emirate's Diploma cohorts are small per school, so a Higher Level subject with few local teachers has a genuinely thin specialist pool, and scarcity pricing follows. Enrolment is spread between the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, and the newer mainland communities, which makes any in-home rate carry a meaningful travel component. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools here, and its inspection and fee processes shape school budgets, which in turn shape what families have left for tutoring.

This page is organised around the money. It publishes the bands with sources, names the variables that move them, places tutoring cost next to school fees and exam entry so the figure has context, compares provider models on what is actually inside the price, and sets out what a quote should itemise before you agree to it. It also says what the money cannot buy, because the two most expensive mistakes in this market are paying for a guarantee nobody can give and paying for work that must be the student's own. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visiting is a service offered only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.programmesIntro: Price varies by programme more than by city, because the assessments differ and so does the preparation a tutor has to do between sessions. Here is what each stage of the IB typically costs to support, and what drives the figure in Abu Dhabi.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The cheapest stage to support, because there are no external papers and the content does not require a subject specialist. Market rates sit at the lower end of the published bands. The cost driver is frequency rather than rate: early literacy and number work needs short, regular sessions, so a monthly figure matters more than an hourly one.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the competing cost at this stage is usually Arabic support, which many families buy separately because it is mandated alongside the licensed curriculum. Budgeting for both at once is the realistic version, and two short sessions a week on different subjects is a very different monthly figure from one longer session.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Mid-band pricing, because the tutor needs to know the four-criterion assessment model rather than only the subject. The hidden cost here is marking: criterion-referenced feedback on a task takes real time between sessions, and a quote that excludes it is cheaper on paper and worth less in practice.
programmes.countryNote: The Middle Years to Diploma transition drives most of the spend in this emirate, and it is the point where families often buy more hours than they need. A clearer and cheaper approach is to find out which criterion is dragging a subject down before buying a term, because the answer usually narrows the work to one skill rather than a whole subject.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The most expensive stage and the one where the spread between providers is widest. Higher Level subjects sit at the top of the specialist band because the pool of tutors who genuinely teach them is small. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run roughly AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma cohorts are small per school, which thins the local specialist supply in any one Higher Level subject. That is the clearest scarcity premium in the emirate, and it is also the strongest argument for online delivery: a figure driven up by geography rather than expertise is a figure worth removing.

programmes.name: The Diploma core: internal assessment, Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge
programmes.description: Usually bought as a short block rather than as weekly hours, timed to the school's draft deadlines. Priced in the specialist band because the work is feedback-heavy rather than teaching-heavy. A block of six to eight sessions across a term is the typical shape, and it should be quoted as a block with the deadlines named.
programmes.countryNote: This is where the worst value in the UAE market sits. One provider found in the wider search results sells finished internal assessments at AED 3,750. That is not expensive tutoring, it is a malpractice risk for the student, and it is the one line item a parent should refuse outright regardless of what it is called.

abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.subjectsIntro: Subject is the second biggest variable in a quote after level, because supply differs sharply. Below are the subjects Abu Dhabi families ask for most, with a note on what drives the price in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most requested and best supplied Diploma subject, which keeps it near the middle of the specialist band rather than the top. Higher Level carries a premium because proof and calculus depth narrow the pool. Hours are also the heaviest here, which makes the monthly figure larger even at an ordinary rate.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Priced similarly to Analysis and Approaches but with thinner supply at Higher Level, because fewer tutors have taught the modelling and statistics content in depth. A tutor quoting the same rate for both routes without asking which one your child takes is quoting a subject name rather than a course.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Reliable scarcity premium at Higher Level across the UAE. The extra paper and the additional topics mean more preparation between sessions, which shows in the rate. Families often get better value buying fewer hours on the specific topics that are failing than a standing weekly slot across the syllabus.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Similar band to Physics, with an additional cost pressure around the internally assessed work, where data analysis feedback is time-consuming. Expect a block quote for that rather than an hourly one, and expect it to be more expensive per hour than ordinary teaching time.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Better supplied than Physics and Chemistry, so usually slightly cheaper at the same level. The cost here hides in volume: the content load means more hours rather than a higher rate, and a family budgeting on an hourly figure alone often underestimates the term.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Mid-band and well supplied. Diagram and evaluation technique responds quickly to correction, which means fewer hours are often genuinely enough, and that is worth knowing before buying a year. Higher Level quantitative questions are reliable marks and cheap to fix.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Marking-heavy, so the honest rate includes written feedback time and a quote that excludes it is misleading. Supply is reasonable but quality varies widely, because the subject looks teachable by any strong English graduate and is not without knowledge of the markbands.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Mid-band. The cost-effective version of support here is short and specific: application to the organisation in the stem is the band separator, and that can be corrected in a handful of sessions once a marked script has shown that generic answers are what is capping the grade.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Often bought alongside the Diploma because Arabic is mandated in UAE schools, and frequently priced separately. Supply of tutors who know the IB Arabic criteria, as opposed to teaching the language well, is thin, and that gap shows in the rate rather than in availability.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Almost always sold as a block rather than hourly, and the price reflects reading and feedback time rather than teaching. A sensible quote names the number of sessions, the school's deadlines they sit against, and the fact that feedback arrives as questions rather than as text.

abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.regionsIntro: Location changes the price of in-home tuition and almost nothing about the price of online tuition, which is a useful thing to know before comparing quotes. Here is how the travel component actually falls across the emirate.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Central and quick to reach, so the travel loading on an in-home rate is at its lowest here. The constraint families report is quiet study space rather than cost, which is why online sessions and a decent headset are the common answer.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Short runs to nearby schools but a limited local tutor pool, so in-home quotes here tend to reflect scarcity rather than distance. Online removes the scarcity rather than the distance, which is the more valuable of the two.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: The longest school transport runs in the emirate, which pushes sessions past 17:30 and puts any visiting tutor into evening traffic in both directions. That travel time is inside the in-home rate whether it is itemised or not.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Mushrif
regions.note: Established central districts with the densest local tutor supply, and therefore the most competitive in-home pricing in Abu Dhabi. Also where sibling bookings are most common, which is the one arrangement that genuinely lowers the per-child cost.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Newer catchment, growing cohorts, thin local specialist supply in any single Higher Level subject. Quotes here can look high for reasons that have nothing to do with teaching quality, which is exactly the premium online delivery removes.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Mussafah
regions.note: Large mainland catchment with long inbound journeys. In-home rates carry the heaviest travel loading in the emirate, and families here are the most likely to find that an online quote is simply a different number rather than a compromise.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Also under ADEK, and far enough out that the local specialist pool for a Higher Level subject is genuinely thin. Scarcity, not distance, is what prices tuition here, and it is the clearest case in the emirate for buying a specialist remotely.

regions.name: Al Dhafra and the Western Region
regions.note: Very limited local provision at Diploma level. Any in-home arrangement involves a long journey priced into the hour, and for most Higher Level subjects there is no local option at any price. Online is the market rather than an alternative to it.

schoolClusters.city: Island schools: Saadiyat, Al Reem and Yas
schoolClusters.note: Where most of the emirate's IB provision sits. Fees at this end of the market are high, which compresses what families have left for tutoring and makes the number of hours more negotiable than the rate. Students we support here are frequently buying a short block before an internal deadline rather than a standing weekly slot.

schoolClusters.city: The mainland corridor: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: A wider fee range and a wider curriculum mix, so tutoring budgets vary more here than anywhere in the emirate. Internal deadlines cluster in the same weeks across several of these schools, which is also when local specialist availability is tightest and effective rates are highest.

abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named only as market context for Abu Dhabi. IB Gram has no affiliation, partnership or endorsement arrangement with any school named on this page, and quotes no school's fees as fact.
abu-dhabi/ib-tuition.modesIntro: The same hourly rate buys quite different things depending on how it is packaged. Three arrangements, with what each actually costs over a term and what is usually inside and outside the price.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one across a term
modes.description: The cheapest per hour of the three and the easiest to budget, because the monthly figure is stable. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Ask explicitly whether marking between sessions is inside that.
bullets: Stable monthly figure, easiest to plan around
Lowest per-hour rate of the three arrangements
Check whether between-session marking is included

modes.title: A short block before the papers
modes.description: More hours over fewer weeks, usually at the same or a slightly higher rate because it lands in the busiest months. The total is larger and the planning window is shorter, which makes it the arrangement where buying the wrong subject is most expensive. A marked diagnostic before the block is the cheapest insurance available.
bullets: Higher total, shorter window, less room to correct a wrong choice
Books into the months when specialist availability is tightest
Diagnostic first is cheaper than a wasted block

modes.title: A core block for internal assessment and Extended Essay deadlines
modes.description: Priced as a block of six to eight sessions against named school deadlines rather than hourly, because the work is feedback-heavy. It should be the most clearly itemised thing you buy: number of sessions, which deadlines they sit against, and an explicit statement that feedback arrives as questions rather than as text.
bullets: Quoted as a block with the school's deadlines named
Feedback time is the bulk of the cost, not session time
Refuse any version that offers finished work at any price

sections.heading: What IB tuition in Abu Dhabi costs, with every figure sourced
paragraphs: A qualified subject tutor working online in this market publishes rates of roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour. An IB, IGCSE or A Level specialist runs AED 200 to 450 or more. Those are the two bands most Abu Dhabi Diploma families are choosing between. Below that, AED 45 to 150 buys a budget or university-student tutor, which is useful for homework supervision and rarely enough for Higher Level exam technique. Above it, one provider publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor.

Packages seen in the market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are worth converting to a per-hour figure before comparing, because the session length and the tutor's level differ between them. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session are roughly AED 240 to 600 for budget support, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work.

Every one of those figures comes from a named provider page or from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, read in October 2026. None of them is an IB Gram price. We do not publish a rate card on this page because our quote follows a free trial lesson and a marked diagnostic paper, and quoting a term before anyone has read your child's work is guesswork dressed as a price. What we will say is which band we sit in once we know the subject and level.

One number is genuinely fixed and worth knowing: the MoHRE private tuition work permit is granted free of charge for two years. Any tutor or agency charging you for a permit, or citing permit costs as a reason for a higher rate, is charging for something that costs nothing.

sections.heading: The seven variables that actually move the number here
paragraphs: A single headline rate is close to useless because seven things change it, and six of them are within your control or at least within your knowledge. Understanding them is the difference between negotiating and guessing. They are, roughly in order of how much they move a quote: level, subject supply, whether marking is included, session length, the month you book, how many children are involved, and location, which matters only for in-home arrangements.

Level is the biggest. A Higher Level Diploma subject and a Middle Years subject are not the same product, and the gap between them is usually larger than the gap between two providers at the same level. Subject supply is second and is specific to this emirate: Abu Dhabi Diploma cohorts are small per school, so the pool of tutors who have genuinely taught a given Higher Level subject is thin, and scarcity prices accordingly.

The variable that most often explains a suspiciously cheap quote is marking. Criterion-referenced feedback on a written task, or a marked timed paper with the losses categorised, takes real time between sessions. A rate that covers only contact time is cheaper and buys less, and the difference does not show until the end of the term when there is nothing to read. Ask explicitly, and ask for the quote itemised.

The month matters more than families expect. Demand concentrates around internal assessment deadlines and the external paper season, and specialist tutors fill up first. Booking in those weeks means choosing from a smaller pool at the top of the band, which is a real cost rather than a sales tactic. Location, finally, is a travel loading on in-home rates only, heaviest in Mohammed Bin Zayed City, Al Ain and the Western Region, and absent entirely from an online arrangement.

sections.heading: Tutoring cost in context: fees, entry and the full Diploma
paragraphs: An hourly rate in isolation is hard to judge. Put next to the other numbers a family in this emirate is already paying, it becomes a decision rather than a shock. The table below sets tutoring against the costs that surround it, using only figures that can be sourced or that you can obtain directly from your own school and exam centre.

A deliberate omission: this page does not publish Abu Dhabi school fee figures. Fees vary enormously by school and year group and are set through the emirate's own regulatory process, so quoting a band would be inventing a number. Your school publishes its own, ADEK is the authority that governs private schools in the emirate, and that is where to read it. What can be said as context is from Dubai, where the Knowledge and Human Development Authority confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees for the 2026-27 academic year under Dubai's second economic incentives package.

Exam entry is the cost families most often forget, and it only applies if your child is sitting outside a school as a private candidate. It is paid to the registered exam centre, varies by subject count, and has its own deadline that sits months before the papers. If the Diploma is being taken through a school, entry is inside the fees and the question does not arise.

The number that deserves the most thought is the two-year total. A standing weekly session in one Higher Level subject across both Diploma years is a large commitment, and many families would be better served by a smaller, sharper pattern: a diagnostic each term, a short block where the diagnostic shows a problem, and a core block around the internal assessment and Extended Essay deadlines. That is usually both cheaper and better targeted than continuous hours, and it is the arrangement a good tutor will suggest if asked what they would do with your budget.

sections.heading: Provider models compared on what is inside the price
paragraphs: Every provider in this market compares itself to an unnamed alternative that is worse. A more useful comparison is between models, because the model determines what is inside the hour. There are five you will realistically encounter in Abu Dhabi, and the differences are structural rather than a matter of quality.

A specialist agency assigns a tutor and takes a margin for vetting and replacement. An international marketplace lists tutors who set their own rates, which gives you range and puts the verification burden on you. An independent freelance tutor is usually the cheapest per hour and carries no replacement arrangement if it does not work. A tuition centre with premises sells group hours at a low per-head rate and is regulated as an institute rather than as an individual. A platform like this one matches a tutor and runs the record-keeping.

The questions that separate them are the same five whatever the model: what is the hourly rate, is marking between sessions inside it, is the tutor's MoHRE permit verified, what happens if the match is wrong, and is there a free trial with the actual tutor rather than a sales call. A provider that cannot answer all five quickly is not necessarily bad, but you are buying something less defined than you think.

One caution about pricing claims across models. Do not take any provider's published rate, including those on this page, as current without checking the date it was read. One competitor's structured pricing data contradicts the figures printed on the same page, and another's discount table contradicts itself. Every figure here is dated to October 2026 and attributed, which is the standard worth holding any provider to, including us.

sections.heading: Hidden extras, and what a quote should itemise before you pay
paragraphs: The gap between two quotes for the same subject at the same level is usually not the rate. It is what is bundled. A quote that itemises is easier to compare and harder to pad, and asking for one is a reasonable request that takes a provider five minutes.

Six lines are worth insisting on. The hourly rate and the session length, stated separately, so the per-hour figure is yours rather than theirs. Whether marking and preparation between sessions is included. Whether materials are included, and what they are, because a provider should not be sending you past papers and mark schemes at all. Whether there is a rescheduling arrangement and what notice it needs. Whether anything is payable up front and what happens if you stop after one session. And whether the quoted figure includes VAT.

On that last point, this page states only the obvious: ask whether a quoted AED figure includes VAT, and ask the provider for their tax registration number if they claim to charge it. We do not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition as a general matter, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority citation and this page does not have one. Any provider asserting the treatment confidently without a citation is telling you something about how they handle facts.

Two things should never appear as a line item. A charge for the tutor's permit, which is free. And anything described as producing, completing or supplying assessed work, at any price, under any label. One provider in the wider UAE results prices finished internal assessments at AED 3,750; the correct response to that line on a quote is to leave, because the risk it creates sits with your child rather than with the seller.

sections.heading: Why the exam and deadline season reprices this market
paragraphs: Published rate cards in this market do not move much across the year. The effective price does, and it moves for a reason worth understanding: supply of genuine subject specialists is finite, and demand is extremely seasonal. The result is that the same AED 250 an hour buys a different quality of tutor in October than it does eight weeks before the papers.

The seasonality is driven by school calendars rather than by providers. Internal assessment and Extended Essay draft deadlines cluster in the same weeks across several Abu Dhabi schools, because they all have to feed the same external submission points. Mock windows cluster similarly. Then the external paper season arrives and every family who had been thinking about it starts calling at once. A specialist with eight weekly slots fills them in that first fortnight.

Cambridge and Pearson dates show the same shape in the IGCSE market and are publishable because they are sourced. Cambridge's March 2027 series closed final entries on 27 November 2026 for an exam period from 3 February to 4 March 2027, with forecast grades due 27 February 2027 and results on Direct on 13 May. Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 final timetable ran to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For the IB, no session or results date is published on this page: the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so any date would be unverified, and your child's Diploma coordinator is the authority on it.

The practical consequence is simple and slightly unwelcome. If you already suspect you will want support in the spring, the cheapest and best-matched version of it is booked in the autumn. That is not an argument about outcomes, which nobody can promise. It is an argument about who is still available.
bullets: Rate cards are stable; effective prices are not, because supply is finite
Internal deadlines cluster across schools, so demand arrives in waves
Cambridge and Pearson dates are sourced and usable; IB dates are not verified here
Confirm every IB date with your school's Diploma coordinator

sections.heading: What the money cannot buy, at any rate
paragraphs: Three things are for sale in this market that should not be, and all three are expensive precisely because they are unverifiable. Knowing what they are protects a budget better than any negotiation.

The first is a promised outcome. No tutor can promise a score, a specific improvement or a university place, and a provider offering one is selling a claim rather than a service. Several competitors publish satisfaction percentages, self-asserted star ratings and student counts with no stated sample, date or method; one shows two different review figures on the same page. Treat an unevidenced number as a reason for caution rather than confidence, and apply the same standard to us.

The second is regulatory approval. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, the Sharjah Private Education Authority, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE as an institution, the IB or any examination board, and does not claim one. A tutoring business with premises and staff needs a permit from the relevant emirate authority, and an individual tutor needs the MoHRE private tuition permit. Neither of those makes a platform accredited, and the phrase describing tutors as regulator-approved is the single most misleading thing available in this market.

The third is completed assessed work. The IB requires internal assessments, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay to be the student's own, submitted through a school accountable for authenticity. A tutor may explain criteria, model technique on other material, ask questions about a draft and mark practice. No tutor text goes into a submission. Also, no provider should be supplying IB subject guides, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables as downloads: those belong to the IB, and redistributing them is copyright infringement regardless of how common it is.
bullets: No grade, score or admission can be promised, and no honest provider will
IB Gram holds no regulator or board accreditation and claims none
Assessed work must be the student's own; feedback is questions, not prose
Subject guides and mark schemes are referenced and linked, never redistributed

sections.heading: Who you are legally paying, and how to check
paragraphs: Before the price matters, the permit does. Private tutoring in the UAE is lawful and regulated: the MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 Regarding the Introduction of Private Tuition Work Permits. It is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students.

MoHRE's service page is listed as Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing. It shows no fee, states a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, and amounts circulating online could not be verified, so none appears here.

Abu Dhabi carries one additional rule that bears directly on who you should be paying. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. This has been reported in the press rather than read from the current policy document, so check the exact wording against ADEK's own publication. The principle is sound regardless: the person who marks your child's school assessments should not also be paid to prepare them for it.

What to do with this is a two-minute conversation. Ask any individual tutor, including ours, whether they hold the MoHRE permit and to show it. Ask a centre which authority licenses it and for the permit reference. Both answers are checkable, both questions are routine, and the willingness to answer tells you a great deal about where your money is going.
